careers-health-physio.title: Physiotherapy & allied health
careers-health-physio.description: Anatomy for movement, rehabilitation principles and common conditions, everyday ergonomics, and the career path to physiotherapy (BPT/MPT) and other allied health professions in India. General education, not medical advice.

courses.title: Anatomy for movement
courses.summary: The working knowledge of bones, joints, muscles, movement planes and the spine that physiotherapists, fitness trainers, coaches and dancers use every day — explained through real movements like climbing stairs, bowling and lifting a child.
outcomes: Learners can classify joints and name typical movements at each
Learners can explain agonist/antagonist pairs and concentric, eccentric and isometric contractions
Learners can describe movements using anatomical position, planes and axes
Learners can describe the regions and curves of the spine and the role of the trunk muscles

lessons.title: Bones and joints

scenes.text: Ravi, a first-year physiotherapy student in Mangaluru, holds a model knee. 'It just bends one way,' he says. 'Like a door hinge.'
His tutor, Dr. Fernandes, asks him to bend his knee to 90° while sitting and gently turn his foot in and out. 'Notice anything?'
Ravi sees his shin rotate a little. 'So it's mostly a hinge, but not perfectly.'
'Exactly,' says Dr. Fernandes. 'Classifications help you think. Real joints are a bit more interesting.'

steps.title: What bones do
steps.body:
The adult skeleton has about **206 bones**. They:
- provide a **framework** and levers for movement,
- **protect** organs (skull–brain, ribs–heart and lungs),
- store **minerals** such as calcium and phosphate,
- contain **marrow**, where blood cells are made.

Bone is living tissue: it remodels in response to load. This is why weight-bearing exercise helps bone density, and why long bed rest or space flight weakens bone.

steps.title: Three kinds of joints by structure
steps.body:
- **Fibrous joints:** bones joined by dense connective tissue; little or no movement (sutures of the skull).
- **Cartilaginous joints:** joined by cartilage; slight movement (intervertebral discs between vertebrae, pubic symphysis).
- **Synovial joints:** a joint cavity with **synovial fluid**, **articular (hyaline) cartilage** covering bone ends, a **joint capsule**, and usually ligaments. These are the freely movable joints that physiotherapists work with most.

steps.title: Types of synovial joint
steps.body:
- **Hinge:** movement mainly in one plane — elbow (humero-ulnar), knee (a modified hinge), finger joints between phalanges.
- **Pivot:** rotation around one axis — the joint between the first two neck vertebrae (atlas and axis) lets you shake your head 'no'; forearm rotation at the radio-ulnar joints.
- **Ball-and-socket:** movement in all planes — shoulder and hip.
- **Condyloid (ellipsoid):** two planes — wrist (radiocarpal), knuckles (metacarpophalangeal).
- **Saddle:** two planes with great range — base of the thumb (carpometacarpal), which allows opposition.
- **Plane (gliding):** small sliding movements — between the small bones of the wrist and foot.

steps.title: Ligaments, tendons and cartilage
steps.body:
- **Ligaments** connect **bone to bone** and stabilise joints (e.g., the anterior cruciate ligament, ACL, in the knee).
- **Tendons** connect **muscle to bone** (e.g., the Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel).
- **Hyaline cartilage** gives smooth joint surfaces; the knee also has two **menisci** of fibrocartilage that improve fit and spread load.

A common student mistake is mixing up ligaments and tendons. Memory trick: *L*igament *L*inks bone to bone.

steps.title: Worked example: bowling in cricket
steps.body: During a fast bowler's delivery: the **shoulder** (ball-and-socket) moves through a big arc; the **elbow** (hinge) must stay within the permitted straightening limit under cricket's laws; the **wrist** (condyloid) flicks; the **front knee** (modified hinge) braces on landing; the **spine** rotates through many small joints. Physiotherapists analyse exactly these joints to reduce injury risk, for example in the lower back of young fast bowlers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Move your thumb to touch each fingertip (opposition — saddle joint). Shake your head 'no' (pivot). Draw a circle with your straight arm (ball-and-socket). Bend your elbow (hinge). Name each joint type as you go.

activity.prompt: Match each joint to its type.

quiz.q: Ligaments connect...
quiz.why: Ligaments connect bone to bone and stabilise joints. Tendons are the ones that connect muscle to bone.

quiz.q: Which is a ball-and-socket joint?
quiz.why: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, with the femoral head sitting in the acetabulum. The knee and elbow are hinge-type joints, and the ankle is mainly a hinge joint.

quiz.q: Synovial joints are characterised by...
options: a joint cavity with synovial fluid
quiz.why: Synovial joints have a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid, which lubricates them and allows free movement. Fibrous joints and fused bones allow little or no movement.

quiz.q: The joint that allows thumb opposition is a...
quiz.why: The thumb's carpometacarpal joint is a saddle joint, which allows opposition of the thumb to the fingers. Hinge and pivot joints cannot do this.

quiz.q: Why does weight-bearing exercise help bones?
options: Bone remodels in response to load
quiz.why: Bone is living tissue that remodels in response to load, so weight-bearing exercise makes it stronger. It does not remove calcium or make bones lighter.

sources: Standard anatomy texts (e.g., Gray's Anatomy for Students)

lessons.title: Muscles: how they make and control movement

scenes.text: Asha, 62, from Nagpur, tells her physiotherapist Sameer: 'Climbing stairs is fine. Coming down hurts my knees and feels shaky.'
Sameer explains that going down, her thigh muscles work while lengthening, controlling her body against gravity — an eccentric contraction.
He gives her slow sit-to-stand exercises: standing up (concentric) and sitting down slowly over three seconds (eccentric).
After six weeks Asha says, 'The stairs at the temple don't scare me anymore.'

steps.title: Muscle basics
steps.body:
There are three muscle types: **skeletal** (voluntary, moves bones), **cardiac** (heart) and **smooth** (in organs and blood vessels). For movement we focus on skeletal muscle.

A muscle attaches via tendons, usually at an **origin** (the more fixed end) and an **insertion** (the end that moves more). When it contracts, it **pulls** — muscles cannot push. This is why muscles work in pairs.

steps.title: Roles: agonist, antagonist, synergist, stabiliser
steps.body:
- **Agonist (prime mover):** the main muscle producing a movement. Bending the elbow: **biceps brachii** (with brachialis).
- **Antagonist:** opposes the movement and must relax or control it. For elbow bending: **triceps brachii**.
- **Synergist:** helps the agonist or removes unwanted movement.
- **Stabiliser (fixator):** holds a nearby joint steady so the movement can happen efficiently — e.g., shoulder muscles stabilising while you curl a weight.

Roles swap depending on the movement: when straightening the elbow, triceps becomes the agonist.

steps.title: Three kinds of contraction
steps.body:
- **Concentric:** muscle shortens while producing force (thigh muscles when standing up from a chair).
- **Eccentric:** muscle lengthens while producing force, controlling movement (thigh muscles when sitting down slowly or going downstairs).
- **Isometric:** muscle produces force without changing length (holding a plank; pushing against a wall).

Eccentric work can produce high forces and is commonly associated with delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) after unfamiliar exercise. It is also used deliberately in rehabilitation, for example in some tendon programmes.

steps.title: Worked example: sit-to-stand
steps.body:
**Standing up:** quadriceps (front of thigh) and gluteus maximus (buttock) work **concentrically** to extend knee and hip. Calf muscles and trunk muscles stabilise.

**Sitting down slowly:** the same quadriceps and gluteal muscles work **eccentrically** — they are still the main muscles, now controlling the lowering. A common error is thinking the hamstrings 'pull you down'; gravity does that, and the quadriceps brakes it.

That is why weakness often shows up first as 'plopping' into a chair.

steps.title: Key muscle groups to know
steps.body:
- **Quadriceps** (4 muscles, front of thigh): extend the knee; rectus femoris also flexes the hip.
- **Hamstrings** (back of thigh): flex the knee and extend the hip.
- **Gluteus maximus:** hip extension; **gluteus medius:** stabilises the pelvis when standing on one leg.
- **Gastrocnemius and soleus** (calf): plantarflex the ankle (point the foot) via the Achilles tendon.
- **Rotator cuff** (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis — 'SITS'): stabilise and rotate the shoulder.
- **Deltoid:** lifts the arm.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Stand on one leg next to a wall for support. Watch in a mirror whether the opposite side of your pelvis drops. If it does, the gluteus medius of the standing leg may be weak or not working well. Physiotherapists use this kind of observation (related to the Trendelenburg sign) all the time.

activity.prompt: Which contraction type is the main working muscle doing?

items.text: Quadriceps while standing up from a chair
Quadriceps while walking downstairs
Trunk muscles while holding a plank
Biceps lifting a bag of rice towards you
Biceps slowly lowering the bag back down
Calf muscles while standing on tiptoe and holding still
Hamstrings slowing the leg at the end of a football kick

quiz.q: When you bend your elbow, the antagonist is...
quiz.why: When the biceps flexes the elbow it is the agonist, and the triceps opposes it as the antagonist. The deltoid and quadriceps work at other joints.

quiz.q: Sitting down slowly into a chair mainly uses the quadriceps...
quiz.why: When you sit down slowly, the quadriceps lengthen while controlling the descent against gravity, which is an eccentric contraction.

quiz.q: Which muscle stabilises the pelvis when standing on one leg?
quiz.why: Gluteus medius stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance. If it is weak, the opposite hip drops.

quiz.q: Muscles can only...
quiz.why: Muscles can only pull by contracting; they cannot push. That is why they work in opposing pairs.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a rotator cuff muscle?
quiz.why: The rotator cuff is the SITS group: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. The deltoid is a larger shoulder muscle outside the cuff.

lessons.title: The language of movement: planes and axes

scenes.text: Lucia, a contemporary dancer in Lisbon, visits physiotherapist Tiago with hip pain during side kicks.
Tiago writes: 'Pain at end of hip abduction in the frontal plane; external rotation pain-free.' Lucia laughs: 'You've turned my dance into a code!'
Tiago explains: the code lets any physio, surgeon or coach anywhere in the world understand exactly which movement hurts.
Together they plan exercises that strengthen her hip through that exact movement.

steps.title: Anatomical position
steps.body:
All movement descriptions start from the **anatomical position**: standing upright, facing forward, arms by the sides, **palms facing forward**, feet together.

Directional terms: **anterior** (front) / **posterior** (back); **superior** (above) / **inferior** (below); **medial** (towards midline) / **lateral** (away); **proximal** (nearer the trunk) / **distal** (further away). Example: the wrist is *distal* to the elbow.

steps.title: Three planes, three kinds of movement
steps.body:
- **Sagittal plane** divides the body into left and right. Movements: **flexion** and **extension** (nodding, squatting, kicking a ball forward, bending the elbow).
- **Frontal (coronal) plane** divides front and back. Movements: **abduction** (away from midline) and **adduction** (towards midline), side bending (lateral flexion) of the trunk. Example: a jumping jack.
- **Transverse (horizontal) plane** divides top and bottom. Movements: **rotation** (internal/medial and external/lateral), and forearm **pronation/supination**. Example: turning to look over your shoulder, a golf swing.

steps.title: Special movement words
steps.body:
- **Ankle:** dorsiflexion (toes up) and plantarflexion (point the foot).
- **Foot:** inversion (sole turns in — the common ankle-sprain direction) and eversion (sole turns out).
- **Forearm:** supination (palm up, 'holding soup') and pronation (palm down).
- **Shoulder blade (scapula):** elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, upward and downward rotation.
- **Thumb:** opposition.

steps.title: Worked example: describe a badminton smash
steps.body:
- Shoulder: **external rotation** then rapid **internal rotation** (transverse plane) with **flexion/abduction**.
- Elbow: rapid **extension** (sagittal).
- Forearm: **pronation** (transverse).
- Trunk: **rotation** (transverse).
- Front knee: **flexion** to absorb landing (sagittal).

Real sports movements combine several planes — physiotherapists break them down to find which component is painful or weak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that anatomical position has **palms forward** — this changes what 'lateral' means for forearm bones (the radius is lateral, on the thumb side).
- Mixing up abduction (**away**, think 'abduct = take away') and adduction (**add** to the body).
- Calling all bending 'flexion': side bending of the trunk is **lateral flexion** in the frontal plane.

activity.prompt: Which plane does each movement mainly occur in?

items.text: Nodding 'yes'
A jumping jack (arms out to the sides)
Shaking your head 'no'
Squatting
Turning a doorknob (forearm rotation)
Side bending the trunk to touch your knee
Kicking a football straight ahead
A side-step in salsa moving the leg away from midline

quiz.q: Flexion and extension happen in which plane?
quiz.why: Flexion and extension happen in the sagittal plane, which divides the body into left and right parts. The frontal plane has abduction and adduction.

quiz.q: Moving the arm out to the side away from the body is...
quiz.why: Abduction is movement away from the body's midline, such as raising the arm out to the side. Adduction brings it back.

quiz.q: Pointing your foot downward is...
quiz.why: Pointing the foot down, towards the sole, is plantarflexion. Dorsiflexion lifts the foot up.

quiz.q: The most common ankle sprain happens with the sole rolling...
quiz.why: Most ankle sprains occur with inversion, the sole rolling inwards, which stresses the lateral ligaments. Eversion sprains are less common.

quiz.q: In anatomical position, the palms face...
quiz.why: In the standard anatomical position, the person stands upright with palms facing forward. It's the reference for describing movements.

lessons.title: The spine, posture and the trunk

scenes.text: Mohan, 28, a software developer in Hyderabad, reads online that slouching 'destroys your spine' and starts sitting bolt upright all day. By evening his back aches more than before.
His physiotherapist, Dr. Kavya, explains: 'Your spine is strong and made to move. Holding any position for hours — even a perfect one — is what tires it.'
She suggests changing position often, short walks, and building general strength.
A month later Mohan says, 'I stopped fearing my spine. That alone helped.'

steps.title: Regions of the spine
steps.body:
The vertebral column usually has:
- **7 cervical** vertebrae (neck),
- **12 thoracic** (upper and mid back; ribs attach here),
- **5 lumbar** (lower back; the largest, carrying the most load),
- the **sacrum** (5 fused vertebrae) and the **coccyx** (tailbone).

Between most vertebrae are **intervertebral discs** — a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel-like centre (nucleus pulposus) — which absorb and share load. The spinal cord runs through the vertebral canal, and nerves exit between vertebrae.

steps.title: Natural curves
steps.body:
Seen from the side, a healthy spine has curves:
- **Cervical lordosis** (curving inwards),
- **Thoracic kyphosis** (curving outwards),
- **Lumbar lordosis** (inwards).

These curves help absorb shock and balance the head over the pelvis. People's curves vary widely and research has **not** found a single 'correct posture' that prevents back pain. Seen from behind, a sideways curve is called **scoliosis**, which should be assessed by a professional, especially in growing children.

steps.title: The trunk muscles
steps.body:
The trunk is supported by a team of muscles: **rectus abdominis** (the 'six-pack' — flexes the trunk), **obliques** (rotation and side bending), **transversus abdominis** (deep, wraps around like a corset), **erector spinae** and **multifidus** (along the back of the spine), the **diaphragm** above and the **pelvic floor** below.

For most people, general strength and fitness of the whole body is more useful than isolated 'core' exercises alone.

steps.title: Myth versus evidence
steps.body:
- **Myth:** 'Slouching damages your spine.' **Evidence:** sustained positions may cause discomfort, but no single posture has been shown to cause back pain. Variety and movement matter more.
- **Myth:** 'Never bend your back to lift.' **Evidence:** the spine is designed to bend; what matters is being prepared and strong for the loads you lift, and building up gradually.
- **Myth:** 'A disc bulge on a scan explains my pain.' **Evidence:** disc bulges are common in people *without* any back pain, and become more common with age.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. See a doctor urgently if back pain comes with: numbness around the genitals or buttocks (saddle area), new difficulty controlling bladder or bowels, progressive leg weakness, fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, or after significant trauma such as a fall or accident. In an emergency in India, call **112**.

steps.title: Try this: the next posture
steps.body: Set a reminder every 30–45 minutes while you study or work. When it goes off, change position: stand, stretch, walk to fill water, or simply shift how you sit. Physiotherapists often say: *your best posture is your next posture.*

statements.s: The lumbar spine usually has 5 vertebrae.
statements.why: Cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5.

statements.s: Research shows one perfect sitting posture prevents back pain.
statements.why: No single posture has been shown to prevent back pain; changing position helps comfort.

statements.s: Disc bulges on scans are common even in people without back pain.
statements.why: Imaging findings must be interpreted with symptoms.

statements.s: The thoracic spine normally curves outwards (kyphosis).
statements.why: Cervical and lumbar regions curve inwards (lordosis).

statements.s: New loss of bladder control with back pain can wait for a routine appointment.
statements.why: It may signal cauda equina syndrome — an emergency.

quiz.q: How many cervical vertebrae are there usually?
quiz.why: Humans usually have seven cervical vertebrae, including the atlas (C1) and axis (C2).

quiz.q: Which curve is normal in the lumbar spine?
quiz.why: The lumbar spine normally has a lordosis, an inward curve. Kyphosis is an outward curve, as in the thoracic spine, and scoliosis is a sideways curve.

quiz.q: Which symptom with back pain needs urgent medical attention?
options: Saddle numbness and new bladder problems
quiz.why: Saddle numbness and new bladder problems are red flags for cauda equina syndrome, which needs urgent care. The others are common non-urgent complaints.

quiz.q: 'Your best posture is your next posture' means...
quiz.why: 'Your best posture is your next posture' means changing position regularly. Staying in any single position for long causes discomfort.

quiz.q: Which deep muscle wraps around the abdomen like a corset?
quiz.why: Transversus abdominis is the deepest abdominal muscle and wraps around the trunk like a corset. The rectus abdominis is the surface 'six-pack' muscle.

sources: NICE guideline NG59 (low back pain and sciatica)

questions.q: Tendons connect...
questions.why: Tendons connect muscle to bone, while ligaments connect bone to bone.

questions.q: The hip is a ___ joint.
questions.why: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, which allows movement in all planes. A hinge allows bending in one plane only.

questions.q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there usually?
questions.why: There are usually 12 thoracic vertebrae, and the ribs attach to them. Cervical has 7 and lumbar has 5.

questions.q: Bringing the arm back towards the body from the side is...
questions.why: Adduction brings a limb back towards the body's midline. Abduction moves it away.

questions.q: Holding a wall-sit without moving is a(n) ___ contraction of the quadriceps.
questions.why: In a wall-sit, the quadriceps produce force without changing length, which is an isometric contraction. Concentric shortens and eccentric lengthens.

questions.q: Turning your palm up is...
questions.why: Turning the palm up is supination, easily remembered as 'holding soup'. Pronation turns the palm down.

questions.q: Which plane contains rotation movements?
questions.why: Rotation happens in the transverse (horizontal) plane. Sagittal has flexion and extension, and frontal has abduction and adduction.

questions.q: Lowering a dumbbell slowly from a curl, the biceps works...
questions.why: Lowering the dumbbell slowly makes the biceps lengthen under control, which is an eccentric contraction. Lifting it is concentric.

questions.q: In a one-leg stand the opposite hip drops. Which muscle is most likely weak on the standing side?
questions.why: If the opposite hip drops during a one-leg stand, the gluteus medius on the standing side is likely weak. This is the Trendelenburg sign.

questions.q: The knees' menisci are made of...
questions.why: The menisci are made of fibrocartilage, which deepens the joint surface and distributes load. Hyaline cartilage covers the bone ends.

questions.q: A scan shows a disc bulge in a person with no symptoms. The best interpretation is...
options: such findings are common and must be interpreted with symptoms
questions.why: Disc bulges are common in people without pain, so scan findings must be interpreted with symptoms. Stopping exercise or surgery isn't needed just because of a scan.

questions.q: Which back-pain feature is a red flag?
options: Stiffness in the morning for 10 minutes
Unexplained weight loss and history of cancer
questions.why: Unexplained weight loss with a history of cancer is a red flag that may signal serious disease. Pain after driving, short morning stiffness and pain that eases with movement are usually benign.

questions.q: During a sit-to-stand, which statement is correct?
options: Quadriceps work concentrically to stand and eccentrically to sit
Hamstrings pull you down when sitting
questions.why: In sit-to-stand, the quadriceps shorten (concentric) to stand and lengthen under control (eccentric) to sit. Muscles pull, they don't push.

questions.q: A fast bowler's shoulder moves through flexion and internal rotation. Which planes are involved?
questions.why: Flexion is in the sagittal plane, and rotation is in the transverse plane, so a bowling shoulder uses both. Real movements combine planes.

lessons.title: The rehabilitation cycle and pain science

scenes.text: Fatima, 48, a tailor in Lucknow, has had shoulder pain for two months. She can't reach the top shelf of her shop.
Physiotherapist Arvind asks about her work, sleep and worries, tests her movement and strength, and asks: 'What would you most like to be able to do again?' 'Lift fabric rolls onto the top shelf.'
They set a goal: lift a 3 kg roll onto the top shelf without pain above 3/10, within six weeks.
Each week Arvind increases the exercise load a little. By week six Fatima reaches the shelf — and understands why gradual load worked.

steps.title: The rehab cycle
steps.body:
Physiotherapy usually follows a cycle:
- **1. Subjective assessment:** history — what happened, symptoms, what makes it better or worse, general health, red flags, work, goals, beliefs and worries.
- **2. Objective assessment:** observation, range of motion, strength, special tests, function (e.g., sit-to-stand, walking).
- **3. Clinical reasoning:** a working hypothesis of the problem and contributing factors.
- **4. Goals:** agreed with the patient.
- **5. Intervention:** education, exercise, manual therapy where helpful, activity advice.
- **6. Re-assessment:** are we making progress? Adjust.
- **7. Discharge and self-management plan.**

The **biopsychosocial model** reminds us that biology, thoughts, emotions, work and social life all affect recovery.

steps.title: Worked example: SMART goals
steps.body:
Weak goal: *'Improve shoulder.'*

SMART goal: *'Fatima will lift a 3 kg fabric roll onto the top shelf (at shoulder height plus 20 cm) with pain no more than 3/10, within 6 weeks.'*
- **S**pecific — a real task
- **M**easurable — weight, height, pain score
- **A**chievable — realistic for her condition
- **R**elevant — matters for her work
- **T**ime-bound — 6 weeks

steps.title: Progressive loading
steps.body:
Tissues — muscle, tendon, bone — adapt to the loads we place on them. Too little load and they weaken; too much too soon and they become irritated.

Progression can change: **resistance** (weight), **repetitions and sets**, **speed**, **range**, **complexity** (from stable to unstable), and **function** (from exercise to real tasks). A common guide is to allow mild, short-lived discomfort that settles within about 24 hours, while avoiding sharp or steadily worsening pain — your physiotherapist sets the exact rules for your case.

steps.title: Modern pain science
steps.body:
**Pain is produced by the brain as a protective output**, based on signals from the body plus context — memories, beliefs, mood, environment. It is real, but it does not always equal the amount of tissue damage.

This explains why: chronic pain can persist after tissues have healed; fear and stress can increase pain; understanding pain (pain neuroscience education) can reduce fear and improve activity. Saying 'hurt does not always mean harm' must be done carefully — it does not mean the pain is imaginary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the scan instead of the person.
- Passive treatments only (machines, massage) without active exercise or education.
- Total rest for weeks — usually slows recovery for common musculoskeletal problems.
- Copying a programme from a video without assessment.
- Ignoring red flags such as unexplained weight loss, fever, night pain that doesn't change with position, or neurological symptoms — these need medical review.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of a small physical goal of your own (e.g., 'walk to the market and back without knee pain'). Rewrite it as a SMART goal. Then list three ways you could progress it gradually.

activity.prompt: Put the rehabilitation cycle in order.
items: Agree SMART goals with the patient

quiz.q: Which goal is SMART?
options: Walk 1 km without a stick within 8 weeks
quiz.why: 'Walk 1 km without a stick within 8 weeks' is specific, measurable and time-bound. 'Get better' or 'exercise more' are vague.

quiz.q: The biopsychosocial model considers...
options: biology, thoughts, emotions and social factors
quiz.why: The biopsychosocial model looks at biology, thoughts, emotions and social factors together. Recovery depends on the whole person, not just the tissue.

quiz.q: Which statement about pain is accurate?
options: Pain is a protective output of the brain influenced by context
quiz.why: Pain is a protective output of the brain, shaped by context, and is real. It doesn't always match tissue damage, and education can change it.

quiz.q: Progressive loading means...
options: gradually increasing demands so tissues adapt
quiz.why: Progressive loading gradually increases the demands so tissues can adapt and get stronger. Maximum weight from day one risks injury.

quiz.q: For common musculoskeletal problems, weeks of total rest usually...
quiz.why: For most musculoskeletal problems, long total rest slows recovery. Staying appropriately active is usually recommended.

lessons.title: Low back pain: what really helps

scenes.text: Rajesh, 41, drives an auto-rickshaw in Chennai. After lifting a heavy suitcase for a passenger, his lower back 'catches'. He fears he has 'slipped a disc' and stays in bed for four days.
At the government hospital physiotherapy department, Dr. Meena screens for red flags — none. She explains most back pain is not dangerous and that gentle activity speeds recovery.
She teaches him simple movements, advises short walks and gradually returning to driving with breaks.
Two weeks later Rajesh is back at work. 'I thought my back was broken,' he says. 'It just needed movement and confidence.'

steps.title: The big picture
steps.body: Low back pain is the **leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide** (Global Burden of Disease studies). Most cases — around **90%** — are classed as **non-specific low back pain**: no single damaged structure can be reliably identified. Most acute episodes improve considerably within weeks, although recurrences are common.

steps.title: Red flags first
steps.body:
Screen for signs of serious causes, which are uncommon but important:
- **Cauda equina syndrome:** saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel problems, sexual dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms — emergency.
- **Infection:** fever, recent infection, IV drug use, immune suppression.
- **Cancer:** history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50 with new pain, constant night pain.
- **Fracture:** significant trauma, osteoporosis, long-term steroid use.
- **Progressive neurological deficit:** worsening leg weakness or foot drop.

If present, refer to a doctor promptly. India emergency: **112**.

steps.title: What evidence-based guidelines recommend
steps.body:
International guidelines (e.g., NICE NG59 and the Lancet 2018 series) broadly agree on first-line care for non-specific low back pain:
- **Reassurance and education:** the spine is strong; pain does not mean serious damage.
- **Stay active** and continue normal activities as far as possible, including work with adjustments.
- **Exercise therapy** — many types help (strength, walking, yoga, pilates-style); the best one is the one the person will do.
- **Psychological approaches** (e.g., cognitive-behavioural) for persistent pain with distress.
- Manual therapy only as part of a package including exercise.

**Not recommended routinely:** imaging (X-ray or MRI) without red flags, long bed rest, and for many patients, passive electrotherapy as a main treatment. Medicines should be discussed with a doctor.

steps.title: Worked example: words matter
steps.body:
Unhelpful words: *'Your disc has slipped,' 'Your spine is degenerating,' 'Never lift again.'* These can increase fear and avoidance.

Helpful words: *'Your back is strong. Pain is a sign it's sensitive right now, not that it's broken. Gentle movement will help it settle. We'll build up what you can do.'*

Research on fear-avoidance shows that frightening beliefs can predict worse outcomes.

steps.title: Practical self-management
steps.body:
- Keep moving: short walks several times a day.
- Change positions often; take breaks during long drives.
- Use heat if it feels comfortable.
- Return to work gradually rather than waiting for zero pain.
- Build general strength and fitness once the acute phase settles.
- See a physiotherapist or doctor if pain is not improving after a few weeks, is severe, or any red flags appear.

a.text: You are a physio student shadowing. A 35-year-old office worker has had back pain for 5 days after gardening. No red flags. She asks for an MRI. What do you suggest your supervisor discuss?

choices.label: Explain that scans are not usually helpful without red flags, and focus on education and staying active.
choices.feedback: Consistent with guidelines; scans often show harmless changes that increase worry.

choices.label: Order an MRI to be safe.
choices.feedback: Without red flags, imaging rarely changes management and can cause fear.

b.text: She worries: 'If I move, will I damage it?' What's the best reply?

choices.label: 'Your back is strong. Gentle movement helps it settle; we'll build up gradually.'
choices.feedback: Reassurance plus a plan reduces fear-avoidance.

choices.label: 'Yes, rest in bed for two weeks.'
choices.feedback: Bed rest tends to slow recovery.

c.text: The MRI shows 'mild disc bulges at L4–5'. She is now terrified. How do you help?

choices.label: Explain such findings are common in people without pain and focus on activity.
choices.feedback: Good recovery — interpreting findings in context reduces fear.

choices.label: Tell her she needs surgery.
choices.feedback: Surgery is not indicated for this presentation.

d.text: Two weeks later she has rested and feels stiffer and more fearful. What now?

choices.label: Re-educate, start a graded activity and exercise plan.
choices.feedback: It's never too late to change course.

end1.text: Guideline-based care: screen red flags, reassure, keep active, exercise, and review if not improving.

quiz.q: Roughly what proportion of low back pain is non-specific?
quiz.why: About 90% of low back pain is non-specific, with no single identifiable structural cause.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag for cauda equina syndrome?
options: Saddle numbness and new bladder problems
quiz.why: Saddle numbness with new bladder problems is a red flag for cauda equina syndrome, a medical emergency. Morning stiffness and tight hamstrings are not.

quiz.q: Routine MRI for non-specific back pain without red flags is...
quiz.why: Routine MRI for non-specific back pain without red flags is not recommended because it rarely changes treatment and may increase fear.

quiz.q: Which is first-line care?
quiz.why: First-line care for back pain is education, staying active and exercise, as guidelines recommend. Surgery, long bed rest and avoiding work are not.

quiz.q: Which phrase is most helpful for a patient?
options: You have the back of an 80-year-old.
Your back is strong; it's sensitive right now and movement will help.
quiz.why: 'Your back is strong; it's sensitive right now and movement will help' reduces fear and encourages activity. The other phrases are frightening and can cause fear-avoidance.

scenes.text: Kiran, 19, twists his ankle in a college football match in Goa. A friend says, 'Ice it and don't walk for two weeks.'
In the same clinic, Saroja, 66, has knee osteoarthritis. 'My knees are worn out,' she says. 'I should save them by not walking.'
Physiotherapist Anil gives both of them the same core message in different words: protected movement and gradual loading help tissues recover and joints feel better.
Kiran is jogging in four weeks. Saroja, after eight weeks of strengthening, walks to her daughter's house again.

steps.title: Ankle sprains
steps.body:
Most ankle sprains are **inversion** injuries that stretch or tear the **lateral ligaments** (often the anterior talofibular ligament). Grades range from mild stretch to complete tear.

The **Ottawa ankle rules** help clinicians decide whether an X-ray is needed — for example, bone tenderness at specific points or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the clinic. If you cannot bear weight or there is bone tenderness, get assessed.

steps.title: PEACE & LOVE (2019)
steps.body:
An updated acronym for soft-tissue injuries (Dubois & Esculier, 2019), which goes beyond the older RICE:

**Immediately — PEACE:**
- **P**rotect: limit movement that increases pain for 1–3 days.
- **E**levate the limb above the heart when possible.
- **A**void anti-inflammatories early on (the authors suggest they may interfere with healing) — discuss medicines with a doctor; ice use is also questioned.
- **C**ompress with a bandage or taping to limit swelling.
- **E**ducate: avoid unnecessary passive treatments; let the body recover actively.

**After the first days — LOVE:**
- **L**oad: let pain guide a gradual return to normal activity.
- **O**ptimism: confident expectations are linked to better outcomes.
- **V**ascularisation: pain-free cardio exercise to boost blood flow.
- **E**xercise: restore mobility, strength and **balance (proprioception)** — this reduces the risk of re-spraining.

steps.title: Knee osteoarthritis (OA)
steps.body:
OA is a whole-joint condition involving cartilage, bone, the joint lining and surrounding muscles. It is common with age and also linked to previous injury, body weight and genetics.

**Core treatments in international guidelines:**
- **Education** about the condition and self-management.
- **Exercise** — especially strengthening the quadriceps and hip muscles, plus aerobic activity such as walking or cycling. Exercise is recommended regardless of age or X-ray severity.
- **Weight management** where appropriate.

Other options (medicines, injections, braces, surgery such as knee replacement) are decided with doctors when core treatment is not enough.

steps.title: 'Wear and tear' — a misleading phrase
steps.body: Calling OA 'wear and tear' makes people think every step uses up their knee. In fact, appropriate loading helps cartilage health and strong muscles reduce pain. X-ray severity often does not match how much pain a person feels. Structured programmes (for example the Danish GLA:D education-and-exercise programme) have reported reduced pain for many participants.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: General education only. Seek medical review for: inability to bear weight, obvious deformity, rapid severe swelling, a hot red joint with fever (possible infection — urgent), locking of the knee, or pain that is not improving after a few weeks.

activity.prompt: Match each letter of PEACE & LOVE to its meaning.
pairs: Protect: limit painful movement for 1–3 days
Load: gradual return guided by pain

quiz.q: Most ankle sprains involve which movement?
quiz.why: Most ankle sprains happen with inversion, where the sole rolls inwards and stresses the lateral ligaments.

quiz.q: What does the 'L' in LOVE stand for?
quiz.why: In LOVE, L stands for Load: gradual, pain-guided loading helps healing. The rest is Optimism, Vascularisation and Exercise.

quiz.q: A core treatment for knee OA in guidelines is...
quiz.why: Guidelines recommend exercise and education as core treatment for knee osteoarthritis, at all ages and severities. Rest and avoiding walking weaken the joint.

quiz.q: Why is 'wear and tear' a misleading description of OA?
options: Appropriate loading helps; X-ray severity often doesn't match pain
It means the joint is infected
quiz.why: 'Wear and tear' is misleading because appropriate loading helps joints, and X-ray severity often doesn't match pain. The phrase can cause fear and avoidance.

quiz.q: Balance exercises after an ankle sprain help to...
quiz.why: Balance exercises after an ankle sprain retrain proprioception, which reduces the risk of re-injury. They don't weaken ligaments or cause swelling.

lessons.title: Stroke rehabilitation basics

story.title: Mr. Thomas learns to walk again

scenes.text: In Kottayam, Annamma notices her husband Thomas, 67, suddenly cannot lift his right arm and his speech is slurred. She remembers FAST and calls 112 immediately.
At the hospital he receives emergency treatment. Two days later physiotherapist Divya begins helping him sit, balance and stand.
Every day they practise real tasks — standing from a chair, stepping, reaching for a cup — many, many times.
Three months later Thomas walks to church with a stick. 'The repetition was boring,' he admits, 'but it rebuilt me.'

steps.title: Recognise a stroke: BE FAST
steps.body:
A stroke is a medical emergency. Common warning signs:
- **F**ace drooping on one side,
- **A**rm (or leg) weakness on one side,
- **S**peech difficulty — slurred or confused,
- **T**ime to call emergency services — in India, **112**.

Some campaigns add **B** (sudden balance loss) and **E** (sudden eye/vision problems): BE FAST. Some treatments that dissolve or remove clots work only within hours, so speed matters.

steps.title: What stroke does
steps.body: A stroke happens when blood supply to part of the brain is blocked (**ischaemic** — most common) or a blood vessel bleeds (**haemorrhagic**). Effects depend on the area affected: weakness on one side (**hemiparesis**), sensory loss, changes in muscle tone (spasticity), balance problems, speech and swallowing problems, visual field loss, neglect of one side, fatigue, mood changes and memory or thinking difficulties. Rehabilitation is done by a team: doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech-language therapists, psychologists and social workers.

steps.title: Neuroplasticity and practice
steps.body:
The brain can reorganise after injury — **neuroplasticity**. Rehabilitation aims to drive this with:
- **Task-specific practice:** practise the actual activity (walking, reaching, standing up), not only isolated exercises.
- **High repetition and intensity:** more practice is generally associated with better outcomes.
- **Meaningful goals:** tasks that matter to the person improve motivation.
- **Early mobilisation** when medically safe, guided by the medical team.
- **Feedback:** knowledge of results and performance.

Much recovery happens in the first months, but improvement can continue for much longer with practice.

steps.title: Worked example: practising sit-to-stand
steps.body:
For Thomas (right-sided weakness):
- Feet back, slightly apart, weight shared on both feet (people often avoid the weak side).
- Lean forward, 'nose over toes'.
- Push up through both legs; therapist guards the weak knee if needed.
- Stand tall, then sit down slowly with control.
- Repeat in sets, increasing repetitions and reducing help over time.

Common mistake: always helping too much. The patient needs to do as much of the effort as safely possible.

steps.title: Family's role
steps.body: Families can help by encouraging practice of daily tasks (rather than doing everything for the person), keeping the home safe from falls, learning safe transfer techniques from the therapist, watching for low mood (common after stroke), and supporting medication and blood-pressure control to prevent another stroke. Caregivers also need rest and support.

statements.s: Sudden face droop, arm weakness or speech trouble means call 112 immediately.
statements.why: Time-critical treatments exist.

statements.s: Ischaemic stroke (a blocked vessel) is more common than haemorrhagic stroke.
statements.why: Most strokes are ischaemic.

statements.s: Task-specific, repetitive practice is a key principle of stroke rehab.
statements.why: It drives neuroplasticity.

statements.s: Families should do every task for the stroke survivor to save their energy.
statements.why: Encouraging safe practice of daily tasks supports recovery.

statements.s: No improvement is possible after the first month.
statements.why: Most recovery is early, but improvement can continue much longer.

quiz.q: In FAST, 'T' stands for...
quiz.why: In FAST for stroke, T means Time to call emergency services, as speed is essential. In India the number is 112.

quiz.q: Weakness on one side of the body is called...
quiz.why: Hemiparesis is weakness on one side of the body ('hemi' means half). Paraplegia affects the legs, and ataxia is poor coordination.

quiz.q: Which is a core principle of stroke rehabilitation?
quiz.why: Stroke rehabilitation relies on task-specific, high-repetition practice, because practice drives neuroplasticity. Passive treatment or avoiding the weak side doesn't.

quiz.q: Who assists with speech and swallowing problems after stroke?
quiz.why: A speech-language therapist helps with speech and swallowing problems after stroke, as part of the multidisciplinary team.

quiz.q: A common mistake when helping a stroke survivor practise standing is...
quiz.why: Giving too much help is a common mistake, since the person needs to do as much as safely possible to relearn. Feedback, goals and encouragement are good.

sources: National stroke guidelines (e.g., NICE NG236, AHA/ASA)

questions.q: SMART goals are...
questions.why: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. It's the standard goal-setting framework in rehab.

questions.q: India's emergency number for a suspected stroke is...
questions.why: 112 is India's single emergency number, so call it for a suspected stroke. 1098 is child help, 14416 is Tele-MANAS, and 181 is a women's helpline.

questions.q: For most acute low back pain, the best advice is...
options: stay active and keep moving within comfort
questions.why: For most acute low back pain, staying active and moving within comfort is best. Bed rest for weeks and avoiding work slow recovery.

questions.q: Which is a core treatment for knee osteoarthritis?
questions.why: Strengthening and aerobic exercise are core treatments for knee osteoarthritis. Total rest and avoiding stairs forever weaken the joint.

questions.q: In PEACE & LOVE, 'O' means...
questions.why: In PEACE & LOVE, the O in LOVE stands for Optimism, since positive expectations are linked to better outcomes.

questions.q: The biopsychosocial model includes...
questions.why: The biopsychosocial model includes biological, psychological and social factors. It is a whole-person approach rather than only tissues or X-rays.

questions.q: Which back pain patient needs urgent medical referral?
options: New bladder retention with saddle numbness
questions.why: New bladder retention with saddle numbness suggests cauda equina syndrome and needs urgent referral. The others are common, non-urgent complaints.

questions.q: The Ottawa ankle rules help decide...
questions.why: The Ottawa ankle rules help decide whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle injury. They reduce unnecessary imaging.

questions.q: Why might frightening words like 'your spine is crumbling' harm recovery?
options: They make patients exercise too much
They increase fear-avoidance, linked to worse outcomes
questions.why: Frightening words increase fear-avoidance, which is linked to worse outcomes. Beliefs shape behaviour and pain.

questions.q: Neuroplasticity after stroke is best promoted by...
options: task-specific, repeated practice of meaningful activities
questions.why: Neuroplasticity after stroke is promoted by task-specific, repeated practice of meaningful activities. Passive treatment or avoiding the weak limb doesn't drive reorganisation.

questions.q: A patient's knee X-ray looks severe but she walks 3 km daily with mild pain. This shows...
options: imaging severity often doesn't match symptoms
questions.why: Imaging severity often doesn't match symptoms, so treat the person, not the image. She walks 3 km with mild pain, so she needn't stop or rush to surgery.

questions.q: Which change is a valid way to progress an exercise?
options: Add resistance, repetitions, speed or complexity gradually
questions.why: Exercises are progressed by gradually adding resistance, repetitions, speed or complexity. Doubling everything daily risks injury, and reducing load only won't build strength.

questions.q: Why does PEACE suggest avoiding anti-inflammatories early after a soft-tissue injury?
options: The authors suggest inflammation is part of healing and these drugs may interfere — discuss with a doctor
questions.why: PEACE suggests avoiding anti-inflammatories early because inflammation is part of healing and these drugs may interfere. Medicine decisions belong with a doctor.

questions.q: A patient with persistent back pain, high fear of movement and low mood would most likely benefit from...
options: education, graded activity/exercise and psychologically informed care
questions.why: Persistent pain with fear of movement and low mood calls for education, graded activity or exercise and psychologically informed care. Braces, more scans and bed rest don't address those factors.

courses.title: Everyday ergonomics: desks, phones and lifting
courses.summary: Set up your work or study space, reduce screen-related discomfort, lift and carry sensibly, and prevent falls at home for older family members. Practical, evidence-informed, and honest about myths. General education, not medical advice.
outcomes: Learners can set up a desk, chair and screen to fit their body
Learners can build movement breaks and eye breaks into the day
Learners can plan a lift and carry loads more safely
Learners can check a home for fall hazards and suggest balance exercises for older adults

lessons.title: Setting up a desk that fits you

scenes.text: Neha, 30, a chartered accountant in Ahmedabad, has worked from her dining table on a laptop for a year. Her neck and wrists ache every evening.
Her physiotherapist friend Jaydeep visits and builds a setup in 20 minutes: a stack of old books under the laptop, a cheap external keyboard and mouse, and a cushion behind her back.
He also sets a reminder on her phone to stand up every 40 minutes.
Two weeks later Neha says the evening aches are much less. 'It cost less than a pizza.'

steps.title: The chair
steps.body:
- Feet flat on the floor or on a footrest.
- Knees roughly level with or slightly below the hips.
- Back supported — use the chair's lumbar support or a small cushion/rolled towel.
- A small gap between the seat edge and the back of the knees.
- Armrests (if any) low enough that shoulders stay relaxed.

steps.title: Screen, keyboard and mouse
steps.body:
- **Screen** about an arm's length away, with the **top of the screen at or slightly below eye level**, directly in front of you.
- **Keyboard and mouse** close, so elbows are by your sides at roughly 90°, wrists fairly straight.
- **Laptops:** a laptop forces a choice — screen too low or keyboard too high. For long work, raise the laptop on a stand or books and use a separate keyboard and mouse.
- Reduce glare: screen side-on to windows, not facing or backing onto them.

steps.title: Honest evidence
steps.body: Good setup improves comfort, and many people find it helps. But research has not shown that a perfect workstation alone prevents all neck or back pain. Other factors matter too: total sitting time, movement, stress, sleep and general fitness. So the best approach combines a reasonable setup **plus** regular movement.

steps.title: Eyes: the 20-20-20 habit
steps.body: Every **20 minutes**, look at something about **20 feet (6 metres)** away for **20 seconds**. This relaxes the focusing muscles of the eyes and reminds you to blink — people blink less when staring at screens, which can dry the eyes. See an eye specialist if you have persistent headaches, blurred vision or eye strain.

steps.title: Try this now
steps.body: Sit at your usual workspace. Check: feet supported? Back supported? Screen top at eye level and an arm's length away? Elbows near 90° and shoulders relaxed? Fix one thing today using what you already have — books, a cushion, a box.

options: At or slightly below eye level
quiz.why: The top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level. This keeps the neck in a comfortable, neutral position.

quiz.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
options: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
quiz.why: The 20-20-20 rule says every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. This relaxes eye focusing and encourages blinking.

quiz.q: For long laptop work, the best fix is...
options: raise the laptop and use a separate keyboard and mouse
quiz.why: Raise the laptop and use a separate keyboard and mouse. This separates screen height from keyboard height, so neither the neck nor the arms are strained.

quiz.q: According to research, which matters along with setup?
options: Regular movement, stress, sleep and fitness
quiz.why: Setup alone does not prevent all pain. Regular movement, stress, sleep and fitness also matter.

lessons.title: Phones, study marathons and moving more

scenes.text: Aarav, 17, in Kota, studies for 10 hours a day for NEET, mostly sitting on his bed, looking down at books and his phone.
He gets neck stiffness and headaches. He wonders if he's ruining his spine forever.
His coaching centre's wellness session explains: it's mostly sustained position and too little movement. They suggest study blocks with movement breaks and a proper desk.
Aarav starts 50-minute study blocks with 5-minute breaks, a daily 30-minute badminton game and better sleep. His headaches ease — and his concentration improves.

steps.title: Phone neck: what's real
steps.body:
Looking down bends the neck forward and increases the load the neck muscles hold. You may have seen dramatic claims that phones are causing horns on skulls or permanent damage — those claims are not well supported.

What is reasonable: long periods in any single position can cause stiffness and discomfort. Practical fixes: raise the phone closer to eye level, use a stand for videos, and — most of all — take breaks and move.

steps.title: Break up sitting
steps.body:
Long uninterrupted sitting is linked with poorer health outcomes. WHO's 2020 physical activity guidelines advise adults to **limit sedentary time** and replace it with activity of any intensity, and recommend **at least 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week** for adults (and an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous activity for children and adolescents aged 5–17), plus muscle-strengthening activities.

Easy strategy: a 2–5 minute movement break every 30–60 minutes.

steps.title: Worked example: a 3-minute desk break
steps.body:
- Stand up and walk to get water (30 s).
- Shoulder rolls backwards × 10.
- Gentle neck turns left and right × 5 each, slowly.
- Chin tucks (make a gentle double chin) × 10.
- Reach both arms overhead and stretch × 3.
- 10 sit-to-stands from your chair.

All movements should feel comfortable; stop anything that causes sharp pain or dizziness.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: See a doctor if neck pain comes with: arm weakness or numbness, severe headache unlike usual, dizziness or visual disturbance, fever, after an injury, or if pain doesn't improve after a few weeks. General education, not medical advice.

activity.label: How many minutes do you usually sit without a break?

bands.text: Great — frequent breaks. Keep it up and add some vigorous activity in the week.
Reasonable. Try a 2–5 minute movement break at the end of each block.
Long stretches. Set a timer for 45–50 minutes and stand up when it rings.
Very long. Break it into blocks; your body and your focus will both benefit.

quiz.q: WHO's 2020 guidelines recommend how much moderate aerobic activity per week for adults?
quiz.why: WHO 2020 recommends at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week for adults, plus muscle strengthening and less sitting.

quiz.q: Which is a well-supported fix for phone-related neck discomfort?
options: Breaks and movement, phone nearer eye level
quiz.why: Breaks and movement, and holding the phone nearer eye level, help phone-related neck discomfort. The main issue is staying in one position for long.

quiz.q: Neck pain with arm numbness and weakness should...
options: be solved with a new phone
quiz.why: Neck pain with arm numbness and weakness is a neurological sign and should be checked by a doctor. Stretching alone or ignoring it isn't enough.

quiz.q: Children and teens (5–17) are advised to average how much moderate-to-vigorous activity daily?
quiz.why: WHO 2020 advises children and teens aged 5 to 17 to average 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day.

sources: WHO Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020)

lessons.title: Lifting, carrying and preventing falls at home

scenes.text: Babu, 35, a delivery worker in Kolkata, carries heavy loads up stairs all day. His mother, 74, lives with him and nearly slipped in the bathroom last week.
At a free workplace health camp, a physiotherapist shows Babu how to plan lifts, keep loads close and split heavy loads into two trips.
She also gives him a home safety list: a non-slip mat, a grab bar, a night light, removing loose rugs.
His mother starts simple daily balance exercises holding the kitchen counter. Months later she says, 'I feel steadier on my feet.'

steps.title: Planning a lift
steps.body:
- **Think first:** how heavy? Can it be split, pushed or carried by two people? Where is it going? Is the path clear?
- **Get close:** keep the load close to your body — the further away, the more strain.
- **Stable base:** feet apart, one slightly forward.
- **Avoid twisting while lifting:** turn by moving your feet.
- **Smooth, controlled movement** rather than jerking.
- **Use aids:** trolleys, straps, ramps.

**Honest evidence:** studies have not shown that teaching 'correct lifting technique' alone prevents back pain. The spine can bend safely. What helps most is avoiding sudden unfamiliar loads, building strength for your work, good planning and aids.

steps.title: Falls in older adults
steps.body:
Falls are a leading cause of injury in older people worldwide (WHO). Risk factors include muscle weakness, poor balance, some medicines (e.g., sedatives), poor vision, foot problems, low blood pressure on standing, and home hazards.

Exercise programmes that include **balance and strength** training — such as the **Otago Exercise Programme** — have been shown in research reviews to reduce falls in older people living at home.

steps.title: Home hazard check
steps.body:
- Non-slip mats in bathroom and near water storage.
- Grab bars by the toilet and bathing area.
- Good lighting, including night lights to the toilet.
- Remove loose rugs, wires and clutter from walkways.
- Handrails on both sides of stairs if possible.
- Commonly used items within easy reach (no climbing on stools).
- Well-fitting footwear with grip (not loose slippers).
- Regular eye check-ups and medicine reviews with a doctor.

steps.title: Worked example: safe balance practice
steps.body:
Holding a kitchen counter, with someone nearby at first:
- Stand with feet together for 10 seconds.
- Stand heel-to-toe (one foot in front of the other) for 10 seconds.
- Rise up on toes slowly × 10.
- Stand on one leg for 5–10 seconds each side.
- 10 sit-to-stands from a firm chair.

Progress slowly. A physiotherapist can tailor the programme. Stop if dizzy, and see a doctor about any falls or near-falls.

quiz.why: Keeping a load close to your body reduces strain, because a longer distance increases the lever arm on the back.

quiz.q: What does research say about teaching 'correct lifting technique' alone?
options: It has not been shown to prevent back pain on its own
quiz.why: Teaching lifting technique alone has not been shown to prevent back pain. Planning, strength and aids also matter.

quiz.q: Which exercise type helps reduce falls in older adults?
quiz.why: Balance and strength training reduce falls in older adults, for example the Otago Exercise Programme. Bed rest and stretching alone don't.

quiz.q: Which is a home fall hazard?
quiz.why: Loose wires across walkways are a trip hazard. Grab bars, handrails and night lights help prevent falls.

questions.q: The top of a computer screen should be...
options: at or slightly below eye level
questions.why: The top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level, which reduces neck strain.

questions.q: The 20-20-20 rule is about...
questions.why: The 20-20-20 rule is about eye breaks: every 20 minutes look 20 feet away for 20 seconds. It isn't about sleep, lifting or diet.

questions.q: When lifting, you should turn by...
questions.why: When lifting, turn by moving your feet rather than twisting your back under load. Twisting under load strains the spine.

questions.q: Which is a fall-prevention measure?
questions.why: Grab bars and night lights reduce fall risk. Dim lighting, loose rugs and slippery floors raise it.

questions.q: For long laptop work, the recommended setup is...
options: laptop raised plus separate keyboard and mouse
questions.why: For long laptop use, raise the laptop and add a separate keyboard and mouse. This separates screen and keyboard heights.

questions.q: WHO's adult guideline for moderate aerobic activity per week is...
questions.why: WHO's 2020 guideline for adults is at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week.

questions.q: Which statement about posture is most accurate?
options: Sitting upright all day is best
One perfect posture prevents all pain
questions.why: Changing position regularly helps comfort, as variety matters more than one perfect posture. Slouching doesn't cause permanent damage.

questions.q: Which medicine-related factor can increase fall risk in older adults?
questions.why: Sedatives can cause drowsiness and unsteadiness, raising fall risk in older adults. Review any medicine with a doctor.

questions.q: A delivery worker must carry a 30 kg load up stairs. The best plan is...
options: carry it fast in one go
split the load or use help/aids where possible
questions.why: For a heavy 30 kg load, split it or use help and aids where possible. Carrying it fast, at arm's length or twisting increases strain.

questions.q: Which neck-pain symptom needs medical review?
options: Stiffness after a long study session
Mild ache that eases with movement
questions.why: Arm weakness and numbness with neck pain are neurological symptoms needing medical review. Stiffness, tight shoulders and mild aches that ease are usually not worrying.

questions.q: Why does research not support lifting-technique training alone for preventing back pain?
options: Back pain has many contributors; planning, load management and strength also matter
questions.why: Back pain has many contributors, so planning, load management and strength also matter, not technique alone. That's why technique training alone isn't supported.

questions.q: An older adult wants to start balance exercises at home. The safest first step is...
options: supported exercises holding a counter, ideally with guidance from a physio
single-leg stands with eyes closed in the middle of the room
questions.why: The safest start is supported exercises, such as holding a counter, ideally guided by a physio. Eyes-closed single-leg stands in an open room risk a fall.

questions.q: Which combination gives the best overall approach for an office worker with recurrent neck discomfort?
options: Reasonable setup, regular movement breaks, physical activity and managing stress and sleep
questions.why: A multi-factor approach fits the evidence: reasonable setup, regular movement, physical activity, and managing stress and sleep. A chair or brace alone doesn't solve it.

courses.title: Becoming a physiotherapist (and other allied health careers)
courses.summary: What physiotherapists actually do, the BPT and MPT path in India, specialisations, regulation under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act 2021, and a look at related careers such as occupational therapy, speech-language pathology and more.
outcomes: Learners can describe the work and settings of physiotherapists
Learners can outline the BPT (including internship) and MPT path and admission routes
Learners can name physiotherapy specialisations
Learners can compare physiotherapy with other allied health careers and decide which suits them

scenes.text: 8 am: Dr. Priyanka, a physiotherapist in a Pune hospital, helps a man walk for the first time after knee replacement surgery.
11 am: in the ICU she does chest physiotherapy with a patient on a ventilator to help clear secretions.
4 pm: at a cricket academy she runs an injury-prevention session for under-16 fast bowlers.
6 pm: she sees a 5-year-old with cerebral palsy and teaches his parents play-based exercises. 'Every day is different,' she says.

steps.title: The job in one paragraph
steps.body: Physiotherapists **assess, diagnose movement-related problems and treat** people of all ages using exercise, education, manual therapy, and electrophysical agents where useful. They work to restore movement and function, reduce pain, prevent injury and disability, and help people stay active. In India the title 'Dr.' is used by many physiotherapists by convention, but physiotherapists are not medical doctors and do not prescribe medicines.

steps.title: Where they work
steps.body: Hospitals (orthopaedic wards, ICU, neurology, paediatrics), outpatient clinics, private practice, sports teams and academies, gyms and fitness centres, rehabilitation centres, schools for children with disabilities, home-care services, corporate ergonomics, old-age homes, research and teaching, and community-based rehabilitation in rural areas.

steps.title: Main specialisations
steps.body:
- **Musculoskeletal / orthopaedic** (backs, joints, post-surgery)
- **Sports**
- **Neurological** (stroke, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's)
- **Cardiorespiratory / cardiopulmonary** (ICU, heart and lung rehab)
- **Paediatric** (developmental delay, cerebral palsy)
- **Geriatric** (falls, frailty)
- **Women's health / pelvic health** (pregnancy, postpartum, continence)
- **Community / rehabilitation**
- **Oncology rehabilitation** and others.

steps.title: Is it for you?
steps.body: Physiotherapy suits people who enjoy **science (especially anatomy and physiology)**, like **working with their hands and with people**, have **patience** (progress can be slow), communicate clearly, are physically active enough to be on their feet all day, and get satisfaction from small improvements. It is less suited to someone who wants a desk-based job or quick results.

items.back: Musculoskeletal / post-operative physiotherapy: early walking, range of motion, strength.
Cardiorespiratory physiotherapy: airway clearance, positioning, breathing exercises.
Paediatric neuro-physiotherapy: play-based motor learning, family training.
Sports physiotherapy: load management, technique, strength.

items.front: Woman after childbirth with leaking urine
items.back: Pelvic health physiotherapy: pelvic-floor muscle training.
Geriatric physiotherapy: balance and strength, home safety.

quiz.q: Physiotherapists in India...
options: treat movement-related problems mainly through exercise, education and manual therapy
quiz.why: Physiotherapists treat movement problems mainly with exercise, education and manual therapy. They are not medical doctors, and they don't prescribe medicines or perform surgery.

quiz.q: Chest physiotherapy in the ICU belongs to which specialisation?
quiz.why: Chest physiotherapy in the ICU belongs to cardiorespiratory physiotherapy, which deals with heart and lung care.

quiz.q: Pelvic-floor training after childbirth is part of...
quiz.why: Pelvic-floor training after childbirth is part of women's or pelvic health physiotherapy, a growing specialisation.

quiz.q: Which trait especially suits physiotherapy?
options: Patience and enjoying working with people
quiz.why: Patience and enjoying working with people suit physiotherapy, since progress is often gradual and hands-on.

lessons.title: The BPT–MPT path in India

scenes.text: Zainab, 17, from Srinagar, studies Physics, Chemistry and Biology. She loves sport and wants to help injured athletes.
Her school counsellor explains the Bachelor of Physiotherapy: four years of study plus a six-month internship.
They check how colleges in her state admit students — some use NEET-UG scores, some their own or state entrance tests, some Class 12 marks.
Zainab writes her plan: BPT, then an MPT in Sports Physiotherapy, and volunteering at local tournaments along the way.

steps.title: BPT: Bachelor of Physiotherapy
steps.body:
- **Eligibility:** usually Class 12 with **Physics, Chemistry and Biology** (and English), with a minimum percentage set by the university/state.
- **Duration:** typically **4 years + 6 months compulsory rotatory internship** (4½ years).
- **Admission:** varies — some states and institutions use **NEET-UG** scores, others conduct their own entrance tests or use Class 12 marks. Check each college's official prospectus.
- **Subjects:** anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, biomechanics, exercise therapy, electrotherapy, pathology, pharmacology basics, orthopaedics, neurology, cardiorespiratory, community physiotherapy, research methods, and supervised clinical postings.

steps.title: MPT: Master of Physiotherapy
steps.body:
- **Duration:** usually **2 years** after BPT.
- **Specialisations** commonly offered: musculoskeletal/orthopaedics, sports, neurology, cardiopulmonary, paediatrics, community, women's health and others.
- Includes advanced clinical work and a research dissertation.
- After MPT: specialist clinical roles, teaching (with university norms), and PhD for research careers.

steps.title: Regulation
steps.body: India passed the **National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP) Act, 2021**, which lists physiotherapy among the recognised allied and healthcare professions and sets up a national commission and state councils for standards and registration. Implementation (registers, councils) has been rolling out over time and some states have had their own physiotherapy councils. Check the current registration requirements in your state before you practise.

steps.title: Check before you join
steps.body:
- Is the college affiliated to a recognised university?
- Does it have an attached hospital or enough clinical postings?
- Are faculty qualified (MPT/PhD)?
- Is the internship real and supervised?
- Avoid short 'diploma in physiotherapy' courses that promise the same career as a BPT — they generally do not lead to registration as a physiotherapist.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List three colleges you'd consider. For each, write: admission route, fees, attached hospital, and internship details. Visit or email at least one and ask to see the physiotherapy department.

activity.prompt: Complete the career path.
activity.text: A Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT) usually takes ___ years of study plus a ___-month internship. A Master of Physiotherapy (MPT) usually takes ___ years. Students generally need Physics, Chemistry and ___ in Class 12.

quiz.q: A BPT in India typically lasts...
quiz.why: A BPT in India typically takes 4 years plus a 6-month internship, about 4½ years in all.

quiz.q: Which Class 12 subject group is usually required for BPT?
quiz.why: BPT usually requires Class 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Biology (PCB), along with English.

quiz.q: Which Act lists physiotherapy among allied and healthcare professions?
quiz.why: The NCAHP Act 2021, the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, lists physiotherapy among recognised professions.

quiz.q: Why should you check whether a college has an attached hospital?
options: Clinical postings are essential for learning
quiz.why: Check for an attached hospital because clinical postings give essential supervised hands-on training. Canteen and parking don't affect learning.

sources: National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act 2021

scenes.text: Arjun, 8, in Bhubaneswar, was born with cerebral palsy. Each week he sees a whole team.
His physiotherapist works on walking; his occupational therapist on holding a pencil and buttoning his shirt; his speech-language pathologist on clearer speech and safe swallowing.
A prosthetist-orthotist makes his ankle-foot orthoses; a special educator adapts lessons at school.
At his school sports day Arjun completes the 50-metre walk. Six professionals cheer from the crowd.

steps.title: Occupational therapy (BOT/BOTh)
steps.body: **Occupational therapists** help people do the everyday 'occupations' of life — self-care, work, school, play — after illness, injury or disability. Examples: hand rehabilitation, sensory integration for children, adapting a kitchen after stroke, returning to work, mental-health rehabilitation. In India the undergraduate degree is usually 4 years plus a 6-month internship.

steps.title: Speech-language pathology and audiology (BASLP)
steps.body: **Audiologists and speech-language pathologists** assess hearing, fit hearing aids, and treat speech, language, voice, fluency (stammering) and swallowing problems. In India the BASLP degree is regulated by the **Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI)**, and practitioners register with RCI.

steps.title: More allied and healthcare careers
steps.body:
- **Prosthetics and orthotics** (artificial limbs and braces) — RCI-regulated.
- **Optometry** — eye examinations and vision correction.
- **Medical laboratory technology**, **radiology/imaging technology**, **operation theatre technology**, **dialysis technology**.
- **Nutrition and dietetics.**
- **Clinical psychology** and **rehabilitation psychology** (RCI).
- **Special education** (RCI-recognised courses).
- **Sports science / strength and conditioning**, **nursing** (regulated separately), **paramedics/emergency medical technicians**.

steps.title: How to choose
steps.body:
Ask yourself:
- Do I prefer **movement and the body** (physio), **daily activities and adaptations** (OT), **communication** (speech), **technology and lab work** (imaging, lab tech), **devices** (prosthetics), or **food and health** (dietetics)?
- Spend a day shadowing two different professionals. Your feelings on the day are very useful data.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the professional.
pairs: A man learning to cook again after stroke
A woman needing an artificial leg
A footballer after knee ligament surgery
An older adult with hearing loss
A diabetic needing a meal plan

quiz.q: Which professional mainly helps with everyday activities like dressing and writing?
quiz.why: Occupational therapists help people with daily activities like dressing and writing. Physiotherapists focus more on movement and strength.

quiz.q: In India, speech-language pathologists and audiologists register with...
quiz.why: Speech-language pathologists and audiologists register with the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), which regulates BASLP.

quiz.q: Who makes artificial limbs and braces?
quiz.why: A prosthetist-orthotist makes artificial limbs (prostheses) and braces (orthoses).

quiz.q: The best way to test whether a career suits you is to...
quiz.why: Shadowing professionals for a day gives real exposure to the work, which is the best way to test a career fit. Guessing or reading salaries doesn't.

questions.q: A BPT usually includes an internship of...
questions.why: A BPT usually includes a 6-month internship after 4 years of study.

questions.q: Which professional treats stammering?
questions.why: A speech-language pathologist treats stammering, a fluency disorder. Physiotherapists and radiologists don't.

questions.q: MPT stands for...
questions.why: MPT stands for Master of Physiotherapy, a 2-year postgraduate degree.

questions.q: Which is a physiotherapy specialisation?
questions.why: Cardiorespiratory is a physiotherapy specialisation covering ICU and heart and lung rehab. Radiology, dermatology and pharmacology are different fields.

questions.q: Occupational therapists focus on...
questions.why: Occupational therapists focus on everyday activities and participation, such as self-care, work, school and play. They don't do surgery or X-rays.

questions.q: Admission to BPT in India is...
options: varies by state and institution (NEET-UG scores, own tests or Class 12 marks)
questions.why: BPT admission varies by state and institution, using NEET-UG scores, own tests or Class 12 marks. Always check each prospectus.

questions.q: Which Act created a national framework for allied and healthcare professions including physiotherapy?
questions.why: The NCAHP Act 2021 created a national framework for allied and healthcare professions, including physiotherapy. The other Acts cover IT, child protection and mental health.

questions.q: Prosthetics and orthotics in India are regulated by...
questions.why: Prosthetics and orthotics in India are regulated by the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI).

questions.q: A red flag when choosing a physiotherapy college is...
questions.why: No supervised clinical postings is a red flag, because clinical training is essential. Recognised affiliation, an attached hospital and qualified faculty are good signs.

questions.q: Which statement is accurate?
options: Physiotherapists use the 'Dr.' title by convention in India but are not medical doctors
A short diploma equals a BPT
questions.why: Physiotherapists in India use the 'Dr.' title by convention but are not medical doctors. They can't prescribe painkillers, and physiotherapy isn't only for athletes.

questions.q: A student loves communication, language and working with children. Which allied career may fit best?
questions.why: Speech-language pathology fits a student who loves communication, language and working with children. Radiology, prosthetics and dialysis technology are less linked to those interests.

questions.q: A child with cerebral palsy needs help with walking, writing and swallowing. Which team best fits?
options: Physio, occupational therapist and speech-language pathologist
questions.why: A child with cerebral palsy needs several professionals: a physio for walking, an occupational therapist for writing, and a speech-language pathologist for swallowing. Multidisciplinary care fits best.

questions.q: Before practising after graduation, a new physiotherapist should...
questions.why: After graduation, check current national or state registration requirements, since regulation is being implemented and varies by state. Just starting may break the rules.

careers-psychology-counselling.description: Learn to listen well, build real counselling micro-skills, handle boundaries, confidentiality and risk safely, and map the path to becoming a psychologist or counsellor in India.

courses.title: Being a good listener (for anyone)
courses.summary: A practical course for friends, parents, teachers, managers and anyone people come to when they are upset. You will learn why we jump to advice, how to give full attention, how to reflect feelings, and when a conversation needs more help than a friend can give.
outcomes: Learners can explain the difference between listening to reply and listening to understand
Learners can use attention, silence and open questions to help someone talk
Learners can reflect content and feelings without parroting
Learners can recognise warning signs that need a trusted adult or professional, and know India's helpline numbers

lessons.title: Why real listening is rare

scenes.text: Ananya, 15, in Pune, comes home after a maths test and says, 'I think I messed it up. I'm so tired of this.'
Her father, worried, answers in one breath: 'You should have started revising earlier. From tomorrow, no phone after 8. I'll find a tutor.' Ananya goes quiet and shuts her door.
Later her grandmother Kamala sits beside her and says only, 'Tired of it... tell me.' Ananya talks for ten minutes: the test, a fight with a friend, feeling she is always behind.
At the end Ananya says, 'Maybe I do need help with algebra.' She found the same solution her father offered, but this time it was hers.

steps.title: Hearing is not listening
steps.body:
**Hearing** is your ears picking up sound. **Listening** is choosing to understand what the other person means and feels.

People often listen at one of three levels:
- **Waiting to talk** — you are planning your next sentence.
