- **Listening to reply** — you hear the problem and immediately look for a fix or a story of your own.
- **Listening to understand** — your only goal for now is to see the situation the way *they* see it.

Most of the time, someone who is upset needs level three first. Advice, if needed at all, works much better *after* they feel understood.

steps.title: The 'fixing reflex'
steps.body:
Counsellors have a name for the urge to jump in and correct or solve: the **righting reflex** (a term from Motivational Interviewing). It comes from caring — we want the pain to stop — and from our own discomfort with someone else's sadness.

The problem: when we fix too fast, the other person may feel judged, rushed, or that their feelings are 'wrong'. They often stop talking, so we never hear the real issue. In Ananya's story the test was only the first layer.

steps.title: Worked example: two replies
steps.body:
Friend: *'My boss shouted at me in front of everyone today.'*

**Reply A (fixing):** 'Just ignore him. Or update your CV, there are better jobs.'

**Reply B (listening):** 'In front of everyone? That sounds humiliating. What happened?'

Reply B does three things: it shows you heard the important detail (*in front of everyone*), it names a likely feeling (*humiliating*), and it opens the door with a question. Reply A may even be good advice, but it closes the conversation.

steps.title: Common listening blocks
steps.body:
Watch for these in yourself — everyone does them:
- **Interrupting** or finishing their sentences.
- **One-upping:** 'That's nothing, when it happened to me...'
- **Minimising:** 'Don't be silly, it's not a big deal.'
- **Premature advice:** solutions before you understand the problem.
- **Judging:** 'Why would you even do that?'
- **Half-attention:** checking your phone, looking around.
- **Forced positivity:** 'Everything happens for a reason!'

None of these make you a bad person. They are habits, and habits can be changed.

steps.title: Ask what they need
steps.body:
A simple, respectful question solves a lot of confusion:

**'Do you want me to just listen, or would you like ideas?'**

Many people say 'just listen' at first and ask for ideas later. Some genuinely want practical help right away (for example, how to reach the hospital). Asking shows respect for their choice.

steps.title: Try this today
steps.body: In your next three conversations, count silently how many times you feel the urge to interrupt, give advice or tell your own story. Do not judge yourself — just notice. Noticing the reflex is the first step to controlling it.

activity.prompt: Your cousin says: 'I didn't get selected for the college team.' Sort each reply.

items.text: Oh no. You were really hoping for that one.
Teams don't matter, focus on studies.
How are you feeling about it?
I got rejected three times, so you're lucky.
Do you want to talk about it, or shall we just get chai?
You should have practised more.
That's disappointing. What happened at the trials?
Everything happens for a reason!

quiz.q: What is the main goal of 'listening to understand'?
options: To see the situation as the other person sees it
quiz.why: Understanding comes first; solutions, if needed, come later and work better once the person feels understood.

quiz.q: The urge to jump in and correct or solve someone's problem is called the...
quiz.why: 'Righting reflex' is the Motivational Interviewing term for the caring but unhelpful urge to fix things immediately.

quiz.q: Which reply is an example of minimising?
options: It's not a big deal, stop worrying.
quiz.why: Minimising tells the person their feelings are too big for the situation, which usually makes them stop sharing.

quiz.q: A friend is upset and you are not sure whether they want advice. What is the best move?
options: Ask: 'Do you want me to listen, or would ideas help?'
Give advice anyway, it saves time
Change the subject to cheer them up
quiz.why: Asking 'Do you want me to listen, or would ideas help?' respects their choice and avoids guessing wrong. Giving unwanted advice or changing the subject can leave them unheard.

quiz.q: In Ananya's story, why did the grandmother's approach work better?
options: She let Ananya talk and reach her own solution
She agreed the test was unfair
quiz.why: Feeling heard allowed Ananya to explore the deeper problems and arrive at her own plan.

sources: Miller & Rollnick, Motivational Interviewing (concept of the righting reflex)

lessons.title: Active listening: attention, silence and open questions

scenes.text: Joseph is a hostel warden in Kochi. One evening he finds Priya, a first-year student from Assam, sitting alone on the steps.
He puts his phone in his pocket, sits at a comfortable distance at an angle, not towering over her, and says, 'You seem quiet tonight. How are things going?'
Priya shrugs. Joseph waits. After about ten seconds of silence she says, 'I miss home. The food, my language, everything.'

Joseph nods: 'Mm. What do you miss most?' She talks about her mother's cooking and how no one here understands her jokes. By the end she is smiling a little and agrees to join the North-East students' group on Sunday.

steps.title: Attending: listening with your body
steps.body:
Before you say anything, your body tells the person whether you are really there. Counselling textbooks (Gerard Egan) summarise this as **SOLER**:
- **S**it facing them squarely, or at a slight angle.
- **O**pen posture — arms not tightly crossed.
- **L**ean slightly towards them.
- **E**ye contact — natural, not staring.
- **R**elaxed — calm, not fidgeting or rushing.

**Cultural note:** in many Indian families and many cultures, steady eye contact with elders or across genders can feel uncomfortable. Sitting side-by-side, walking together or talking while doing a task can feel safer. Adapt to the person; the goal is that they feel *attended to*, not that you follow rules.

steps.title: Silence and minimal encouragers
steps.body:
Most of us rush to fill silence. Yet a few seconds of quiet gives the person time to find words for something hard. Count slowly to five in your head before speaking.

**Minimal encouragers** are tiny signals that say 'keep going': 'Mm', 'I see', 'Go on', a nod, or repeating one key word ('Everything?'). They keep the person in charge of the story.

steps.title: Open versus closed questions
steps.body:
**Closed questions** can be answered with yes, no or one word: 'Did you have a fight?' 'Are you OK?' They are useful for facts.

**Open questions** invite a story: 'What happened?' 'How are you feeling about it?' 'What's been the hardest part?' They usually start with *what*, *how*, or *tell me about*.

Be careful with **'why'** questions ('Why did you do that?') — they can sound like blame. 'What led up to that?' asks the same thing more gently.

steps.title: Worked example: turning closed into open
steps.body:
- 'Are you stressed?' becomes 'How are you feeling these days?'
- 'Did your parents get angry?' becomes 'How did your parents react?'
- 'Is it the exam?' becomes 'What's on your mind?'
- 'Why didn't you tell me?' becomes 'What made it hard to talk about?'

Notice the open versions do not assume an answer. 'Is it the exam?' puts your guess in their mouth; 'What's on your mind?' lets them tell you it is actually something else.

steps.title: Mistakes beginners make
steps.body:
- **Question rapid-fire:** five questions in a row feel like an interrogation. Ask one, then listen.
- **Leading questions:** 'You must be angry, right?' tells them what to feel.
- **Too much nodding and 'mm':** done mechanically, it looks fake.
- **Forgetting the phone:** a single glance at a notification tells the person they are second priority.

steps.title: Try this: the 70/30 conversation
steps.body: Ask a family member, 'What was the best and the hardest part of your day?' Aim for them to talk about 70% of the time. Use only open questions, encouragers and silence. Afterwards notice: what did you learn that you would have missed if you had talked more?

activity.prompt: Match each closed question with a better open question.
pairs: What was that like for you?

quiz.q: What does the 'O' in SOLER stand for?
quiz.why: In SOLER, the O stands for Open posture, along with Squarely facing, Leaning in, Eye contact and Relaxed. It shows you are available to listen.

quiz.q: Which is an open question?
options: What has been the hardest part?
quiz.why: It cannot be answered with yes or no and invites the person to tell their story.

quiz.q: Why should 'why' questions be used carefully?
quiz.why: 'Why did you...' can feel accusing. 'What led up to...' gets the same information more gently.

quiz.q: A person goes silent after saying something difficult. A good listener usually...
options: Fills the gap immediately with advice
Waits calmly for a few seconds
quiz.why: After a difficult statement, a good listener waits calmly for a few seconds. Silence gives the person time to find words, while rushing or changing topic shuts them down.

quiz.q: Strict eye contact rules may need adapting because...
options: In some cultures and situations it can feel uncomfortable
Counsellors should never look at clients
quiz.why: Attending is about the person feeling attended to; sitting side-by-side or walking may feel safer for some.

lessons.title: Reflective listening and empathy

story.title: Farah and Zoya after the driving test

scenes.text: In Hyderabad, Zoya fails her driving test for the second time and calls her best friend Farah, crying.
Farah's first thought is to say, 'At least you didn't crash!' Instead she says, 'Second time... you sound really let down.'
Zoya: 'Not just let down. Embarrassed. My younger brother passed first time.' Farah: 'So it's also about feeling compared with him.' Zoya: 'Yes! Exactly that.'
Zoya says later that the call helped more than any advice. Feeling understood made her calm enough to book a few more practice lessons.

steps.title: What reflective listening is
steps.body:
A **reflection** is a short statement (not a question) that tells the person what you understood. It works like a mirror: they hear their own experience back and can confirm, correct or go deeper.

Two main types:
- **Reflecting content (paraphrasing):** the facts and situation in your own words. 'So the test was today and you were marked down for parking.'
- **Reflecting feeling:** the emotion behind the words. 'You sound really let down.'

A good reflection is brief, uses your own words, and ends with a downward tone — a statement, not a question.

steps.title: Empathy versus sympathy
steps.body:
**Sympathy** is feeling *for* someone from the outside: 'Oh, poor you.' It can create distance, or make the person feel pitied.

**Empathy** is trying to understand the experience *from the inside*, as if you were in their place, while remembering it is theirs, not yours. The psychologist Carl Rogers described it as sensing the other person's world 'as if' it were your own, without losing the 'as if'.

Empathy does not mean agreeing. You can understand why someone feels furious with their sister without agreeing that they should stop speaking to her.

steps.title: Worked example: levels of reflection
steps.body:
Speaker: *'Everyone at my new office already has friends. I eat lunch at my desk.'*

- **Parroting (weak):** 'Everyone already has friends and you eat at your desk.'
- **Paraphrase:** 'You're new and haven't found your group yet.'
- **Feeling reflection:** 'That sounds lonely.'
- **Deeper reflection (guess at meaning):** 'You're starting to wonder if you'll ever fit in there.'

Deeper reflections are powerful but they are guesses. If you are wrong, the person will correct you, and that correction is useful too.

steps.title: Grow your feeling vocabulary
steps.body:
Many people only use 'good', 'bad', 'stressed' and 'angry'. Try more precise words:
- Instead of *sad*: disappointed, lonely, hurt, discouraged, grieving.
- Instead of *angry*: annoyed, frustrated, betrayed, resentful, furious.
- Instead of *scared*: nervous, uneasy, overwhelmed, panicky, dreading.
- Instead of *happy*: relieved, proud, hopeful, excited, content.

The right word often makes a person say, 'Yes, that's it,' and feel deeply understood.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Starting every sentence with 'So what I'm hearing is...'** — it sounds scripted. Vary it or just say the reflection.
- **Getting the intensity wrong:** calling deep grief 'a bit upset' minimises it; calling mild irritation 'rage' exaggerates it.
- **Turning it into a question every time:** 'You feel lonely?' A statement invites more depth.
- **Reflecting, then immediately advising:** give the reflection space to land.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Next time someone shares something, try just one reflection of feeling before you say anything else. Notice whether they say more, correct you, or relax.

a.text: Your friend calls: 'I didn't get the internship. I really thought this one was mine.' What do you say first?

choices.label: 'You really thought this one was yours. That must sting.'
choices.feedback: A clear reflection of both content and feeling.

choices.label: 'There are hundreds of internships, apply for another.'
choices.feedback: Probably true, but it skips past how they feel right now.

choices.label: 'Did you prepare properly?'
choices.feedback: This can sound like blame at a painful moment.

b.text: Friend: 'It does. And now I'm scared my parents will think I'm wasting time.' What next?

choices.label: 'So it's not just the internship — you're worried about what your parents will think.'
choices.feedback: Excellent, you picked up the new, deeper worry.

choices.label: 'Your parents won't care, relax.'
choices.feedback: You cannot know this, and it dismisses the fear.

c.text: Your friend goes quiet: 'Yeah... maybe. Anyway.' The conversation is closing. How can you recover?

choices.label: 'Sorry, I jumped in. I think you're really disappointed. Tell me what happened.'
choices.feedback: Repairing is a real skill. Naming your mistake and returning to listening often reopens the conversation.

choices.label: Change the topic to a film.
choices.feedback: The chance to support them is lost for now.

d.text: Friend: 'Exactly. Thanks for getting it. Could you help me think how to tell them?' Now they are asking for ideas — and you can offer some together.

choices.label: Brainstorm together how to talk to the parents.
choices.feedback: Advice works best when the person asks for it after feeling heard.

end1.text: Well done. You reflected feelings, spotted the deeper worry, and offered help only once it was wanted.

end2.text: This path ended early. Try again and see what happens when you reflect the feeling first.

quiz.q: A reflection is best delivered as...
options: A repetition of their exact words
A short statement in your own words
quiz.why: Statements invite the person to go deeper; exact repetition (parroting) feels mechanical.

quiz.q: Which is a reflection of feeling?
quiz.why: 'You sound betrayed' names the emotion behind the words, which is a reflection of feeling. The others share your experience, ask a question or give advice.

quiz.q: Empathy means...
options: Telling them how you would feel
Agreeing with everything the person says
Understanding their experience from their point of view, while knowing it is theirs
Feeling sorry for them from a distance
quiz.why: Empathy is understanding their experience from their point of view while knowing it is theirs. It isn't agreeing with everything or feeling sorry from a distance.

quiz.q: If your reflection is wrong, what usually happens?
options: You must apologise for a long time
The person corrects you, which helps you understand better
quiz.why: Corrections are useful information; a sincere attempt to understand is rarely harmful.

quiz.q: Calling someone's deep grief 'a bit upset' is a mistake of...
quiz.why: Calling deep grief 'a bit upset' understates the feeling, which is a mistake of intensity. Matching the intensity shows you really understand.

sources: Carl Rogers, A Way of Being (empathy)

lessons.title: Limits, secrets and when to get help

story.title: Kabir and the message at midnight

scenes.text: Kabir, 16, from Lucknow, gets a late-night message from his friend Rohan: 'I'm so tired of everything. Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me. Don't tell anyone.'
Kabir feels scared and unsure. He wants to be loyal, but this feels too big.

He replies: 'I'm really glad you told me. Are you thinking about ending your life?' Rohan writes: 'Sometimes.' Kabir says: 'I care about you too much to keep this secret. Can we tell your mum or our class teacher together tomorrow? If you feel unsafe tonight, please call 14416 or 112.'
The next morning they talk to their school counsellor. Rohan later tells Kabir, 'I was angry for one day. Now I'm grateful.'

steps.title: A listener is not a therapist
steps.body:
Good listening helps enormously, but friends, parents and colleagues are not trained to treat depression, trauma, addiction or crises. Knowing your **limits** is part of being a good listener.

Your job as a supportive person is to:
- listen and take the person seriously,
- stay calm and non-judgemental,
- help them connect with the right help,
- look after yourself too.

steps.title: Situations that always need more help
steps.body:
Bring in a trusted adult or professional when someone:
- talks about **wanting to die, ending their life or hurting themselves**,
- is being **hurt, abused or threatened** by someone,
- is planning to **hurt someone else**,
- seems confused, very unwell, or is using alcohol or drugs dangerously,
- has stopped eating, sleeping or functioning for a long time.

If there is immediate danger, call **112** (all emergencies in India). For children in difficulty, **1098** (Childline). For mental health support, **Tele-MANAS: 14416**.

steps.title: Asking directly does not 'put the idea in their head'
steps.body:
Many people fear that asking 'Are you thinking about suicide?' might make it more likely. Research reviews have found that asking directly does **not** increase suicidal thoughts and may bring relief, because the person finally feels allowed to talk.

Use clear words. Vague phrases like 'You're not going to do anything silly, are you?' signal that you want a 'no'.

steps.title: Secrets you should never promise to keep
steps.body:
It is fine to keep ordinary private things private. But **never promise total secrecy before you know what the secret is.** A kind way to say it:

*'I'll keep what you tell me private, unless I'm worried you or someone else could get hurt. Then I'd need to get help — and I'd try to do it with you.'*

This is the same rule professional counsellors follow: confidentiality has **limits** when there is serious risk of harm.

steps.title: Worked example: helping someone reach help
steps.body:
- **Acknowledge:** 'Thank you for trusting me with this.'
- **Ask:** 'Are you thinking of hurting yourself?'
- **Stay:** do not leave them alone if they are in immediate danger.
- **Connect:** 'Who can we tell together — a parent, teacher, doctor?' Offer to sit with them while they call.
- **Follow up:** check in the next day. Reaching out once is not the end.

steps.title: Look after the listener
steps.body: Hearing someone's pain can leave you sad, anxious or drained. That is normal. Talk to someone you trust (without sharing more details than needed), sleep, move your body, and remember: you are not responsible for fixing another person's life. Getting them to help *is* helping.

statements.s: If a friend says 'Don't tell anyone' about wanting to die, you must keep the promise.
statements.why: Safety comes before secrecy. Tell a trusted adult or call a helpline, ideally together with your friend.

statements.s: Asking directly about suicide can bring relief and does not plant the idea.
statements.why: Research reviews support asking clearly and calmly.

statements.s: In India, 14416 is the Tele-MANAS mental health helpline.
statements.why: Tele-MANAS is the national tele-mental health service; 112 is for any emergency.

statements.s: A good listener should try to be the person's only support.
statements.why: No one person can carry this. Connecting them to more support is the caring choice.

statements.s: It is normal for a listener to feel drained after a heavy conversation.
statements.why: Listeners need care too: rest, and talk to someone you trust.

quiz.q: Your friend says, 'Promise you won't tell anyone what I'm about to say.' What is wisest?
options: Say you'll keep it private unless someone could get hurt
quiz.why: Saying you'll keep it private unless someone could get hurt keeps trust and is honest that safety comes first. Promising everything may force you to break your word.

quiz.q: Which is the all-emergency number in India?
quiz.why: 112 is India's single all-emergency number. 1098 is Childline and 14416 is Tele-MANAS, and 100 is only for police.

quiz.q: Which phrase asks about suicide clearly?
options: Are you thinking about ending your life?
You won't do anything silly, will you?
Cheer up, it's not that bad.
quiz.why: 'Are you thinking about ending your life?' is clear, direct language that tells the person it's safe to answer honestly. Asking about suicide does not plant the idea.

quiz.q: Which situation is beyond what a friend should handle alone?
options: A friend being hurt at home
A friend who lost a cricket match
A friend annoyed about a film
quiz.why: Abuse or harm always needs a trusted adult or authorities; for children, 1098 can help.

quiz.q: After connecting a friend with help, a good next step is to...
options: Check in on them in the following days
quiz.why: Checking in on your friend in the following days shows ongoing care and helps you notice if they need more support. Ignoring it or posting online does not help.

sources: Dazzi et al. 2014, review on asking about suicide
WHO, Preventing suicide: a resource series

questions.q: Hearing differs from listening because listening...
options: involves choosing to understand meaning and feeling
questions.why: Hearing is just sensing sound, while listening involves choosing to understand meaning and feeling. It is an active effort.

questions.q: Which is an open question?
options: How has this week been for you?
questions.why: An open question like 'How has this week been for you?' invites a fuller answer. Questions such as 'Are you tired?' or 'Did you eat?' can be answered with just yes or no.

questions.q: India's mental health helpline Tele-MANAS can be reached at...
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, India's mental health helpline, is 14416 (or 1-800-891-4416). 1098 is Childline, 108 is ambulance and 101 is fire.

questions.q: 'At least you didn't crash!' is an example of...
questions.why: 'At least you didn't crash!' pushes the person's feeling aside with forced positivity, which is minimising. A reflection of feeling would name the fear or upset instead.

questions.q: Minimal encouragers are...
options: small signals like 'mm' or a nod that invite the person to continue
questions.why: Minimal encouragers are small signals like 'mm' or a nod that invite the person to keep talking. They let the speaker stay in charge of the story.

questions.q: SOLER is a guide for...
questions.why: SOLER is Egan's guide to non-verbal attending: Squarely, Open posture, Lean, Eye contact, Relaxed. It should be adapted to the person's culture.

questions.q: Speaker: 'I studied all night and still blanked out.' Which is the best feeling reflection?
questions.why: 'That sounds really frustrating' names the likely emotion as a statement, so it is a feeling reflection. 'Blanked out?' is only a question, and the others give advice or dismiss the feeling.

questions.q: Empathy differs from sympathy because empathy...
options: tries to understand from inside the person's experience
questions.why: Empathy tries to understand from inside the person's experience, while sympathy feels for someone from the outside, often with pity. Empathy doesn't mean agreeing or advising.

questions.q: 'Why did you do that?' can be rephrased more gently as...
questions.why: 'What led up to that?' asks for the same information as 'Why did you do that?' but with less blame. 'Why' can sound like an accusation.

questions.q: A friend tells you they are being hit at home and asks you to keep it secret. Best response?
options: Explain you care too much to keep it secret and help them tell a trusted adult or 1098
Keep the secret to stay loyal
questions.why: Violence at home needs adult or professional help, so explain that you care too much to keep it secret and help them tell a trusted adult or call 1098. Confronting the parent may increase the danger.

questions.q: You made a fixing reply and your friend went quiet. The best repair is...
options: Acknowledge you jumped in and return to listening
questions.why: Acknowledging that you jumped in and returning to listening repairs the moment and reopens the conversation. Repeating advice or changing the subject deepens the distance.

questions.q: Which statement about asking about suicide is supported by research reviews?
options: Asking directly does not increase risk and may bring relief
It should only be done by doctors
questions.why: Research reviews find that asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and may bring relief. Clear, caring questions are recommended, and anyone can ask.

questions.q: A colleague shares something heavy; afterwards you feel low for two days. The most appropriate step is...
options: Tell the whole team the story
Look after yourself and talk to someone you trust, without unnecessary details
questions.why: Listeners need support too; protect the other person's privacy while caring for yourself.

questions.q: Speaker: 'My parents keep comparing me with my cousin, the doctor.' Which is a deeper (meaning) reflection?
options: 'It sounds like you wonder whether you'll ever be enough for them.'
questions.why: It guesses at the underlying meaning — offered tentatively, the person can confirm or correct.

courses.title: Counselling skills: foundations for trainees
courses.summary: For psychology and social-work students, teachers, HR staff and volunteers on helplines. Covers the helping relationship, core micro-skills (OARS), contracting, boundaries and confidentiality, basic suicide-risk assessment and safety planning, referral, supervision and self-care. General education — real practice requires supervised training.
outcomes: Learners can describe Rogers' core conditions and the working alliance
Learners can use open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries in a session
Learners can contract confidentiality and explain its limits, including Indian legal duties
Learners can carry out a basic, structured suicide-risk conversation and a safety plan
Learners can recognise when and how to refer, and why supervision matters

scenes.text: Meenal, an MA Counselling Psychology trainee in Bengaluru, meets her first client at a college counselling centre: Arjun, 19, who 'just wants tips to stop overthinking'.
She has a list of techniques ready. But her supervisor reminded her: 'In the first session, the technique is the relationship.'
Meenal explains confidentiality, asks what Arjun hopes to get from counselling, and mostly listens. Arjun opens up about his parents' divorce.
At the end Arjun says, 'I didn't expect to talk about that. Can I come next week?' The relationship had started to form.

steps.title: Rogers' core conditions
steps.body:
Carl Rogers, founder of person-centred therapy, proposed that change becomes possible when the helper offers three **core conditions**:
- **Empathy** — accurately understanding the client's inner world and communicating that understanding.
- **Unconditional positive regard** — warm acceptance of the person (not necessarily of every behaviour), without conditions of worth.
- **Congruence (genuineness)** — being real, not hiding behind a professional mask, and not pretending feelings you don't have.

Most modern approaches (CBT, psychodynamic, solution-focused, MI) still rely on these as the foundation.

steps.title: The working alliance
steps.body:
Edward Bordin described the **working alliance** as three parts:
- agreement on **goals** (what we're working towards),
- agreement on **tasks** (what we'll do in sessions),
- a **bond** of trust and respect.

Across many studies, the strength of the alliance is one of the more consistent predictors of how well therapy goes, across different therapy types. This is why rushing to techniques before trust exists often backfires.

steps.title: A simple map of a helping conversation
steps.body:
Gerard Egan's *Skilled Helper* model offers three stages:
- **Stage 1 — Current picture:** What is going on? Help the client tell their story, find blind spots and focus on what matters most.
- **Stage 2 — Preferred picture:** What would be better? What do they want instead?
- **Stage 3 — Way forward:** How will they get there? Strategies, plans, action.

It is not strictly linear; clients move back and forth. But it reminds you not to jump to Stage 3 in minute five.

steps.title: Worked example: opening a first session
steps.body:
*'Hi Arjun, I'm Meenal, a counselling trainee here. We have about 50 minutes. Before we start, a word on privacy: what you say stays between us and my clinical supervisor, who helps me make sure you get good support. The only exceptions are if I'm worried that you or someone else could be seriously harmed, or if a law or court requires it — I'd talk with you first wherever possible. Does that make sense? ... So, what brings you here today?'*

This covers: introductions, time, confidentiality and its limits, supervision, consent, and an open invitation.

steps.title: Counselling is not advice-giving
steps.body:
Common trainee errors:
- **Advising:** 'You should move out.' Clients rarely follow advice they didn't help create.
- **Rescuing:** taking over problems the client can handle.
- **Over-sharing:** long stories about your own life. Brief, purposeful self-disclosure can help; frequent self-disclosure shifts focus to you.
- **Diagnosing too early:** labels in session one can feel like being put in a box.

The aim is to strengthen the client's own capacity to understand and act.

steps.title: Try this: write your opening
steps.body: Write your own 60-second opening script for a first session in your setting (school, college, NGO, workplace). Include name and role, time, confidentiality and limits, and an open question. Say it aloud until it sounds natural, not recited.

activity.prompt: Match each concept with its description.
pairs: Accurately sensing and communicating the client's inner world
Warm acceptance of the person without conditions of worth
Being genuine rather than hiding behind a role
Agreement on goals and tasks plus a bond of trust
Exploring the preferred picture — what the client wants instead
Taking over problems the client could handle

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Rogers' core conditions?
quiz.why: Rogers' core conditions are empathy, congruence and unconditional positive regard. Interpretation is a psychodynamic technique, not a core condition.

quiz.q: Bordin's working alliance includes agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and...
quiz.why: Bordin's working alliance has three parts: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and the emotional bond between client and counsellor.

quiz.q: In Egan's model, Stage 3 focuses on...
quiz.why: In Egan's three-stage model, Stage 1 is the current picture, Stage 2 the preferred picture and Stage 3 the way forward, which is planning and action.

quiz.q: Unconditional positive regard means...
options: accepting the person warmly without conditions of worth
quiz.why: Unconditional positive regard is warm acceptance of the person without conditions of worth. Accepting the person is different from approving of every behaviour.

quiz.q: Why should trainees mention supervision in the first session?
options: Because informed consent includes who else may hear about their case
quiz.why: Informed consent includes telling clients who else may hear about their case, such as a supervisor. Clients have a right to know how their information is used.

scenes.text: Daniel, a nurse-counsellor in a Nairobi clinic, sees Grace, 45, who has been told by her doctor to stop smoking. She crosses her arms: 'Everyone keeps lecturing me.'
Daniel doesn't lecture. He asks, 'What do you enjoy about smoking, and what's not so good about it?'
He reflects: 'It's your only quiet time in a busy day — and you're also worried about your breathing when you play with your grandson.'
Grace pauses. 'My grandson... yes. Maybe I could start by not smoking in the house.' Daniel summarises and affirms her idea. She leaves with a plan she made herself.

steps.title: The four OARS
steps.body:
Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) summarises core micro-skills as **OARS**:
- **O — Open questions:** 'What would you like to be different?'
- **A — Affirmations:** genuine recognition of strengths or efforts: 'You came even though you were nervous — that took courage.'
- **R — Reflections:** statements of what you understand: simple or complex.
- **S — Summaries:** collecting several points together, then checking: 'Let me see if I've got this...'

These are used in almost every counselling approach, not only MI.

steps.title: Simple and complex reflections
steps.body:
- **Simple reflection** stays close to what was said: 'You're tired of the lectures.'
- **Complex reflection** adds meaning, feeling or the unspoken: 'You want people to trust that you can make your own decisions.'
- **Double-sided reflection** captures ambivalence: 'Part of you values your quiet smoke breaks, and part of you is worried about your health.'

A common training guideline is to offer more reflections than questions — many MI trainers aim for about two reflections per question. Too many questions make clients passive.

steps.title: Worked transcript
steps.body:
**Client:** I've missed four classes this week. I just can't get out of bed.
**Counsellor (R, simple):** Getting out of bed has been really hard.
**Client:** Yeah, and then I feel guilty all day.
**Counsellor (R, complex):** So it's not laziness — it's heavy, and the guilt makes it heavier.
**Client:** Exactly.
**Counsellor (O):** What's different on the days you do make it?
**Client:** When my roommate drags me to breakfast.
**Counsellor (A):** You noticed what helps — that's useful.
**Counsellor (S):** So: mornings are very hard, guilt adds weight, and company makes a difference. Did I miss anything?

steps.title: Affirmations that land
steps.body:
Affirmations must be **genuine and specific**, about effort or values, not empty praise.
- Weak: 'You're amazing!'
- Strong: 'You kept going to work through a really hard month. That shows how much your family matters to you.'

Avoid affirmations that sound like evaluation ('Good job!') — it positions you as the judge.

steps.title: Mistakes to avoid
steps.body:
- **Question-answer trap:** question, answer, question, answer... the client waits for you to lead.
- **Summarising too often:** every two minutes feels mechanical; use summaries at transitions and endings.
- **Hidden advice in questions:** 'Have you thought about just talking to your mother?' is advice dressed as a question.
- **Ignoring ambivalence:** pushing only the 'change' side often triggers the client to argue the other side.

steps.title: Try this: code a conversation
steps.body: Record (with permission) or recall a 5-minute supportive conversation. Count your open questions, closed questions, reflections, affirmations and summaries. Is your reflection-to-question ratio below 1? Practise replacing some questions with reflections.

activity.prompt: Classify each counsellor statement.

items.text: What would a good week look like for you?
You've been trying hard to keep the peace at home.
You're frustrated that nobody asks what you want.
So far you've mentioned sleep, the fights at home and worries about money — is that right?
How has this been affecting your studies?
It took courage to come here today.
Part of you wants to leave the job, and part of you is scared of the gap on your CV.
Let me pull together what we covered today before we plan next steps.

quiz.q: OARS stands for...
quiz.why: OARS from Motivational Interviewing stands for Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections and Summaries. These are the core micro-skills.

quiz.q: 'Part of you wants X, and part of you wants Y' is a...
quiz.why: 'Part of you wants X, and part of you wants Y' is a double-sided reflection. It captures ambivalence without taking sides.

quiz.q: Which is a genuine, specific affirmation?
options: You kept attending college during a very painful month.
quiz.why: 'You kept attending college during a very painful month' recognises a specific effort, so it is a genuine affirmation. 'Good job!' is general praise, and 'That's correct' is only feedback.

quiz.q: 'Have you thought about just apologising?' is risky because...
options: it is advice disguised as a question
quiz.why: 'Have you thought about just apologising?' is advice disguised as a question. The client may feel steered rather than heard.

quiz.q: Many MI trainers aim for roughly how many reflections per question?
quiz.why: Many MI trainers aim for about two reflections per question. Reflections help clients go deeper, while too many questions make them passive.

lessons.title: Boundaries and confidentiality

scenes.text: Sana counsels employees through a workplace wellbeing service in Gurugram. After a few good sessions, her client Vikram sends her a friend request on Instagram and a box of sweets for Diwali.
Sana likes Vikram and doesn't want him to feel rejected. But she also knows that being 'friends' would change their work.

In the next session she says warmly: 'Thank you for thinking of me. I keep my personal social media separate from clients so this space stays fully yours — it's not about you.' She checks her service's policy on small festival gifts and shares the sweets with the team, telling him so.
Vikram says he understands. The boundary actually made him trust her more.

steps.title: Contracting: agreeing the frame
steps.body:
At the start, a counsellor agrees the **frame** of the work with the client (often in writing):
- session length, frequency and fees (if any),
- how to cancel or reschedule,
- how to contact the counsellor between sessions, and what to do in an emergency,
- confidentiality and its limits,
- record-keeping and supervision,
- the client's right to ask questions or end counselling.

This is part of **informed consent**: the client chooses to begin with clear knowledge of what they are agreeing to.

steps.title: Confidentiality and its limits
steps.body:
Confidentiality is central: clients need to know their story won't travel. But it is **not absolute**. Typical limits:
- **Serious risk of harm** to the client or others (e.g., suicide risk, threats of violence).
- **Child protection:** in India the **POCSO Act, 2012** (Section 19) requires anyone who knows or suspects a sexual offence against a child to report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police.
- **Court orders** or other legal requirements.
- **Supervision:** case discussion with a supervisor, usually anonymised.

India's **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** also gives persons with mental illness a right to confidentiality of their mental-health information, with specific exceptions. Rules evolve — check current law and your organisation's policy.

steps.title: Boundaries protect the client
steps.body:
Boundaries are the professional limits that keep the relationship safe and focused on the client's needs.
- **Dual relationships:** avoid being a client's friend, business partner, landlord or relative while counselling them. In small towns, overlaps can't always be avoided — then discuss them openly and seek supervision.
- **Sexual or romantic relationships with clients are never acceptable** in any counselling ethics code.
- **Gifts:** small tokens may be culturally appropriate; follow your organisation's policy and reflect on meaning. Large gifts or money are not accepted.
- **Time and contact:** consistent session lengths; clear rules about messaging.
- **Touch:** generally avoided; if ever considered (e.g., a handshake), it is the client's comfort and consent that matters, and cultural and gender norms count.

steps.title: Worked example: explaining a limit
steps.body:
Client: *'Promise you'll never tell anyone what I say.'*

Counsellor: *'What you share stays here. The rare exceptions are if I believe you or someone else is in serious danger, if a child is being harmed, or if a court requires it. Even then, I would try to talk with you first about what happens next. Is there something worrying you about sharing?'*

This is honest, calm, and turns the worry into something to explore.

steps.title: Boundary slips start small
steps.body:
Serious boundary violations rarely start dramatically. They often begin with small 'crossings': sessions running long for one client, late-night messages, personal favours, sharing your own problems. Not every crossing is harmful, but a pattern is a warning sign.

Ask yourself: *Whose needs is this meeting — mine or the client's? Would I be comfortable discussing this with my supervisor?* If not, bring it to supervision.

steps.title: Records
steps.body: Keep notes factual, brief and secure (locked cabinet or password-protected systems). Write as if the client could read them one day. Avoid storing client details on personal phones or unofficial chat apps.

a.text: You are a school counsellor. Riya, 14, says: 'I'll tell you something only if you promise not to tell my parents.' What do you say?

choices.label: 'I promise, you can tell me anything.'
choices.feedback: Promising total secrecy before you know the content is risky; you may have to break it.

choices.label: 'Most things stay between us. If you or someone else is in danger, I'd need to involve others — and I'd talk to you first.'
choices.feedback: Honest contracting builds real trust.

b.text: Riya tells you an older cousin has been touching her inappropriately. You promised secrecy. What now?

choices.label: Keep the promise.
choices.feedback: This leaves a child at risk and breaches POCSO's reporting duty.

choices.label: Explain gently that you must act to keep her safe, follow the school's child-protection procedure and report as POCSO requires.
choices.feedback: Correct, though trust may be harder now. Next time, explain limits first.

c.text: Riya pauses, then tells you an older cousin has been touching her inappropriately. What do you do?

choices.label: Thank her, reassure her it's not her fault, explain what will happen next, and follow the child-protection procedure and POCSO reporting.
choices.feedback: Child safety and legal duty come first, handled with care and transparency.

choices.label: Call the cousin yourself to confront him.
choices.feedback: Confronting the alleged abuser can put the child at greater risk and harm an investigation.

end1.text: You protected Riya while respecting her as much as possible: belief, reassurance, clear explanation and correct reporting.

end2.text: This path left the child unsafe or broke procedure. In child-protection cases: listen, reassure, don't investigate yourself, report as required.

quiz.q: Which is a recognised limit of confidentiality?
options: The client's parents ask out of curiosity
Serious risk of harm to the client or others
A friend of the counsellor asks
quiz.why: A serious risk of harm to the client or others is a recognised limit of confidentiality. Curiosity from parents or friends is not a reason to disclose.

quiz.q: Under India's POCSO Act, 2012, knowledge of a sexual offence against a child...
options: is handled only by the school principal
must be reported to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit
may be ignored if the family prefers
quiz.why: Under the POCSO Act, 2012, knowing about a sexual offence against a child creates a duty to report to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit. Failure to report is itself an offence.

quiz.q: A romantic relationship between a counsellor and a current client is...
quiz.why: A romantic relationship with a current client is never acceptable. Counselling ethics codes prohibit it because it exploits the power imbalance.

quiz.q: Contracting at the start of counselling is part of...
quiz.why: Contracting at the start of counselling is part of informed consent. The client agrees to the work knowing its frame, such as time, fees and confidentiality.

quiz.q: A useful self-check for boundary decisions is...
options: Will the client like me more?
Whose needs does this meet — mine or the client's?
quiz.why: Ask whose needs a boundary decision meets, yours or the client's. Boundaries exist to keep the work focused on the client.

sources: Common counselling ethics codes (e.g., BACP, ACA)

lessons.title: Risk assessment basics and safety planning

scenes.text: Nikhil volunteers on an emotional-support helpline in Mumbai. A caller, Leela, 32, says quietly, 'I don't see the point of anything anymore.'
Nikhil remembers his training: stay calm, ask directly. 'Leela, sometimes when people feel this way they think about ending their life. Are you having thoughts like that?'
Leela says yes, for two weeks, but she hasn't made a plan and her sister lives nearby. Nikhil asks gently about plans, means, past attempts and what has kept her going.

Together they write a simple safety plan: warning signs, things that calm her, her sister's number, Tele-MANAS 14416, and an appointment with a doctor. Nikhil consults his shift supervisor before closing the call.

steps.title: Scope: this is an introduction
steps.body: This lesson teaches *basics* that every helper should know. Formal suicide-risk assessment and management is done by trained, supervised professionals. Always follow your organisation's protocol and consult a supervisor. If someone is in immediate danger in India, call **112**; mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body:
Signs that someone may be considering suicide include:
- talking about wanting to die, being a burden, or having no reason to live,
- searching for means,
- withdrawing from people, giving away possessions, saying goodbye,
- sudden calm after a period of deep distress,
- increased alcohol or drug use,
- extreme mood changes, hopelessness, agitation or sleeping problems.

No single sign predicts suicide. Take all talk of suicide seriously.

steps.title: Risk and protective factors
steps.body:
**Risk factors** (raise concern): previous suicide attempt (one of the strongest), mental disorders such as depression, substance misuse, chronic pain or illness, recent losses (relationship, job, exam results), isolation, abuse or violence, access to lethal means, family history of suicide.

**Protective factors** (lower concern): supportive relationships, reasons for living (children, pets, faith, goals), problem-solving skills, access to care, restricted access to means, sense of hope.

Risk is dynamic — it changes over hours and days, so it must be revisited.

steps.title: Worked example: a structured conversation
steps.body:
Ask step by step, calmly:
- **Thoughts:** 'Are you having thoughts of ending your life?'
- **Frequency and intensity:** 'How often? How strong are they?'
- **Plan:** 'Have you thought about how you would do it?'
- **Means:** 'Do you have access to that?'
- **Timing / intent:** 'Have you thought about when? How likely do you think you are to act?'
- **History:** 'Have you ever tried before?'
- **Protective:** 'What has stopped you so far? Who do you have around you?'

Generally, the more specific the plan, the more available the means, the stronger the intent and the more recent a previous attempt, the higher the urgency.

steps.title: Safety planning
steps.body:
A **safety plan** (based on Stanley and Brown's Safety Planning Intervention) is a written, personalised list the person keeps handy:
- 1. My warning signs (thoughts, moods, situations).
- 2. Things I can do on my own to cope (walk, music, prayer, a shower).
- 3. People and places that distract me.
- 4. People I can ask for help (names and numbers).
- 5. Professionals and helplines (doctor, counsellor, 14416, 112).
- 6. Making my environment safer (reducing access to means — e.g., a family member keeps medicines or pesticides locked away).

It is made **with** the person, in their words, not handed to them.

steps.title: If risk is high
steps.body: If someone has a plan, means and intent, or is in immediate danger: do not leave them alone, remove access to means if safely possible, call 112 or arrange emergency medical care, involve their family or trusted person, and inform your supervisor. Document what was said and done. In India, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Section 115) directs that a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and should receive care, rather than be punished.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of a basic risk conversation in a sensible order.
items: Stay calm and show you are listening
Ask about plan, means and timing
Connect to professional help and follow your protocol

quiz.q: Which is among the strongest risk factors for suicide?
quiz.why: A previous suicide attempt is one of the strongest known risk factors for suicide. Being an introvert, living in a city or liking sad music are not.

quiz.q: A sudden calm after weeks of deep distress can be...
options: a possible warning sign worth checking
quiz.why: A sudden calm after weeks of deep distress can be a warning sign, sometimes because a decision has been made. Gently check by asking, not assuming recovery.

quiz.q: Reducing access to lethal means is...
options: an evidence-supported part of safety planning
quiz.why: Reducing access to lethal means is one of the best-supported suicide prevention strategies and is part of safety planning. It isn't just for police.

quiz.q: A safety plan should be...
options: a contract promising not to die
made with the person, in their own words
quiz.why: Collaborative plans are more likely to be used. 'No-suicide contracts' are not recommended as a substitute.

quiz.q: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be...
options: under severe stress and in need of care
quiz.why: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, Section 115 presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and needs care, not punishment. The government must provide that care.

lessons.title: Referral, endings, supervision and self-care

story.title: When Rahul needed more than counselling

scenes.text: Tanvi, a counsellor at a Chennai college, has seen Rahul for four sessions about exam stress.
Today Rahul says he hasn't slept for three nights, feels his thoughts are racing, has spent all his savings online and is sure he has a special mission.
Tanvi recognises this may need urgent psychiatric assessment. She explains her concern kindly, involves his guardian with his knowledge, and arranges an appointment with a psychiatrist that day.
In supervision later, Tanvi talks through her own worry. Her supervisor says: 'Knowing the edge of your competence is a skill, not a failure.'

steps.title: When to refer
steps.body:
Refer, or seek additional help, when:
- the problem is **beyond your training** (e.g., possible psychosis, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, severe trauma, substance dependence),
- there may be a **medical cause** or need for medication (only doctors — e.g., a psychiatrist — can prescribe),
- **risk** is high,
- you have a **conflict of interest** or dual relationship,
- after a fair trial the work is **not helping**,
- the client needs a **specialist** (legal aid, de-addiction centre, disability services, domestic violence support).

steps.title: Worked example: a warm referral
steps.body:
A cold referral: *'This isn't my area. Here's a number.'*

A warm referral: *'From what you've described — no sleep for days and racing thoughts — I think it's important a psychiatrist sees you, because some of this might need medical help, and they are trained for exactly that. It's not that I don't want to work with you. Can we call together now to book an appointment? And would you like to come back here afterwards to talk?'*

Warm referrals explain *why*, reduce shame, help with the practical steps and, where appropriate, keep the door open.

steps.title: Endings (termination)
steps.body:
Endings matter, especially for clients who have experienced abandonment. Good practice:
- discuss the ending several sessions in advance,
- review progress and what helped,
- plan how the client will keep gains going,
- say how they can return or seek help in future,
- notice feelings about ending — in both of you.

steps.title: Supervision
steps.body: **Clinical supervision** is regular, structured discussion of your casework with an experienced practitioner. It protects clients (quality and safety), supports your learning, and helps you notice your own reactions (sometimes called countertransference) that may affect the work. It is a standard requirement in professional training and many ethics codes expect ongoing supervision or consultation throughout a career.

steps.title: Burnout and vicarious trauma
steps.body:
Helpers are at risk of:
- **Burnout:** emotional exhaustion, cynicism, feeling ineffective — often linked to workload and lack of support.
- **Vicarious (secondary) trauma:** changes in your own beliefs and feelings after repeatedly hearing traumatic stories.

Protective habits: realistic caseloads, supervision, peer support, personal therapy, rest, interests outside work, and clear boundaries around time. Self-care is an ethical duty, because exhausted helpers make more mistakes.

steps.title: Try this: build your referral map
steps.body: List local and national services you could refer to: a psychiatrist or government hospital psychiatry department, a district mental health programme, de-addiction services, women's helpline (181), Childline (1098), Tele-MANAS (14416), legal aid. Note how to contact each and what they offer. Keep it updated.

activity.prompt: Think about your own limits as a helper. Which kinds of problems or people would you find hardest to work with, and what would you do about it? What does your personal 'self-care plan' look like?
activity.hint: Be honest — everyone has limits. Consider: topics close to your own life, signs you're tired, people you can talk to, and how you'll rest.

quiz.q: Which situation most clearly calls for referral to a psychiatrist?
options: Days without sleep, racing thoughts and grandiose beliefs
quiz.why: These could indicate a condition needing medical assessment and possibly medication.

quiz.q: A warm referral includes...
options: explaining why, reducing shame and helping with practical steps
telling the client they are too difficult
quiz.why: A warm referral explains why the referral is being made, reduces shame and helps with practical steps. This increases the chance the client actually gets help.

quiz.q: Clinical supervision mainly serves to...
options: protect clients and support the counsellor's practice
quiz.why: Supervision protects clients and supports the counsellor's practice through quality, safety and learning. It does not replace training or check attendance.

quiz.q: Vicarious trauma refers to...
options: changes in the helper after repeatedly hearing traumatic stories
quiz.why: Vicarious trauma means changes in the helper after repeatedly hearing traumatic stories. It is also called secondary traumatic stress.

quiz.q: In India, who can prescribe psychiatric medication?
quiz.why: Only medical doctors such as psychiatrists can prescribe psychiatric medication, because prescribing requires a medical qualification. Counsellors, social workers and clinical psychologists cannot.

sources: Common counselling ethics codes on competence and referral

questions.q: Which approach did Carl Rogers found?
questions.why: Carl Rogers founded person-centred (client-centred) therapy. Behaviourism, Gestalt and psychoanalysis come from other founders.

questions.q: What does the 'S' in OARS stand for?
questions.why: In OARS, S stands for Summaries, along with Open questions, Affirmations and Reflections.

questions.q: Who can prescribe medication for mental illness in India?
options: A psychiatrist or other medical doctor
questions.why: Only a psychiatrist or other medical doctor can prescribe medication for mental illness in India. Prescribing needs medical registration.

questions.q: 'You've worked so hard to keep your family together' is a(n)...
questions.why: 'You've worked so hard to keep your family together' recognises specific effort and values, which is an affirmation. It is not a question or a summary.

questions.q: Informed consent in counselling includes telling clients about...
questions.why: Informed consent includes telling clients about confidentiality and its limits. They need to know how their information is handled.

questions.q: Which is a protective factor against suicide?
questions.why: Strong supportive relationships protect against suicide through connection and reasons for living. Job loss, isolation and access to lethal means raise risk.

questions.q: Bordin's working alliance is made of...
questions.why: Bordin's working alliance is goals, tasks and bond. Empathy, regard and congruence are Rogers' core conditions, a common mix-up.

questions.q: A client says, 'I want to quit drinking but it's the only way I relax.' The best double-sided reflection is...
options: 'Drinking helps you relax, and you also want to stop.'
questions.why: 'Drinking helps you relax, and you also want to stop' holds both sides of the client's ambivalence, so it is a double-sided reflection. Telling them to quit takes sides.

questions.q: Which law in India creates a duty to report sexual offences against children?
questions.why: The POCSO Act 2012 creates a duty to report sexual offences against children (Section 19). The IT Act, RTE Act and Consumer Protection Act cover other areas.

questions.q: A client has a specific plan, access to means and says they intend to act tonight. The most appropriate response is...
options: Don't leave them alone, call emergency services (112), involve a trusted person and your supervisor
Change the topic to calm them
Ask them to sign a no-suicide contract and leave
questions.why: With a plan, means and intent for tonight, risk is imminent. Don't leave the person alone, call 112, involve a trusted person and your supervisor. A no-suicide contract or waiting a week is unsafe.

questions.q: Which best describes a 'warm referral'?
options: Sending an email without telling the client
Asking the family to decide everything
Explaining reasons, reducing shame and helping the client connect
questions.why: A warm referral explains the reasons, reduces shame and helps the client connect with the new service. This improves follow-through.

questions.q: A counsellor notices she has extended one client's sessions by 20 minutes for several weeks and messages him at night. This is best described as...
options: a sign the client is improving
a pattern of boundary crossings to take to supervision
questions.why: Repeatedly extending one client's sessions and messaging at night is a pattern of boundary crossings. Small crossings can build into violations, so take it to supervision.

questions.q: Why are 'no-suicide contracts' not recommended as a stand-alone intervention?
options: There is little evidence they prevent suicide; collaborative safety plans are preferred
questions.why: There is little evidence that no-suicide contracts prevent suicide, so they are not recommended alone. Collaborative safety plans have stronger support.

questions.q: Which statement about risk assessment is MOST accurate?
options: Risk can be calculated once and filed
Risk is dynamic and should be reviewed as circumstances change
questions.why: Suicide risk is dynamic and changes with events, mood and access to means, so it should be reviewed as circumstances change. A one-time assessment isn't enough.

courses.title: Becoming a psychologist or counsellor in India
courses.summary: Who does what in mental health, the study path from Class 12 to RCI registration as a clinical psychologist, the main fields of psychology and where psychologists work, and how to build real skills and avoid shortcuts. Rules change, so the course shows you how to check current official requirements.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish psychologist, clinical psychologist, counsellor, psychiatrist and psychiatric social worker
Learners can outline the typical academic path to clinical psychology practice in India and the role of the RCI
Learners can describe major fields of psychology and their workplaces
Learners can plan internships, supervised experience and ethical early-career steps

scenes.text: Ishaan, 17, in Jaipur, announces at dinner, 'I want to be a psychologist.' His uncle says, 'So you'll give tablets?' His aunt says, 'So you'll be a counsellor, same thing.'
Ishaan isn't sure. He decides to find out properly.
He learns that psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors and psychiatric social workers often work in the same team but train differently and do different jobs.
At the next dinner he explains it in two minutes. His uncle says, 'So it's a team. Good.'

steps.title: Psychiatrist
steps.body: A **psychiatrist** is a **medical doctor**: MBBS, then a postgraduate degree in psychiatry (MD Psychiatry or DNB). Psychiatrists diagnose mental illnesses, check for physical causes, **prescribe medication**, and may also provide psychotherapy. They are regulated as doctors (National Medical Commission / state medical councils).

steps.title: Clinical psychologist
steps.body: A **clinical psychologist** has studied psychology (BA/BSc and MA/MSc) and then completed an **RCI-recognised professional qualification in clinical psychology**, followed by registration with the **Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI)**. They do psychological assessment (including standardised tests), diagnosis and evidence-based psychotherapy. They do **not** prescribe medication. India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 defines a clinical psychologist by reference to such RCI-recognised qualifications.

steps.title: Counsellor and counselling psychologist
steps.body:
**Counsellors** help people with life problems, stress, relationships, career decisions, adjustment and wellbeing, usually through talking therapies. Many have an MA/MSc in Counselling Psychology or Applied Psychology; others have training in specific settings (schools, addiction, HIV, career guidance).

At present, counselling in India does not have a single national licence in the way medicine does, so quality varies a great deal. Clients and employers increasingly look for a recognised postgraduate degree plus supervised practice.

steps.title: Psychiatric social worker and others
steps.body:
**Psychiatric social workers** typically hold a master's in social work plus specialised training in psychiatric social work. They focus on families, community resources, rehabilitation and social circumstances.

Other team members can include **psychiatric nurses**, **occupational therapists** (daily-living skills and rehabilitation), **special educators**, and **rehabilitation psychologists**.

steps.title: How to check someone's credentials
steps.body:
- Psychiatrist: check medical registration (NMC / state medical council).
- Clinical psychologist: ask for the RCI registration (CRR) number; RCI publishes registered professionals.
- Counsellor: ask about their degree, where they trained, supervised hours and who supervises them.

Be wary of titles like 'certified psychologist' after a short online course — that is not a professional qualification.

activity.prompt: Match each professional with what is typical of their role.
pairs: Medical doctor who can prescribe medication
Talking support for life problems, stress and decisions

quiz.q: Which professional can prescribe medicines for depression?
quiz.why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor and can prescribe medicines for depression. Clinical psychologists, counsellors and social workers cannot prescribe.

quiz.q: In India, clinical psychologists register with...
quiz.why: In India, clinical psychologists register with the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), which regulates their training and registration.

quiz.q: A psychiatrist's typical education is...
quiz.why: A psychiatrist is a doctor with MBBS followed by MD or DNB in Psychiatry. Psychiatry is a medical specialty.

quiz.q: Why should you be cautious about 'certified psychologist' after a short online course?
options: It is not a recognised professional qualification for clinical practice
quiz.why: A short online 'certified psychologist' course isn't a recognised professional qualification for clinical practice. Practice needs recognised degrees and supervised training.

lessons.title: The study path, step by step

scenes.text: Shreya, 16, from Bhopal, wants to be a clinical psychologist working with children. She is in Class 11 with Humanities and Psychology.
With her school counsellor she maps the journey: undergraduate psychology, a master's, then an RCI-recognised clinical training programme with a competitive entrance and interview.
She realises it may take around seven years after Class 12. 'That's long,' she says. The counsellor replies, 'You'll be working with real clients in supervised placements well before the end.'
Shreya bookmarks the RCI website to check which programmes are currently recognised, because rules change.

steps.title: School and undergraduate
steps.body:
- **Class 11–12:** Psychology as a subject helps but is not usually mandatory. Many universities admit students from any stream. Central and many other universities use **CUET** for undergraduate admissions.
- **Undergraduate:** BA or BSc in Psychology (3 years, or 4 years with honours/research under the NEP 2020 framework at many universities). Learn research methods, statistics, developmental, social, cognitive, biological and abnormal psychology.

steps.title: Master's degree
steps.body: MA or MSc in Psychology (2 years), often with a specialisation: **Clinical**, **Counselling**, **Organisational/Industrial**, **Developmental**, **Health**, **Forensic**, etc. This is where you get your first supervised practicum. Many counselling roles (schools, colleges, NGOs, corporate wellbeing) hire at this level.

steps.title: Professional training and RCI registration
steps.body:
To practise as a **clinical psychologist**, you need an **RCI-recognised professional qualification in clinical psychology**. Traditionally this has been the **2-year M.Phil in Clinical Psychology** at RCI-approved institutions (hospitals, medical colleges and universities), with intense supervised clinical work. RCI has been revising and adding recognised programmes, so always check the current list on the RCI website.

After qualifying, you apply for **RCI registration** and receive a registration number. Practising as a clinical psychologist without it is not permitted under the RCI Act.

steps.title: Research and teaching
steps.body: A **PhD** in psychology leads to research and academic careers. To teach in Indian universities and colleges, the **UGC-NET** (or a PhD as per UGC rules) is generally required for Assistant Professor posts. Research careers also exist in public-health projects, NGOs, hospitals and technology companies (for example, user research).

steps.title: Mistakes to avoid
steps.body:
- Assuming a BA Psychology alone qualifies you to do therapy. It does not.
- Joining a 'clinical' programme without checking it is RCI-recognised.
- Ignoring statistics and research methods — they matter in every master's entrance.
- Thinking online certificates replace supervised hours.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your own path as a timeline: your current class, target undergraduate course and entrance, master's specialisation, any professional training, and one backup option (e.g., school counselling or HR). Note one official website you will check each year.

activity.prompt: Arrange a typical route to becoming a registered clinical psychologist in India.
items: Gain entry to an RCI-recognised clinical psychology programme
Complete supervised clinical training and exams
Register with the Rehabilitation Council of India

quiz.q: Which body's recognition matters most for clinical psychology training programmes in India?
quiz.why: The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) recognises clinical psychology training programmes. BCI is for law, NCTE for teaching and AICTE for technical education.

quiz.q: The traditional RCI-recognised professional qualification for clinical psychologists has been...
quiz.why: A 2-year M.Phil with intensive supervised clinical training; check RCI for current programmes.

quiz.q: Is a BA in Psychology alone enough to practise psychotherapy?
options: No — further postgraduate and supervised training is needed
quiz.why: A BA in Psychology is foundational, not professional training. Practising psychotherapy needs postgraduate study and supervised training.

quiz.q: To teach psychology as an Assistant Professor in India you generally need...
options: UGC-NET or PhD as per UGC rules
quiz.why: To teach as an Assistant Professor in India, you generally need UGC-NET or a PhD as per UGC rules. A BA alone or RCI registration is not enough.

sources: Rehabilitation Council of India (official programme list)

lessons.title: Fields of psychology and where they work

scenes.text: Five friends graduate with MA Psychology in Delhi.
Aditi goes into clinical training at a hospital. Faizan joins a school as a counsellor. Grace, from Shillong, joins a tech company's people-analytics team.
Manpreet works with a cricket academy on athletes' focus and pressure. Lakshmi joins an NGO researching maternal mental health in rural Tamil Nadu.
At a reunion they laugh: 'Same degree, completely different jobs.'

steps.title: Major fields
steps.body:
- **Clinical:** assessment and treatment of mental disorders (hospitals, clinics, private practice).
- **Counselling:** life problems, adjustment, relationships, careers (schools, colleges, NGOs, workplaces, online platforms).
- **School / educational:** learning difficulties, behaviour, wellbeing, career guidance.
- **Organisational / industrial (I-O):** hiring, assessment, leadership, culture, wellbeing at work.
- **Health:** behaviour change, chronic illness, pain, adherence.
- **Forensic:** psychology and law — assessments, prisons, juvenile justice, victim support.
- **Sport:** performance, pressure, motivation, injury recovery.
- **Neuropsychology:** brain–behaviour relationships, cognitive assessment after injury or dementia.
- **Developmental, social, cognitive and research psychology.**
- **Applied work** such as user experience (UX) research and behavioural science in policy.

steps.title: Settings
steps.body: Government and private hospitals, district mental health programmes, rehabilitation centres, schools and universities, corporate HR and wellbeing teams, NGOs and public-health projects, helplines and tele-mental-health services, courts and correctional homes, sports academies, research institutes and tech companies.

steps.title: Match field to your strengths
steps.body: Enjoy one-to-one depth and can sit with distress? Clinical or counselling. Love data and systems? I-O, research, UX. Care about justice? Forensic. Love sport? Sport psychology. Interested in children's learning? School/educational. Many people move between fields over a career.

steps.title: Honest realities
steps.body: Training is long and competitive; early salaries in many counselling and NGO roles are modest; emotional load is real. Rewards include meaningful work and growing demand for mental-health services in India. Check job listings in your target field to see current requirements before choosing a specialisation.

cards.back: Assessment, diagnosis and therapy for mental disorders; needs RCI registration in India.
Selection, assessment, leadership, teams and wellbeing at work.
Psychology applied to legal settings: assessments, prisons, juvenile justice.
How brain function relates to behaviour and cognition; assessment after injury, stroke or dementia.
Focus, confidence, pressure, motivation and recovery from injury in athletes.
Learning difficulties, behaviour, wellbeing and career guidance for students.

quiz.q: Which field focuses on hiring, leadership and workplace culture?
quiz.why: Organisational (I-O) psychology applies psychology at work, including hiring, leadership and workplace culture. Forensic, sport and neuropsychology are different fields.

quiz.q: A psychologist assessing memory after a stroke is likely working in...
quiz.why: Assessing memory after a stroke is neuropsychology, which studies the links between brain and behaviour.

quiz.q: Which field works most with courts and prisons?
quiz.why: Forensic psychology applies psychology in legal settings such as courts and prisons.

quiz.q: Which is an honest reality of the field?
options: Early salaries in many counselling roles are modest
quiz.why: Early salaries in many counselling roles are modest. The field is meaningful but demanding, so plan realistically; it has an emotional load and demand exists.

lessons.title: Building real skills and avoiding shortcuts

scenes.text: Sneha, 21, final-year BA Psychology in Kolkata, sees an advert: 'Become a Certified Psychologist in 6 weeks! Start your own practice!'
It costs a lot, and her friends say it's a shortcut. Her professor says, 'Short courses can teach useful skills, but they don't make you a psychologist.'
Sneha instead volunteers at a helpline after their training, does a summer internship at a hospital psychiatry department, and prepares for MA entrances.
Two years later her supervised hours and references help her get into a strong clinical programme.

steps.title: What builds real competence
steps.body:
- **Supervised practice** — the core of learning to help people safely.
- **Internships** at hospitals, NGOs, schools, rehab centres or helplines (most take students for observation and supervised tasks).
- **Research skills** — statistics, reading papers, a small research project or dissertation.
- **Ethics** — knowing confidentiality, consent, boundaries and limits of competence.
- **Personal work** — many trainees find their own therapy helps them understand their reactions.
- **Languages** — counselling in a client's mother tongue is a big advantage in India.

steps.title: Keep a practice log
steps.body: Record each placement: setting, dates, hours, tasks (observation, assessment, co-facilitation), supervisor name and what you learned. Never record identifiable client details in personal notes. A clean log makes applications, references and future registration much easier.

steps.title: Red flags in courses and jobs
steps.body:
- Promises like 'certified psychologist in weeks' or 'open your own clinic without a degree'.
- No information about faculty, supervision or recognition.
- Jobs asking untrained students to do therapy unsupervised.
- Platforms that ask you to diagnose people online after a chat.

Short courses (e.g., in listening skills, mental-health first aid, specific techniques) can be valuable *add-ons* when described honestly.

steps.title: Worked example: asking for an internship
steps.body:
*'Dear Dr. Rao, I'm a second-year BA Psychology student at ___ College. I'm interested in clinical psychology and would be grateful for a chance to observe and assist at your department for four weeks this summer. I have completed coursework in abnormal psychology and research methods, and I understand the importance of confidentiality. I've attached my CV and a letter from my professor. Thank you for considering this.'*

Keep it short, specific, polite, and show you understand professional boundaries.

steps.title: Try this: your next 12 months
steps.body: Pick: one internship or volunteering role, one skill (e.g., statistics software or a second language), one book or course on ethics, and one person in the field to request a 20-minute informational conversation with.

a.text: You're a final-year psychology student. An online platform offers you paid work as a 'therapist' chatting with clients, no supervision needed. What do you do?

choices.label: Accept — it's good money and experience.
choices.feedback: Unsupervised therapy by untrained students can harm clients and you.

choices.label: Decline, and ask your department about supervised placements or helpline volunteering.
choices.feedback: This builds real, safe experience.

b.text: A client tells you they've been planning to end their life. You have no supervisor to call. What now?

choices.label: Give them crisis numbers (112, 14416), stay with them, then contact the platform and leave this role.
choices.feedback: You did the safest thing possible in a bad set-up — but the role itself was unsafe.

choices.label: Tell them to cheer up and end the chat.
choices.feedback: This is dangerous for the client.

c.text: Your department connects you with a helpline that trains volunteers for 40 hours and provides a shift supervisor. Do you also keep a practice log?

choices.label: Yes — dates, hours, tasks and supervisor, with no client details.
choices.feedback: Excellent professional habit.

choices.label: No, it's only volunteering.
choices.feedback: You'll still learn, but a log would make future applications easier.

end1.text: You're building competence safely, with training and supervision — the foundation of a good career.

end2.text: You protected the client, and learned why supervision matters. Seek properly supervised experience next.

end3.text: This could have cost a life. Untrained, unsupervised therapy is unsafe. Try the path again.

quiz.q: What is the core of learning to help people safely?
quiz.why: Supervised practice is the core of learning to help people safely. Videos, books and followers can't replace feedback from a qualified supervisor.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag?
options: 'Certified psychologist in 6 weeks — open your own clinic'
A course listing its faculty and supervision
quiz.why: 'Certified psychologist in 6 weeks' is a red flag because no short course makes someone a psychologist. A master's with practicum or a listed faculty and supervision are good signs.

quiz.q: What should a practice log NOT include?
quiz.why: A practice log should not include identifiable client details, to protect confidentiality. Dates, hours, tasks and the supervisor's name are fine.

quiz.q: Why is speaking a client's mother tongue valuable in India?
options: People often express emotions more fully in their first language
quiz.why: People often express emotions more fully in their first language, so speaking a client's mother tongue helps. It isn't required by law.

questions.q: Which mental-health professional is a medical doctor?
questions.why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor, with MBBS plus MD or DNB in Psychiatry. Social workers, counsellors and clinical psychologists are not doctors.

questions.q: RCI stands for...
questions.why: RCI stands for Rehabilitation Council of India, which regulates rehabilitation professions including clinical psychology.
