questions.q: Which field studies psychology at work?
questions.why: Organisational (I-O) psychology studies psychology at work. Sport, forensic and neuro are other areas.

questions.q: A typical master's in psychology in India lasts...
questions.why: A typical master's in psychology (MA or MSc) in India lasts 2 years.

questions.q: Many central universities use which test for undergraduate admission?
questions.why: Many central universities use CUET-UG for undergraduate admission. CAT is for management, GATE for engineering and NEET-PG for medical postgraduates.

questions.q: Which professional is most associated with families, community resources and rehabilitation?
questions.why: Psychiatric social workers focus on families, community resources and rehabilitation, bringing in the social context.

questions.q: How can you verify a clinical psychologist's credentials?
options: Ask for their RCI registration number
questions.why: You can verify a clinical psychologist by asking for their RCI registration number. RCI maintains a register.

questions.q: Clinical psychologists in India typically...
questions.why: Clinical psychologists in India typically do psychological assessment and psychotherapy. They do not prescribe medicines.

questions.q: Why check the RCI website each year when planning?
options: Recognised programmes and rules can change
questions.why: Check the RCI website each year because recognised programmes and rules can change. Regulators update requirements.

questions.q: Which law defines 'clinical psychologist' with reference to RCI-recognised qualifications?
questions.why: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines 'clinical psychologist' by reference to RCI-recognised qualifications. The other Acts do not.

questions.q: An unsupervised student offered paid online 'therapy' should...
questions.why: An unsupervised student should decline paid online 'therapy' and seek supervised placements. Unsupervised practice is unsafe and unethical.

questions.q: A student wants to work in tech using psychology. Which path fits best?
options: UX research / I-O with strong research methods
questions.why: UX research or I-O with strong research methods uses psychology in tech, for example in people analytics and user studies. School counselling and psychiatry are not tech paths.

questions.q: Which combination best prepares an applicant for a competitive clinical training programme?
options: Strong grades, research methods, supervised placements, a practice log and references
questions.why: Competitive clinical programmes value strong grades, research methods, supervised placements, a practice log and references. Certificates or followers alone don't show this.

careers-sexual-health-pro.title: Sexual health practice: a clinical refresher

courses.title: Foundations: response models, classification and contributors
courses.summary: Revisit the classic and modern models of sexual response, how ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR classify sexual dysfunctions, the biopsychosocial contributors clinicians must screen for, and how sexual health changes across the lifespan. Clinical and non-explicit. Educational overview — always consult current official classification texts and guidelines.

scenes.text: In a Mumbai sexual-medicine clinic, Dr. Nandini sees Meera and Arvind, married 12 years. Meera says, 'I never feel like it out of nowhere anymore. Something must be wrong with me.'
Dr. Nandini draws two diagrams: a straight line (desire, then arousal, then orgasm) and a circle where emotional intimacy and willingness can come first and desire can follow arousal.
Meera recognises herself in the circle. Once she is relaxed and feels close to Arvind, interest often develops. 'So it's responsive, not absent?'
The reframing reduces her distress considerably before any specific treatment begins, and the couple focus on the conditions that help.

steps.title: Masters & Johnson (1966): the four-phase cycle
steps.body:
William Masters and Virginia Johnson, in *Human Sexual Response* (1966), described a laboratory-observed **four-phase cycle**:
- **Excitement** — physiological arousal begins (vasocongestion, increased heart rate).
- **Plateau** — heightened arousal is maintained.
- **Orgasm** — the peak with rhythmic muscular contractions.
- **Resolution** — return to baseline; many men experience a **refractory period**.

**Contribution:** first large systematic physiological study; normalised sexual function as a legitimate scientific topic; led to their therapy programme (*Human Sexual Inadequacy*, 1970) and **sensate focus**.

**Limitations:** physiological and genital focus; desire is assumed rather than described; linear; volunteer sample not representative.

steps.title: Kaplan's triphasic model
steps.body:
Helen Singer Kaplan (1970s) argued that **desire** needed its own place and proposed a three-phase model: **desire → excitement (arousal) → orgasm**. Her work on desire disorders (*Disorders of Sexual Desire*, 1979) helped shape the phase-based classification introduced in **DSM-III (1980)**, in which dysfunctions were organised by phase.

**Limitation:** still linear and assumes that spontaneous desire *precedes* arousal, which does not fit many people's experience, especially in long-term relationships.

steps.title: Basson's circular (intimacy-based) model
steps.body:
Rosemary Basson (2000) proposed a **circular model**, initially to describe many women's experience:
- A person may begin from **sexual neutrality**, with motivations such as wanting **emotional closeness**, intimacy or to please a partner.
- With appropriate context and stimulation, **arousal** develops; **responsive desire** can then emerge.
- Emotional and physical **satisfaction** reinforces intimacy and motivation for the future.
- **Spontaneous desire** can also occur, but is not required for a healthy response.

**Clinical implications:** lack of spontaneous desire is not automatically a disorder; context, relationship, distraction, fatigue and emotional safety matter; treatment often targets conditions for responsive desire. Later research suggests responsive desire is also common in many men and in long-term relationships, and the phases overlap considerably.

steps.title: Worked example: using the models in session
steps.body:
A patient reports 'no desire'. Clarifying questions informed by the models:
- *Spontaneous vs responsive:* 'Once you're relaxed and close to your partner, does interest sometimes develop?'
- *Context:* 'What gets in the way — tiredness, privacy, worries, conflict, pain?'
- *Satisfaction:* 'When intimacy happens, how do you feel afterwards?'
- *Distress:* 'Is this a concern for you, for your partner, or both?'

Psychoeducation about responsive desire alone can reduce distress for some patients — a good example of the 'Limited Information' level of PLISSIT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the linear model as the only 'normal' sequence.
- Pathologising low spontaneous desire without assessing distress, context or the relationship.
- Assuming one model applies by gender; use models as lenses, not boxes.
- Forgetting that research samples behind these models were largely Western; cultural context shapes experience and expression.

quiz.why: Masters & Johnson described four phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution (EPOR), from Human Sexual Response (1966).

options: spontaneous desire must always precede arousal
responsive desire can emerge after arousal and is not in itself a disorder

lessons.title: Classification: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 in overview

scenes.text: Dr. Chidi Okafor, a psychiatrist in Lagos, and Dr. Sana Iqbal, a urologist in Delhi, review a case together online: a 45-year-old man with erection difficulties for eight months, type 2 diabetes and recent work stress.
Dr. Okafor uses DSM-5-TR terms; Dr. Iqbal's hospital codes with ICD. 'Are we even describing the same thing?' she jokes.
They notice ICD-11 lets them record the dysfunction and add qualifiers for both a medical condition and psychological factors, instead of choosing 'organic' or 'psychogenic'.
Their joint plan addresses diabetes control, cardiovascular risk, medication and stress together.

steps.title: DSM-5-TR: the diagnoses
steps.body:
DSM-5 (2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022) lists these **sexual dysfunctions**:
- Delayed Ejaculation
- Erectile Disorder
- Female Orgasmic Disorder
- Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder (desire and arousal merged in DSM-5)
- Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (dyspareunia and vaginismus merged in DSM-5)
- Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder
- Premature (Early) Ejaculation
- Substance/Medication-Induced Sexual Dysfunction
- Other Specified and Unspecified Sexual Dysfunction

steps.title: DSM general criteria and specifiers
steps.body:
Across most diagnoses DSM requires:
- symptoms persisting for a **minimum of approximately 6 months** (not required for substance/medication-induced dysfunction),
- for many diagnoses, occurring on all or almost all (about 75–100%) occasions,
- **clinically significant distress** in the individual,
- not better explained by a non-sexual mental disorder, **severe relationship distress (e.g., partner violence)** or other significant stressors, nor solely by a substance or medical condition.

**Specifiers:** lifelong vs acquired; generalised vs situational; severity (mild, moderate, severe). DSM also asks clinicians to consider partner factors, relationship factors, individual vulnerability, cultural/religious factors and medical factors.

steps.title: ICD-11: a new chapter
steps.body:
ICD-11 (in effect from **1 January 2022**) created **Chapter 17: Conditions related to sexual health**, separate from both mental disorders and diseases of the genitourinary system. It includes:
- **Sexual dysfunctions:** hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction; sexual arousal dysfunctions (female sexual arousal dysfunction, male erectile dysfunction); orgasmic dysfunctions (e.g., anorgasmia); ejaculatory dysfunctions (male early ejaculation, male delayed ejaculation).
- **Sexual pain disorders:** sexual pain-penetration disorder.
- **Gender incongruence** (moved out of the mental disorders chapter).

A key change: ICD-11 **abandons the split between 'organic' and 'non-organic'**. Instead, clinicians add **aetiological qualifiers** — e.g., associated with a medical condition, with psychological or behavioural factors, with use of a psychoactive substance or medication, with lack of knowledge or experience, with relationship factors, or with cultural factors. Several can apply at once.

steps.title: What is classified elsewhere
steps.body: In ICD-11, **compulsive sexual behaviour disorder** sits within impulse control disorders, and **paraphilic disorders** remain in the mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders chapter. Distinguish problems a person finds distressing from variation in sexual interest or frequency that is not a disorder.

steps.title: Worked example: classifying the case
steps.body:
45-year-old man, erection difficulties on most occasions for 8 months, distressed, type 2 diabetes, work stress, no medication cause identified.
- **DSM-5-TR:** Erectile Disorder, acquired, generalised, severity per assessment; note medical factors (diabetes) and stressors.
- **ICD-11:** Male erectile dysfunction, with qualifiers *associated with a medical condition* and *associated with psychological or behavioural factors*.

The integrated ICD-11 approach mirrors clinical reality: most presentations are multifactorial.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Diagnosing without **distress** — a difference in frequency or interest that does not trouble the person is not a disorder.
- Missing **partner violence** or coercion, which DSM explicitly flags.
- Using outdated terms ('frigidity', 'impotence') that are stigmatising and imprecise.
- Quoting criteria from memory — always check the current official text for exact wording before formal diagnosis or research.

options: a new chapter on conditions related to sexual health

quiz.q: ICD-11 replaced the organic/non-organic split with...
options: aetiological qualifiers that can be combined
quiz.why: ICD-11 replaced the organic versus non-organic split with aetiological qualifiers that can be combined. This reflects multifactorial causes.

quiz.q: Which is required for most DSM sexual dysfunction diagnoses?
options: Clinically significant distress in the individual
quiz.why: Most DSM sexual dysfunction diagnoses require clinically significant distress in the individual. A partner's complaint or lab results alone are not enough.

lessons.title: Biopsychosocial contributors, including medications

scenes.text: Kavitha, 34, a teacher in Coimbatore, started an SSRI for depression four months ago. Her mood is much better, but she notices sexual changes and is thinking of stopping the tablets secretly.
Her psychiatrist, Dr. Raghavan, routinely asks every patient on antidepressants about sexual side effects. Kavitha is relieved: 'I was too embarrassed to bring it up.'
They discuss options — timing, dose review, or switching — without stopping abruptly, and she agrees to a plan.
Kavitha stays on treatment. 'If he hadn't asked, I would have stopped and probably relapsed.'

steps.title: Biological contributors
steps.body:
- **Vascular:** hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking, diabetes, atherosclerosis. Erectile dysfunction (ED) shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease and can **precede coronary symptoms by several years** — an opportunity for cardiovascular screening.
- **Neurological:** diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, pelvic surgery.
- **Endocrine:** hypogonadism, thyroid disorders, hyperprolactinaemia, menopause-related oestrogen decline.
- **Pelvic and genital:** infections, dermatological conditions, endometriosis, vestibulodynia, pelvic floor dysfunction, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, prostate conditions.
- **Systemic:** chronic kidney or liver disease, cancer and its treatment, chronic pain, fatigue, sleep disorders.

steps.title: Medications and substances
steps.body:
Commonly implicated:
- **SSRIs and SNRIs:** delayed or absent orgasm, reduced desire, arousal difficulties. Very common and under-reported.
- **Antipsychotics** (especially those raising prolactin).
- **Some antihypertensives** (e.g., thiazide diuretics, some older beta-blockers).
- **5-alpha-reductase inhibitors** (for prostate enlargement), **anti-androgens**.
- **Opioids** (can lower testosterone), some anti-epileptics.
- **Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and other substances.**

Never advise patients to stop prescribed medication on their own; liaise with the prescriber about options such as dose review or switching.

steps.title: Psychological, relational and cultural contributors
steps.body:
- **Individual:** depression, anxiety, **performance anxiety and 'spectatoring'** (monitoring oneself during intimacy — a concept from Masters & Johnson), body-image concerns, trauma history, guilt or shame, low sexual knowledge.
- **Relational:** conflict, poor communication, mismatch in desire, partner's own sexual difficulty, infidelity, lack of privacy (common in shared or joint-family homes), coercion or violence.
- **Cultural and religious:** beliefs about sex, marriage expectations, myths (e.g., about semen loss or virginity), stigma around seeking help.

The **predisposing, precipitating and maintaining factors** framework (the '3 Ps') is a useful way to organise a formulation.

steps.title: Worked example: a 3P formulation
steps.body:
Case: 29-year-old man, situational early ejaculation after marriage.
- **Predisposing:** limited sex education; strong performance pressure from peers' stories; anxious temperament.
- **Precipitating:** first experiences with spouse under pressure of family expectations and little privacy.
- **Maintaining:** spectatoring, avoidance, the couple not discussing it, internet myths, an unregulated 'herbal' product.

The plan follows from the formulation: education, couple communication, behavioural strategies, evidence-based medical options, stopping unregulated products.

steps.title: Screening habits
steps.body:
- Ask about sexual function at baseline **before** starting medicines known to affect it, and again at follow-up.
- Ask about sexual concerns in diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney, cancer, pelvic, spinal and mental-health care.
- Use a normalising lead-in: *'Many people with diabetes notice changes in sexual function. Is that something you've experienced?'*
- Validated questionnaires (e.g., IIEF for erectile function, FSFI for female sexual function) can support but not replace clinical assessment.

options: It shares risk factors and can precede coronary symptoms by several years
It only occurs after heart attacks
quiz.why: ED shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease and can precede coronary symptoms by several years. So it is an opportunity for cardiovascular risk assessment.

quiz.why: SSRIs are the medication class most commonly linked to delayed orgasm, a very common but under-reported effect.

quiz.why: Spectatoring is anxious self-monitoring during intimacy, a concept from Masters & Johnson. It maintains performance anxiety.

quiz.q: The '3 Ps' formulation includes...
quiz.why: The 3 Ps formulation covers predisposing, precipitating and maintaining factors. It is a standard framework for understanding a problem.

quiz.q: A patient wants to stop an antidepressant because of sexual side effects. You should...
options: liaise with the prescriber about options and avoid abrupt stopping
quiz.why: Liaise with the prescriber about options and avoid abrupt stopping, because stopping suddenly risks relapse and discontinuation symptoms.

lessons.title: Sexual health across the lifespan

scenes.text: On Monday, a family doctor in Bengaluru, Dr. Fernandes, sees Rohit, 17, worried that nightfall (wet dreams) is 'making him weak'. She explains it is normal and harmless.
On Wednesday, Ayesha, 31, four months after childbirth and breastfeeding, mentions discomfort and low interest and assumed this was something to stay quiet about.
On Friday, Mrs. Lakshmi, 68, and her husband ask whether intimacy is 'still appropriate at our age'. Dr. Fernandes says, 'Absolutely — let's talk about what would help.'
Each consultation needed a different conversation, but the same respect, accurate information and a chance to ask.

steps.title: Adolescence
steps.body:
Common concerns: puberty timing, nocturnal emissions, masturbation myths, menstruation, body image, orientation and identity questions, contraception and STI knowledge, consent, online pornography and sexting.

Clinical approach: confidential, age-appropriate, non-judgemental, evidence-based education (UNESCO ITGSE 2018). In India, the **POCSO Act, 2012** sets 18 as the age of consent and imposes **mandatory reporting** of sexual offences involving minors — explain limits of confidentiality honestly at the start.

steps.title: Pregnancy and postpartum
steps.body:
- Desire and comfort vary across pregnancy; most couples can continue intimacy unless advised otherwise by their obstetrician (e.g., certain bleeding or placental conditions).
- Postpartum: fatigue, perineal healing, caesarean recovery, pelvic floor changes, low mood, body-image changes and **breastfeeding-related low oestrogen** can cause dryness and discomfort.
- Screen for **postpartum depression**.
- Pelvic health physiotherapy helps with pelvic floor problems and pain.
- Discuss contraception — breastfeeding is not reliable contraception unless specific criteria (LAM) are met.

steps.title: Midlife and menopause
steps.body:
- **Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM):** dryness, discomfort, urinary symptoms related to oestrogen decline. It tends to be **progressive** without treatment, unlike hot flushes, which often improve over time.
- Options include vaginal moisturisers and lubricants, and **local vaginal oestrogen** (prescribed after medical assessment); systemic hormone therapy decisions are individual.
- In men, **testosterone declines gradually** with age; true hypogonadism needs symptoms plus repeated morning blood tests. Erections may need more direct stimulation and refractory periods lengthen.
- Chronic conditions and medications become more common contributors.

steps.title: Older age, illness and disability
steps.body:
Many older adults remain interested in intimacy; health, partner availability and opportunity are bigger barriers than age itself. Ageist assumptions ('not at your age') stop patients asking.

After **myocardial infarction**, cardiology guidance generally supports resuming sexual activity once the person can manage moderate exertion without symptoms — individualised by the treating team. After **cancer, stroke or spinal cord injury**, the **EX-PLISSIT** model is particularly useful. People with **intellectual or physical disabilities** have the same rights to sexual health education and care, with attention to consent capacity and safeguarding.

steps.title: Worked example: opening the conversation with an older couple
steps.body:
*'Many couples your age have questions about intimacy, and it's a normal part of health. Some people find things like arthritis, medicines or dryness make it harder. Would it be helpful to talk about what you've noticed?'*

This normalises, gives permission, mentions common contributors and leaves the choice with them.

steps.title: Common clinician mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming adolescents are not sexually active, or that older adults are not.
- Assuming every patient is heterosexual, married or monogamous.
- Not asking postpartum patients because 'they'll bring it up'.
- Attributing everything to age without checking medications, mood and treatable causes.

activity.prompt: Questions patients often hesitate to ask — and calm, accurate answers.

items.a: No. Nocturnal emissions are a normal part of puberty and adulthood. They do not cause weakness or illness.

items.q: Is it normal to have less interest after having a baby?
items.a: Yes, very common — fatigue, healing, hormonal changes with breastfeeding and new responsibilities all play a part. Discomfort can be treated, and mood should be checked. Speak to your doctor or a pelvic health physiotherapist.

items.q: Is intimacy appropriate in older age?
items.a: Yes. Many people value intimacy throughout life. Changes such as dryness or slower arousal are common and often manageable with medical advice.

items.q: After menopause, does dryness go away on its own?
items.a: Genitourinary symptoms often persist or progress without treatment. Moisturisers, lubricants and, after medical assessment, local vaginal oestrogen can help.

items.q: After a heart attack, when can I resume sexual activity?
items.a: Many people can once they manage moderate exertion without symptoms, but your cardiologist should individualise this — especially regarding certain medicines.

quiz.q: Which statement about genitourinary syndrome of menopause is accurate?
options: It tends to be progressive without treatment
It always resolves within a year
quiz.why: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause tends to be progressive without treatment. Unlike hot flushes it often persists, though effective treatments exist.

quiz.q: Breastfeeding can cause vaginal dryness because...
options: it is associated with low oestrogen
quiz.why: Breastfeeding is associated with low oestrogen, which can cause vaginal dryness. It does not raise oestrogen or cause infection.

quiz.q: In India, the age of consent under POCSO is...
quiz.why: POCSO defines a child as anyone under 18, so for its purposes the age is 18.

quiz.q: Diagnosis of male hypogonadism generally requires...
options: symptoms plus repeated morning testosterone tests
quiz.why: Diagnosing male hypogonadism needs symptoms plus repeated morning testosterone tests. Age alone or a single random test risks over-diagnosis.

quiz.q: Which is a common clinician mistake?
options: Assuming older adults are not sexually active
quiz.why: Assuming older adults are not sexually active is a common clinician mistake. This ageism stops patients getting help.

AHA scientific statement on sexual activity and cardiovascular disease (2012)

questions.q: Who described the excitement–plateau–orgasm–resolution cycle?
questions.why: Masters & Johnson described the excitement–plateau–orgasm–resolution cycle in Human Sexual Response (1966). Kaplan and Basson proposed later models.

questions.q: ICD-11 came into effect in...
questions.why: ICD-11 came into effect on 1 January 2022.

questions.q: Which medication class is most often linked with delayed orgasm?
questions.why: SSRIs are most often linked to delayed orgasm. Antacids, paracetamol and iron do not typically cause it.

questions.q: Which model emphasises intimacy motivation and responsive desire?
questions.why: Basson's model emphasises intimacy motivation and responsive desire. Kaplan added desire as a phase, and Masters & Johnson described the linear cycle.

questions.q: DSM-5 merged dyspareunia and vaginismus into...
questions.why: DSM-5 merged dyspareunia and vaginismus into Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (GPPPD).

questions.q: The '3 Ps' are...
questions.why: The 3 Ps are predisposing, precipitating and maintaining factors, a formulation framework.

questions.q: Which DSM specifier describes onset?
questions.why: The DSM onset specifier is lifelong versus acquired. Lifelong means present since the first sexual experiences.

questions.q: ICD-11 handles aetiology by...
options: requiring a single organic or psychogenic label
questions.why: ICD-11 allows multiple aetiological qualifiers instead of a single organic or psychogenic label. This reflects the multifactorial reality.

questions.q: ED can precede coronary symptoms by...
questions.why: ED can precede coronary symptoms by several years because of shared vascular pathology.

questions.q: Which is classified in ICD-11 Chapter 17?
questions.why: Paraphilic and compulsive sexual behaviour disorders are in the mental disorders chapter.

questions.q: DSM excludes a sexual dysfunction diagnosis when the problem is better explained by...
options: severe relationship distress such as partner violence
questions.why: DSM excludes a sexual dysfunction diagnosis when the problem is better explained by severe relationship distress such as partner violence. Always screen for violence and coercion.

questions.q: A woman reports she rarely feels spontaneous desire but enjoys intimacy once it starts and is not distressed. The most appropriate conclusion is...
options: this may fit responsive desire; without distress it is not a disorder
questions.why: Rarely feeling spontaneous desire but enjoying intimacy once it starts, without distress, fits responsive desire. DSM requires distress, so it isn't a disorder.

questions.q: Why did DSM-III's phase-based classification draw criticism later?
options: It assumed a linear sequence that does not fit many people's experience
questions.why: Linear models were challenged by research supporting overlapping and responsive patterns.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man on a nitrate for angina asks about ED treatment. The key safety point is...
options: PDE5 inhibitors are safe with nitrates
He is too old for treatment
PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates due to risk of severe hypotension
questions.why: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates because of the risk of severe hypotension. Coordinate with cardiology and don't prescribe both.
