lessons.title: Taking a sexual history

scenes.text: In a district hospital in Bhopal, Dr. Imran sees Suresh, 52, for diabetes review. Suresh's wife is in the room. Suresh mentions 'some other problem' and then goes silent.
Dr. Imran asks, 'Would it be all right if we spoke privately for a few minutes? I do that with all patients.' The wife steps out.
He says, 'Many men with diabetes notice changes in erections. Is that something you've experienced?' After a long pause, Suresh nods: 'For a year. I thought it was age.'
A structured history follows — onset, situations, medications, mood, relationship, cardiovascular risk. Suresh leaves with a plan and, for the first time, hope.

steps.title: Setting and permission
steps.body:
- **Privacy:** offer time alone with every patient as routine policy, so no one feels singled out. Consider chaperones and interpreters thoughtfully — family members should not be default interpreters for sexual history.
- **Permission:** 'I'd like to ask some questions about your sexual health, as it's part of overall health. Is that all right?'
- **Confidentiality:** explain what stays confidential and the legal limits (e.g., POCSO for minors; serious risk of harm).
- **Language:** use clear, neutral, medically accurate words; check the patient's own terms and mirror respectful ones. Avoid euphemisms that cause confusion and avoid slang.

steps.title: Normalising and non-assuming questions
steps.body:
- **Normalising statements** reduce shame: 'Many people with X notice Y...'
- **Do not assume** marital status, orientation, gender of partners, monogamy or activity level: 'Are you currently in a relationship? With men, women, or both?' or 'Tell me about your partner or partners.'
- **Ask about safety:** 'Do you ever feel pressured or unsafe in your relationship?'
- **Ladder from general to specific**, and explain why you are asking specific questions.

steps.title: Domains to cover
steps.body:
**The presenting concern:** what exactly, onset (sudden/gradual), duration, **lifelong vs acquired**, **generalised vs situational** (e.g., with partner vs alone; morning erections preserved?), severity, the person's and partner's distress, what they have tried (including unregulated products), goals.

**Medical:** chronic illness (diabetes, CVD, hypertension, thyroid, neurological), surgery and pelvic trauma, obstetric/gynaecological history, urinary symptoms, pain.

**Medications and substances:** prescribed, over-the-counter, herbal, alcohol, tobacco, other drugs.

**Psychological:** mood, anxiety, stress, body image, trauma, beliefs.

**Relational and cultural:** relationship quality, communication, privacy, family pressure, religious or cultural considerations.

**Sexual and reproductive health screen (CDC's '5 Ps'):** Partners, Practices, Protection from STIs, Past STI history, Pregnancy intention/prevention.

steps.title: Worked example: clarifying an ED complaint
steps.body:
- 'When did you first notice this? Did it start suddenly or gradually?'
- 'Does it happen every time, or only in some situations?'
- 'Do you still sometimes wake with erections?' (preserved nocturnal/morning erections and situational patterns suggest psychological contributors are significant, though organic factors may still exist)
- 'Any chest pain or breathlessness on exertion?' (cardiovascular screen)
- 'Which medicines do you take, including for chest pain?' (nitrates — safety)
- 'How is this affecting you and your relationship?'
- 'What would you like to be different?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the history in front of family members by default.
- Visible discomfort, laughter or moral comments.
- Asking only about penetrative intercourse, missing other aspects of intimacy and concerns.
- Missing coercion, violence or trafficking indicators.
- Not asking about unregulated 'sex tonics' — some products have been found to contain undeclared prescription drugs.
- Rushing to prescribe without assessing cardiovascular risk and partner factors.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write three normalising lead-in sentences for your own clinical setting (for example: diabetes clinic, antenatal clinic, psychiatry follow-up). Practise them aloud until they sound natural.

a.text: A 26-year-old woman attends with her mother-in-law for 'not conceiving after one year of marriage'. You suspect there may be more to discuss. What do you do first?

choices.label: Explain that you see all patients alone for part of the visit and ask the mother-in-law to wait outside.
choices.feedback: Routine private time protects autonomy and safety without singling anyone out.

choices.label: Take the full history with the mother-in-law present.
choices.feedback: The patient may not feel free to speak about intimacy, pain or safety.

b.text: Alone, she says quietly that intercourse has not been possible because of pain and fear. How do you continue?

choices.label: Thank her, normalise that this is a common and treatable concern, and ask permission to ask more questions.
choices.feedback: Permission plus normalising builds trust.

choices.label: Tell her she just needs to relax.
choices.feedback: Dismissive and inaccurate; genito-pelvic pain needs assessment.

c.text: The patient says little; the mother-in-law answers for her. You sense discomfort. How do you recover?

choices.label: Explain the routine private part of the consultation and continue alone.
choices.feedback: Good recovery.

d.text: You explore onset (since marriage — lifelong), any pain with medical examinations or tampons, relationship, feelings of safety, beliefs, and her goals. What is an appropriate next step?

choices.label: Offer gentle, consented examination only when she is ready, and discuss a multidisciplinary plan: education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, psychological support and graded exposure.
choices.feedback: Patient-led pacing and evidence-based multidisciplinary care.

choices.label: Insist on an immediate internal examination.
choices.feedback: Forcing examination can be traumatic and reinforce fear; consent and readiness come first.

e.text: This response risks harm and loss of trust. Pause and return to a permission-based approach.

choices.label: Apologise, re-explain, and ask permission to understand more.
choices.feedback: Repair is possible when done sincerely.

end1.text: You created privacy, gave permission, took a structured history and planned consent-based, multidisciplinary care.

quiz.q: Why should time alone be offered to every patient routinely?
options: So no one feels singled out and patients can speak freely, including about safety
quiz.why: Offering time alone routinely means no one feels singled out, and patients can speak freely, including about safety. It protects autonomy and allows disclosure.

quiz.q: Which is a normalising statement?
options: Many people with diabetes notice changes in sexual function — have you?
quiz.why: 'Many people with diabetes notice changes in sexual function — have you?' normalises the issue, reducing shame and inviting disclosure. The other statements shame or dismiss.

quiz.q: CDC's '5 Ps' include Partners, Practices, Protection from STIs, Past STI history and...
quiz.why: The CDC's 5 Ps are Partners, Practices, Protection from STIs, Past STI history and Pregnancy intention or prevention.

quiz.q: Which question helps distinguish situational from generalised ED?
options: Do you still sometimes wake with erections?
quiz.why: Preserved nocturnal or morning erections suggest the physical mechanism works, pointing to significant psychological contributors. It helps separate situational from generalised ED.

quiz.q: Why ask about unregulated 'sex tonics'?
options: Some have contained undeclared drugs and can interact or delay proper care
quiz.why: Ask about unregulated 'sex tonics' because some have contained undeclared drugs, can interact with medicines and may delay proper care.

sources: CDC, A Guide to Taking a Sexual History

scenes.text: Esther, an oncology nurse in Manchester, cares for Priya, 44, who has finished treatment for breast cancer. Priya mentions she 'feels like a different person'.
Esther says, 'Many people notice changes in intimacy and body image after treatment. Would it help to talk about that?' Priya, surprised, says yes.
Esther gives accurate information about treatment-related dryness and fatigue, suggests specific practical steps, and reviews at the next visit.
When Priya's distress about body image remains high, Esther refers her to a psychosexual therapist. 'You opened the door,' Priya tells her.

steps.title: PLISSIT (Annon, 1976)
steps.body:
Jack Annon's model has four progressive levels:
- **P — Permission:** signal that sexual concerns are a legitimate health topic; give permission to talk, and reassure that thoughts, feelings or behaviours within healthy, consensual limits are normal.
- **LI — Limited Information:** provide accurate, relevant facts (e.g., effects of a medicine, normal variation, responsive desire).
- **SS — Specific Suggestions:** tailored, practical advice after assessment (e.g., lubricants, timing medicines, communication exercises, a behavioural technique).
- **IT — Intensive Therapy:** referral for specialist treatment (psychosexual therapy, couple therapy, sexual medicine, trauma therapy).

Most concerns can be addressed at the first two or three levels by trained generalists. Each level requires more skill, knowledge and time.

steps.title: EX-PLISSIT (Taylor & Davis, 2007)
steps.body:
The **Extended PLISSIT** model was developed for people with chronic illness and disability. Key differences:
- **Permission-giving underpins every level**, not only the first — e.g., permission to ask more, to say no, to come back later.
- Each interaction ends with **review**, and the practitioner engages in **reflection** on their own practice.
- Practitioners are encouraged to **challenge their assumptions** (about age, disability, orientation, culture).
- The model is explicitly cyclical: patients may move back and forth between levels.

steps.title: Worked example: four levels, one patient
steps.body:
Patient: 58-year-old man after prostate surgery, worried about erections.
- **P:** 'Many men have questions about erections after this surgery. It's a normal and important topic.'
- **LI:** 'Nerve recovery after surgery can take many months; changes are common and there are treatments.'
- **SS:** 'Your urologist can discuss a rehabilitation plan; some men use tablets, others use a vacuum device. Let's book that discussion.'
- **IT:** If distress, relationship strain or low mood are significant, refer to psychosexual or couple therapy alongside medical care.
- **EX-PLISSIT:** 'Is it all right if I ask about this again next visit?' then review and reflect.

steps.title: Knowing your level
steps.body: Work within your training and scope of registration. A general nurse or physiotherapist may comfortably provide P and LI; SS needs topic-specific competence; IT requires specialist training and supervision. Knowing where to refer is part of competence.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Skipping P and LI and jumping straight to prescriptions.
- Giving Specific Suggestions without adequate assessment (e.g., missing pain, coercion or a medical cause).
- Staying at LI for months when Intensive Therapy is needed.
- Assuming people with disabilities or older adults are not interested in sexual health.

activity.prompt: Which PLISSIT level best fits each response?

items.text: 'Many people have questions about intimacy after a heart attack — it's fine to ask.'
'This blood-pressure medicine can sometimes affect sexual function.'
'A water-based lubricant may help with dryness; let's review in a month.'
Referral to a psychosexual therapist for long-standing trauma-related difficulties
'Responsive desire is common in long relationships.'
Structured couple therapy using a graded programme
'Your concerns are a normal part of health care here.'
'Try discussing the timing of your medicine with your doctor.'

quiz.q: PLISSIT was proposed by...
quiz.why: PLISSIT was proposed by Jack Annon in 1976.

quiz.q: The key feature of EX-PLISSIT is that...
options: permission-giving underpins every level, with review and reflection
quiz.why: EX-PLISSIT (Taylor & Davis, 2007) keeps permission-giving at every level and adds review and reflection. It does not remove the permission level.

quiz.q: 'Specific Suggestions' should follow...
options: adequate assessment of the individual's situation
quiz.why: Specific Suggestions should follow adequate assessment of the individual's situation, so they are tailored and safe. Generic online advice may not fit.

quiz.q: Which level involves referral to a specialist?
quiz.why: Intensive Therapy is the PLISSIT level involving specialist referral, used for complex or persistent concerns.

quiz.q: EX-PLISSIT was developed particularly for...
options: people with chronic illness and disability
quiz.why: EX-PLISSIT was developed particularly for people with chronic illness and disability, though it applies more broadly.

lessons.title: Erectile and ejaculatory concerns: evidence-based overview

scenes.text: Kunal, 33, an engineer in Indore, has been buying an expensive 'herbal tonic' online for early ejaculation for a year. It hasn't helped, and he feels he's 'not a real man'.
A urologist, Dr. Bhatt, takes a full history: lifelong pattern, high anxiety, no ED, no medical illness, and his wife is supportive but frustrated by his avoidance.
Dr. Bhatt explains the condition plainly, offers a combined plan — behavioural techniques, an evidence-based medicine option, and a couple session — and asks him to stop the unregulated product.
Three months later Kunal reports better control and, more importantly, less fear. 'The shame was the bigger problem,' he says.

steps.title: Erectile dysfunction: assessment
steps.body:
- Full history (as in lesson 1), including **cardiovascular risk**, medications (especially **nitrates**), mood and relationship.
- Examination as indicated; blood pressure, BMI, genital and secondary sexual characteristics.
- Investigations commonly include **fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile**, and **morning total testosterone** where hypogonadism is suspected; others as indicated.
- Validated tools (e.g., IIEF-5) to track severity.
- Consider cardiovascular evaluation, as ED may be an early marker of vascular disease.

steps.title: Erectile dysfunction: treatment overview
steps.body:
- **Lifestyle and risk factors:** physical activity, weight management, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol, optimising diabetes and blood pressure.
- **Address contributors:** medication review with the prescriber, treat depression/anxiety, relationship factors.
- **PDE5 inhibitors** (e.g., sildenafil, tadalafil) are first-line oral therapy for many. They require sexual stimulation to work. **Absolutely contraindicated with nitrates** (and certain other drugs such as riociguat) because of the risk of severe hypotension; caution with alpha-blockers and in unstable cardiovascular disease.
- **Other options:** vacuum erection devices, intracavernosal or intraurethral therapies, and penile prosthesis surgery for selected patients — under specialist care.
- **Psychosexual and couple therapy** alone or combined with medication improves outcomes when psychological or relational factors are present.

steps.title: Early (premature) ejaculation
steps.body:
The **ISSM** definition describes: ejaculation that always or nearly always occurs within about **1 minute** of vaginal penetration from the first experiences (**lifelong**), or a clinically significant and bothersome reduction in latency, often to about **3 minutes or less** (**acquired**); inability to delay on all or nearly all occasions; and negative personal consequences such as distress or avoidance. (Definitions are based on research in heterosexual intercourse; clinical judgement is needed for other contexts.)

**Treatment overview:**
- **Education and reassurance**; reduce performance anxiety.
- **Behavioural techniques** such as the **stop-start** and **squeeze** methods, often with a partner, and pelvic floor training.
- **Medication:** on-demand **dapoxetine** (a short-acting SSRI approved for PE in several countries, including India); off-label daily SSRIs; **topical anaesthetic** preparations — prescribed after assessment.
- **If ED coexists, treat ED first**, as anxiety about erections can drive early ejaculation.
- Combined behavioural and medical approaches often work better than either alone.

steps.title: Delayed ejaculation
steps.body: Less common. Review medications (**SSRIs** are a frequent cause), alcohol and substances, neurological conditions (e.g., diabetic neuropathy, spinal injury), pelvic surgery, hormonal factors, and psychological and relational contributors. Management centres on addressing causes, medication review with the prescriber, and psychosexual therapy. Evidence for specific drug treatments is limited.

steps.title: Safety and quackery
steps.body:
- Never recommend PDE5 inhibitors without asking about nitrates and cardiovascular status.
- Counsel against unregulated 'tonics' and online products; some have been found adulterated with prescription drugs.
- Avoid fear-based or moralising messages (e.g., that masturbation causes ED) — they are inaccurate and increase anxiety.
- This is an educational overview; prescribing decisions belong to appropriately registered clinicians following current guidelines (e.g., EAU, AUA, ISSM).

statements.s: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in patients taking nitrates.
statements.why: Risk of severe hypotension.

statements.s: PDE5 inhibitors produce an erection without any sexual stimulation.
statements.why: They enhance the natural response to stimulation.

statements.s: If ED and early ejaculation coexist, guidelines generally suggest treating ED first.
statements.why: ED-related anxiety may drive early ejaculation.

statements.s: SSRIs are a common cause of delayed ejaculation.
statements.why: Review with the prescriber.

statements.s: Herbal sex tonics sold online are always free of prescription drugs.
statements.why: Adulteration has been found in some products.

statements.s: ED may be an early marker of cardiovascular disease.
statements.why: An opportunity for cardiovascular risk assessment.

quiz.q: Which is first-line oral therapy for many men with ED?
quiz.why: PDE5 inhibitors, such as sildenafil and tadalafil, are first-line oral therapy for many men with ED after assessment. Testosterone isn't for all, and herbal tonics are unproven.

quiz.q: The ISSM definition of lifelong early ejaculation refers to a latency of about...
quiz.why: The ISSM definition of lifelong early ejaculation refers to ejaculation within about 1 minute of penetration, plus inability to delay and negative consequences.

quiz.q: Which behavioural techniques are used for early ejaculation?
quiz.why: Stop-start and squeeze are the behavioural techniques used for early ejaculation, often with partner involvement.

quiz.q: Which tests are commonly included in ED work-up?
quiz.why: ED work-up commonly includes glucose or HbA1c and lipids, to screen for vascular and metabolic risk.

quiz.q: Dapoxetine is...
options: a short-acting SSRI used on demand for PE
quiz.why: Dapoxetine is a short-acting SSRI used on demand for premature ejaculation. It is approved for PE in several countries including India; it is not a PDE5 inhibitor.

sources: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health

lessons.title: Desire, arousal, orgasm and genito-pelvic pain: overview and sensate focus

scenes.text: Divya and Harish, married 18 months in Chandigarh, come to a sexual-health clinic. Both families keep asking about 'good news'. Intercourse has not been possible; Divya feels intense fear and pain.
Dr. Gurpreet, a psychiatrist trained in psychosexual therapy, works with a gynaecologist and a pelvic health physiotherapist. A gentle, consented assessment rules out structural problems.

The team explains the fear–tension–pain cycle. Divya learns pelvic floor relaxation, the couple start a staged sensate focus programme with a temporary pause on attempts at intercourse, and Divya uses graded vaginal trainers at her own pace.
Months later the couple report much less fear and a closer relationship. They also learned to tell their families, kindly, that it's private.

steps.title: Low desire and arousal concerns
steps.body:
**Assess:** distress; responsive vs spontaneous desire (Basson); medications (SSRIs, hormonal factors), mood, fatigue, sleep, pain, relationship quality, life stage (postpartum, menopause), stress, trauma.

**Management overview:**
- Psychoeducation (often very effective on its own).
- Address contributors: treat depression, review medicines, manage pain or GSM, improve sleep.
- **Psychological therapies:** CBT and **mindfulness-based approaches** (e.g., programmes developed by Lori Brotto) have supportive evidence for women's desire and arousal concerns; couple therapy where relational issues are central.
- **Medications:** in some countries, flibanserin and bremelanotide are approved for certain premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder, with modest benefit and specific safety considerations; testosterone may be considered for postmenopausal women with HSDD under specialist guidance per international position statements. Availability in India varies — check current regulatory status.

steps.title: Orgasm difficulties
steps.body:
- Assess whether lifelong or acquired; medication effects (especially SSRIs); knowledge and comfort with one's own body; anxiety, spectatoring, relationship and cultural factors.
- **Evidence-based approaches** include education about anatomy and response, **directed self-exploration programmes** (a structured, staged behavioural approach with strong evidence for lifelong female orgasmic difficulties), CBT and sensate focus for couples, and medication review when drug-induced.
- Reassure that many people do not experience orgasm through intercourse alone; this is a normal variation, not a disorder.

steps.title: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration concerns
steps.body:
Includes pain during intimacy, involuntary pelvic floor tightening (historically 'vaginismus') and fear of penetration.
- **Rule out and treat medical causes:** infections, dermatological conditions, vestibulodynia, endometriosis, GSM, postpartum perineal pain.
- **Multidisciplinary care:** gynaecology, **pelvic floor physiotherapy** (relaxation, down-training, biofeedback), **psychological therapy** (CBT, exposure-based approaches, trauma-informed care), and **graded vaginal trainers (dilators)** used by the patient at her own pace.
- **Couple involvement** and a temporary pause on attempts at penetration reduce pressure.
- In India, presentation as **non-consummation of marriage** with family pressure is common — handle with sensitivity and privacy.

steps.title: Sensate focus
steps.body:
Developed by **Masters & Johnson** (1970) and refined since, sensate focus is a **structured series of touch exercises** for couples that removes performance demands.
- Early stages: non-genital, non-demand touch, taking turns, focusing on sensations rather than goals; intercourse is temporarily off the table.
- Later stages gradually reintroduce more intimate contact, guided by the therapist.
- Aims: reduce anxiety and spectatoring, improve communication and awareness, rebuild comfort.

It is guided by a trained therapist, who adapts it for culture, disability, trauma history and the couple's values. Couples report back each session; difficulties are informative, not failures.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Telling patients to 'relax' or 'have a drink'.
- Forcing examinations, or examinations without clear consent and a chaperone offer.
- Treating only one partner when the issue is relational.
- Missing coercion, marital conflict or violence presenting as 'low desire'.
- Over-medicalising normal variation.

activity.prompt: Order a typical multidisciplinary pathway for genito-pelvic pain.
items: Private, permission-based history with normalising statements
Consent-based, patient-paced examination to rule out medical causes
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychological therapy
Graded self-paced use of vaginal trainers
Couple work such as staged sensate focus
Review progress and adjust the plan

quiz.q: Which approach has strong evidence for lifelong female orgasmic difficulties?
quiz.why: Directed self-exploration programmes, a structured behavioural approach, have strong evidence for lifelong female orgasmic difficulties. Antibiotics and tonics do not help.

quiz.q: Sensate focus initially...
options: removes performance demands with staged non-demand touch
quiz.why: Sensate focus begins with staged, non-demand touch that removes performance pressure and spectatoring. It does not require intercourse or focus on orgasm.

quiz.q: Genito-pelvic pain management is best described as...
options: multidisciplinary: medical, physiotherapy, psychological and couple-based
quiz.why: Genito-pelvic pain is best managed by a multidisciplinary team combining medical, physiotherapy, psychological and couple-based care, since the problem is biopsychosocial.

quiz.q: Mindfulness-based therapy has supportive evidence for...
quiz.why: Mindfulness-based therapy has supportive evidence for women's desire and arousal concerns, for example work by Brotto and colleagues.

quiz.q: Not experiencing orgasm through intercourse alone is...
quiz.why: Not reaching orgasm through intercourse alone is a common normal variation. Avoid pathologising it.

sources: Brotto et al., mindfulness-based sex therapy trials
Global Consensus Position Statement on testosterone for women (2019)

questions.q: PLISSIT stands for...
options: Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions, Intensive Therapy
Pain, Lifestyle, Sleep, Stress, Intimacy, Therapy
questions.why: PLISSIT stands for Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions and Intensive Therapy, proposed by Annon in 1976.

questions.q: Which drug class must never be combined with PDE5 inhibitors?
questions.why: Nitrates must never be combined with PDE5 inhibitors, because of the risk of severe hypotension.

questions.q: Sensate focus was developed by...
questions.why: Sensate focus was developed by Masters & Johnson and described in Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970).

questions.q: A normalising statement aims to...
questions.why: A normalising statement aims to reduce shame and invite disclosure. It is a common technique in sexual history taking.

questions.q: Stop-start and squeeze techniques are used for...
questions.why: Stop-start and squeeze are behavioural techniques for early ejaculation.

questions.q: EX-PLISSIT adds...
options: permission at every stage, review and reflection
questions.why: EX-PLISSIT adds permission at every stage, plus review and reflection, to the PLISSIT model (Taylor & Davis 2007).

questions.q: Preserved morning erections with situational ED suggest...
options: significant psychological contributors (though organic factors may coexist)
questions.why: Preserved morning erections with situational ED suggest significant psychological contributors, though organic factors may coexist. It is a clue, not proof.

questions.q: If ED and early ejaculation coexist, a common recommendation is to...
questions.why: When ED and early ejaculation coexist, treating ED first is commonly recommended, since ED anxiety may drive the early ejaculation.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of CDC's 5 Ps?
questions.why: Personality is not one of the CDC 5 Ps, which are Partners, Practices, Protection, Past STI history and Pregnancy intention.

questions.q: A patient with genito-pelvic pain asks to postpone examination. You should...
options: respect her pace, explain options and plan when she is ready
questions.why: Respect her pace, explain options and plan when she is ready. Consent and patient pacing matter, so don't insist or examine under family pressure.

questions.q: A general nurse with basic training is most appropriately positioned to provide...
options: Permission and Limited Information, with referral as needed
questions.why: A general nurse with basic training is best placed to give Permission and Limited Information, referring on as needed. Intensive therapy and prescribing are outside that scope.

questions.q: Low desire presents with marked fear of the partner. The first priority is...
options: assess safety and possible coercion or violence
questions.why: Low desire with marked fear of the partner calls first for a safety assessment for coercion or violence. DSM excludes a dysfunction diagnosis when it is explained by partner violence.

questions.q: Why are combined behavioural and medical approaches often recommended for PE?
options: Evidence suggests combination can outperform either alone and address anxiety
questions.why: Combined behavioural and medical approaches often outperform either alone for PE and also address anxiety. Behavioural methods are not harmful.

questions.q: Which statement about flibanserin and bremelanotide is most accurate?
options: They are first-line for all women with low desire
They are approved in some countries for certain premenopausal women with HSDD, with modest benefit
questions.why: Flibanserin and bremelanotide are approved in some countries for certain premenopausal women with HSDD, with modest benefit. They are not first-line for all, nor PDE5 inhibitors.

courses.title: Culture, diversity and ethics in Indian practice
courses.summary: Practise sexual-health care that fits Indian realities: common myths and culture-bound presentations such as Dhat syndrome, family and marriage pressures, affirming care for sexual and gender minorities within current Indian law, and the ethics of boundaries, consent, chaperones, confidentiality and mandatory reporting. General education, not legal advice.
outcomes: Learners can recognise and respond to common myths and culture-bound presentations such as Dhat syndrome
Learners can adapt communication to family structures, language and gender preferences
Learners can provide affirming care consistent with Indian legal developments (2014, 2018, 2019) and professional guidance
Learners can apply ethical principles: consent, chaperones, confidentiality, POCSO reporting, scope and boundaries

lessons.title: Myths, Dhat syndrome and cultural context in India

scenes.text: Ramesh, 22, from a village near Varanasi, visits a psychiatry OPD complaining of tiredness, poor concentration and 'losing strength through urine'. He has spent his savings at a roadside clinic.
Dr. Shalini listens without laughing or dismissing. She asks about his worries, sleep, mood and what he believes is happening.
She explains, in Hindi and with simple diagrams, that the body continuously produces semen and its loss does not cause weakness. She also screens him and finds moderate depression and anxiety.
With treatment for depression and repeated, respectful education, Ramesh improves. 'Nobody ever explained it without making me feel stupid,' he says.

steps.title: Dhat syndrome
steps.body:
**Dhat syndrome** is a culture-related presentation, described in the Indian subcontinent (first named by N. N. Wig in 1960), in which a person — usually a young man — attributes symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, poor concentration, anxiety or sexual difficulties to **loss of semen** (believed to be lost in urine, through nocturnal emissions or masturbation). The belief has roots in traditional ideas that semen is a precious vital substance.

Clinically, it frequently coexists with **depression, anxiety and somatic symptoms**, and sometimes with sexual dysfunctions such as early ejaculation or ED.

**Management:** empathic listening; exploring the person's explanatory model; clear, culturally sensitive education (semen is continuously produced; its loss does not cause weakness); treating comorbid depression/anxiety; addressing sexual concerns; discouraging unregulated remedies. Dismissing the belief bluntly often leads to doctor-shopping.

steps.title: Common myths you will meet
steps.body:
- Masturbation causes weakness, blindness, ED or infertility — **false**.
- Nightfall (nocturnal emission) is a disease — **false**; it is normal.
- Penis size determines satisfaction or fertility — **misleading**; most men worried about size are within the normal range.
- Bleeding on first intercourse proves virginity — **false**; the hymen varies and many people do not bleed. The 'two-finger test' has been condemned by the Supreme Court of India as violating dignity and privacy, and WHO advises against virginity testing.
- Menstruating people are 'impure' — a cultural belief, not a health fact.
- 'Sex tonics' increase strength — no evidence; some are adulterated.

steps.title: Family, marriage and privacy
steps.body:
- Many patients live in **joint or crowded households**, limiting privacy — a real contributor to sexual difficulties.
- **Arranged marriages** can mean couples meet with little prior knowledge of each other or of sexual health; early marriage-related anxiety, non-consummation and pressure to conceive are common presentations.
- **Family members** may accompany patients and expect to be present; offer private time routinely and explain why.
- **Gender of clinician:** some patients prefer a clinician of the same gender; accommodate where possible.
- **Language:** use the patient's language and words they find respectful; use trained interpreters rather than family for sensitive topics where possible.

steps.title: Worked example: responding to a belief respectfully
steps.body:
Patient: *'Doctor, I lose dhat in my urine and that's why I feel weak.'*

Unhelpful: *'That's nonsense. Nothing is wrong with you.'*

Helpful: *'Many young men have shared this worry with me, and I can see it's been troubling you for a long time. Can you tell me what you have noticed and what you think is happening? ... Let me explain what we know about how the body makes semen, and also check other reasons you may feel tired — like sleep, stress or low mood, which are very treatable.'*

This honours the patient's experience, gives accurate information and opens the door to treating comorbid conditions.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Laughing at or dismissing beliefs.
- Assuming all Indian patients share the same beliefs — India's diversity is enormous across regions, religions, castes, classes and urban/rural settings.
- Imposing your own values about marriage, religion or sexuality.
- Ignoring structural barriers: cost, travel, stigma, lack of private space.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a short, respectful explanation of nocturnal emissions and of semen production for a worried 18-year-old, in the language you most often use with patients. Avoid jargon, avoid moralising, keep it non-explicit.

statements.s: Dhat syndrome often coexists with depression and anxiety.
statements.why: Screen and treat comorbidity.

statements.s: Masturbation causes infertility.
statements.why: A myth with no scientific basis.

statements.s: Absence of bleeding on first intercourse proves a woman was not a virgin.
statements.why: Hymen anatomy varies; virginity testing has no scientific validity.

statements.s: Bluntly dismissing a patient's explanatory model often leads to doctor-shopping.
statements.why: Respectful exploration is more effective.

statements.s: Lack of privacy in shared homes can contribute to sexual difficulties.
statements.why: A real-world contextual factor.

quiz.q: Dhat syndrome centres on the belief that...
options: loss of semen causes weakness and other symptoms
quiz.why: Dhat syndrome centres on the belief that loss of semen causes weakness and other symptoms. It has been described in the Indian subcontinent.

quiz.q: Who first named Dhat syndrome?
quiz.why: N. N. Wig first named Dhat syndrome, in 1960.

quiz.q: The best initial response to a patient's culture-related belief is...
options: empathic exploration followed by clear education
quiz.why: Respond to a culture-related belief with empathic exploration followed by clear education. Ignoring, ridiculing or simply agreeing with it doesn't help.

quiz.q: Why offer private time even when family accompanies the patient?
options: It is required by POCSO only
To allow free disclosure, including of safety concerns
quiz.why: Offering private time even when family accompanies the patient allows free disclosure, including safety concerns. It protects autonomy.

quiz.q: WHO's position on virginity testing is that it...
options: has no scientific validity and should not be performed
quiz.why: WHO says virginity testing has no scientific validity and should not be performed. WHO and UN agencies have called for its elimination.

sources: Wig 1960; Prakash 2007, Indian J Psychiatry (Dhat syndrome review)
WHO/UN Human Rights/UN Women, Eliminating virginity testing (2018)

lessons.title: Affirming care for sexual and gender diversity

scenes.text: Aman, 27, a gay man in Kolkata, has avoided doctors for years after one told him to 'get married and you'll be cured'.
At a new clinic, Dr. Ruksana's intake form asks 'partner(s)' without assumptions. She asks in a matter-of-fact way about partners and protection.
For the first time Aman discusses STI testing, vaccinations and HIV prevention options openly.
'You didn't flinch,' he says. Dr. Ruksana replies, 'This is just healthcare.'

steps.title: Indian legal developments
steps.body:
- **2014 — NALSA v. Union of India:** the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify their gender and recognised a 'third gender'.
- **2018 — Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India:** the Supreme Court read down Section 377 of the then Indian Penal Code to decriminalise consensual sexual acts between adults, including same-sex relations.
- **2019 — Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act:** prohibits discrimination against transgender persons, including in healthcare, and provides for identity certification and welfare measures.
- India's criminal code is now the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, in force from 1 July 2024.
- **2022:** India's **National Medical Commission** advised that 'conversion therapy' constitutes professional misconduct.

This is general education, not legal advice; laws and their interpretation evolve.

steps.title: Professional consensus
steps.body: Major health bodies do not regard homosexuality or bisexuality as disorders. ICD-11 moved **gender incongruence** out of mental disorders into the sexual-health chapter, reflecting that gender diversity is not a mental illness while preserving access to gender-affirming care where needed. Attempts to change sexual orientation or gender identity ('conversion therapy') lack evidence of benefit and are associated with harm.

steps.title: Affirming communication
steps.body:
- Use inclusive forms and questions: 'partner(s)', 'What name and pronouns would you like me to use?'
- Ask about practices and protection based on behaviour, not identity labels.
- Do not ask unnecessary questions out of curiosity (e.g., about surgical status when irrelevant to the visit).
- Know relevant preventive care: STI screening based on practices, hepatitis B and HPV vaccination where appropriate, HIV prevention (including PrEP where available and indicated), mental-health screening given minority stress.
- Be alert to family rejection, forced marriage pressures and violence; know local support organisations.

steps.title: Worked example: correcting a mistake
steps.body:
You misgender a patient. Instead of a long apology that centres your discomfort:

*'Sorry — she. Let me continue: so the pain started in March...'*

Brief correction, then move on. Make a note in the record (with consent) so colleagues use the right name and pronouns.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Assuming heterosexuality or marriage.
- Suggesting marriage or 'treatment' to change orientation — unethical and identified as professional misconduct by the NMC.
- Outing a patient to family without consent.
- Treating every health issue as related to identity, or ignoring identity where it is relevant (minority stress).

activity.prompt: Match each development with its year or content.
pairs: 2014: recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify gender
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
Moved out of the mental disorders chapter
India's criminal code in force from 1 July 2024

quiz.q: Which judgment decriminalised consensual adult same-sex relations in India?
quiz.why: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual adult same-sex relations by reading down Section 377 of the then IPC. NALSA concerned transgender rights.

quiz.q: 'Conversion therapy' is...
options: lacking evidence of benefit, associated with harm, and deemed misconduct by India's NMC
quiz.why: Conversion therapy lacks evidence of benefit and is associated with harm, and India's NMC deems it professional misconduct. It is unethical practice.

quiz.q: Which is an affirming intake question?
options: Tell me about your partner or partners.
quiz.why: 'Tell me about your partner or partners' makes no assumptions about gender or number, so it is affirming. The other questions assume or judge.

quiz.q: After misgendering a patient, the best response is...
quiz.why: After misgendering, give a brief correction and continue. Long apologies or asking them to explain gender shift the focus away from the patient.

quiz.q: ICD-11 places gender incongruence in...
quiz.why: ICD-11 places gender incongruence in conditions related to sexual health (Chapter 17), not in mental disorders.

sources: Supreme Court of India: NALSA (2014), Navtej Singh Johar (2018)

lessons.title: Ethics, boundaries and the law in practice

scenes.text: Dr. Vikram, a sexual-medicine specialist in Jaipur, gets a friendly WhatsApp message from a patient inviting him for coffee 'to say thanks'.
The same week, a 16-year-old girl attending for period pain mentions she is in a sexual relationship with a 23-year-old man.

Vikram declines the coffee politely and moves communication to the clinic's official channel. For the adolescent, he explains his legal duty, consults the hospital's child-protection lead and follows the POCSO reporting procedure, keeping her informed and supported.
In peer supervision he says, 'Neither decision felt easy. Both were about protecting people.'

steps.title: Professional boundaries
steps.body:
- **Sexual contact or romantic relationships with patients are never acceptable.** Most professional codes also prohibit them with former patients in many circumstances, and with patients' close family where it exploits the professional relationship.
- **Language and conduct:** clinical, respectful, non-explicit; no jokes or comments about a patient's body; no unnecessary questions.
- **Digital boundaries:** use official channels; don't accept social media requests from patients; never share explicit images or request them.
- **Self-disclosure:** minimal and only when clearly in the patient's interest.
- Notice warning signs in yourself: special treatment of one patient, secrecy, extended sessions, personal contact.

steps.title: Consent and chaperones
steps.body:
- **Intimate examinations** need a clear explanation of why, what it involves and that the patient can stop at any time; obtain and document consent.
- **Offer a chaperone** for intimate examinations regardless of the gender of patient and clinician; record the offer and the response. Respect the patient's preference about a same-gender clinician where possible.
- Use trauma-informed practice: explain each step, ask permission, minimise exposure, give control.
- Capacity: assess and document; involve legal processes for people who lack capacity.

steps.title: Confidentiality and mandatory reporting
steps.body:
- Keep records secure and share only on a need-to-know basis with consent.
- **POCSO Act, 2012:** any person (including health professionals) who knows or has reason to believe that a sexual offence has been committed against a child (under 18) must report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police; failure to report is an offence. This duty applies even when adolescents describe the activity as consensual — a recognised ethical tension. Follow the law and institutional child-protection procedures, explain the process honestly to the young person, and keep caring for them.
- **Medical termination of pregnancy:** the MTP Act requires confidentiality of the woman's identity.
- **Adult survivors of sexual violence:** offer medical care, emergency contraception and STI prophylaxis as indicated, documentation, and information about reporting options; follow applicable law and Ministry of Health guidelines for medico-legal care.
- Emergency in India: **112**; women's helpline **181**; Childline **1098**.

steps.title: Scope and titles
steps.body: In India, 'sexologist' is not a separate statutory profession with its own register. Clinicians who practise sexual medicine come from medicine (psychiatry, urology/andrology, gynaecology, dermatology-venereology, family medicine) or from clinical psychology and counselling. Practise within the scope of **your own registration** (e.g., only registered medical practitioners prescribe), and be honest about qualifications. Advertising miracle cures or making unverifiable claims breaches professional ethics and may break advertising laws.

steps.title: Self-awareness and supervision
steps.body: Sexual-health work can stir clinicians' own values, embarrassment, history and biases. Regular supervision or peer consultation, personal reflection and, where helpful, personal therapy support ethical practice. Ask: *Am I imposing my values? Am I avoiding a topic because I'm uncomfortable? Would I be comfortable if a colleague observed this consultation?*

a.text: A patient you've treated for months sends a warm message on your personal number suggesting dinner 'as friends'. What do you do?

choices.label: Decline kindly, restate the professional relationship and move contact to official channels; note it and discuss in supervision.
choices.feedback: Clear, kind boundary-setting protects the patient and the therapeutic work.

choices.label: Accept — it's only dinner.
choices.feedback: This blurs boundaries and risks exploitation; most codes prohibit such relationships.

b.text: Later, a 15-year-old tells you she is sexually involved with an adult neighbour and begs you not to tell anyone. What do you do?

choices.label: Explain kindly that the law requires you to report to keep her safe, involve the child-protection lead, report under POCSO and continue supporting her.
choices.feedback: Correct legal and ethical action, delivered with care.

choices.label: Keep it confidential to preserve trust.
choices.feedback: This breaches POCSO's reporting duty and leaves a child at risk.

c.text: An adult woman requests an intimate examination for pain. She seems anxious. What is best practice?

choices.label: Explain the purpose and steps, obtain consent, offer a chaperone, let her stop at any time and document.
choices.feedback: Consent, chaperone offer and trauma-informed care.

choices.label: Proceed quickly to reduce her anxiety without explaining.
choices.feedback: Skipping consent and explanation can be distressing and is unethical.

e1.text: Boundary violation risk. Return and choose a professional response.

choices.label: Go back and reconsider.
choices.feedback: Try again.

e2.text: A child remains unsafe and you have breached the law. Reconsider.

choices.label: Go back and reconsider.
choices.feedback: Try again.

choices.label: Go back and reconsider.
choices.feedback: Try again.

end1.text: You maintained boundaries, met legal duties and provided consent-based, trauma-informed care.

quiz.q: A romantic relationship with a current patient is...
quiz.why: A romantic relationship with a current patient is never acceptable, because it exploits the professional relationship. Consent doesn't fix the power imbalance.

quiz.q: A chaperone should be offered for intimate examinations...
options: regardless of patient and clinician gender
quiz.why: Offer a chaperone for intimate examinations regardless of patient and clinician gender. It is standard good practice, and the offer should be documented.

quiz.q: Under POCSO, a health professional who learns of a sexual offence against a 16-year-old must...
options: keep it confidential if she says it's consensual
quiz.why: Under POCSO, a health professional who learns of a sexual offence against anyone under 18 must report to the police or SJPU. Mandatory reporting applies even if she says it is consensual.

quiz.q: In India, 'sexologist' is...
options: not a separate statutory profession; practise within your own registration
a separate statutory profession with its own register
quiz.why: In India, 'sexologist' is not a separate statutory profession. Practise within the scope of your own registration.

quiz.q: India's women's helpline number is...
quiz.why: India's women's helpline is 181. Childline is 1098, Tele-MANAS is 14416 and the emergency number is 112.

sources: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Guidelines for medico-legal care for survivors of sexual violence (2014)

questions.q: India's criminal code in force since 1 July 2024 is the...
questions.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code and came into force on 1 July 2024.

questions.q: The Childline number in India is...
questions.why: Childline in India is 1098, for children in difficulty. 181 is the women's helpline, 14416 is Tele-MANAS and 112 is the emergency number.

questions.q: Nocturnal emissions are...
questions.why: Nocturnal emissions are normal physiology, not a disease or a sign of weakness or infertility.

questions.q: Dhat syndrome frequently coexists with...
questions.why: Dhat syndrome frequently coexists with depression and anxiety, so screen for and treat them.

questions.q: Which case recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify gender?
questions.why: NALSA v Union of India (2014) recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify their gender.

questions.q: A chaperone offer should be...
questions.why: A chaperone offer should be documented along with the patient's response. It is good practice, not something to keep secret.

questions.q: What does WHO say about virginity testing?
options: It has no scientific validity and should be eliminated
questions.why: WHO says virginity testing has no scientific validity and should be eliminated, as in the 2018 WHO/UN joint statement.

questions.q: The 2019 Transgender Persons Act prohibits...
questions.why: India's Transgender Persons Act 2019 prohibits discrimination, including in healthcare. It does not ban gender-affirming care or name changes.

questions.q: The best response to a patient's culture-related explanatory model is...
options: explore it respectfully, then educate accurately
questions.why: Explore the patient's explanatory model respectfully, then educate accurately. Agreeing, ridiculing or referring immediately doesn't help engagement.

questions.q: A 17-year-old discloses a consensual relationship with a 17-year-old classmate. Under POCSO...
options: a reporting duty still applies; follow procedure and seek legal guidance — a recognised ethical tension
no reporting duty applies because both are minors
questions.why: POCSO applies to all under 18; clinicians often seek institutional and legal guidance.

questions.q: A colleague advertises 'guaranteed cure in 7 days' for sexual problems. This is...
options: an ethical breach and potentially unlawful advertising
questions.why: Advertising a 'guaranteed cure in 7 days' makes unverifiable claims that mislead patients, so it is an ethical breach and may be unlawful.

questions.q: After misgendering a patient, the most appropriate action is...
options: brief correction and continue; update records with consent
ask the patient to justify their identity
questions.why: After misgendering, briefly correct and continue, and update records with the patient's consent. Don't ask them to justify their identity.

questions.q: A counsellor (not a medical practitioner) offering sexual-health services should...
options: work within counselling scope and refer for medical assessment and prescribing
questions.why: A counsellor who is not a medical practitioner should stay within counselling scope and refer for medical assessment and prescribing. Prescribing PDE5 inhibitors would be outside scope.

questions.q: Which combination best reflects culturally competent care in India?
options: Routine private time, patient's language, respectful exploration of beliefs, attention to privacy and family pressures
Assume all patients share one culture
questions.why: Culturally competent care combines routine private time, the patient's language, respectful exploration of beliefs, and attention to privacy and family pressures. Assuming one culture does not.

lessons.title: How learning actually works

scenes.text: Ms. Anita Thomas teaches Class 8 science in Thrissur. Her students do well in class but forget most of it by the term exam.
She tries one change: every lesson begins with a five-minute, no-marks quiz on things taught last week and last month.
At first students groan. By the term exam their scores have risen, and they say revision feels easier.
'I didn't teach more,' she tells colleagues. 'I made them remember more often.'

steps.title: Memory: working and long-term
steps.body:
**Working memory** — what we can hold in mind at once — is small; most people can juggle only a few new items at a time. **Long-term memory** is vast. Learning means building organised knowledge in long-term memory so that it can be used without overloading working memory.

**Cognitive load theory** (John Sweller) suggests that when too much new information arrives at once, learning suffers. Good teaching breaks content into steps, removes distractions and builds on what students already know.

steps.title: Retrieval practice and spacing
steps.body:
- **Retrieval practice:** recalling information from memory (quizzes, flashcards, 'write everything you remember') strengthens memory more than re-reading. This is often called the **testing effect**. Low-stakes or no-stakes quizzes work best.
- **Spaced practice:** revisiting material over days and weeks beats cramming the same total time in one go.
- **Interleaving:** mixing different types of problems (e.g., alternating area and perimeter questions) helps students learn *when* to use each method, especially in maths.

These are among the most robust findings in learning research.

steps.title: Worked examples and dual coding
steps.body:
- **Worked examples:** novices learn faster by studying fully solved problems and then gradually solving more themselves ('I do, we do, you do'). As expertise grows, worked examples help less and independent problem-solving helps more.
- **Dual coding:** combining words with diagrams, timelines or flowcharts can help, as long as the visuals carry meaning and aren't decorative clutter.
- **Elaboration:** asking 'why' and 'how' questions connects new ideas to existing knowledge.

steps.title: Myth: learning styles
steps.body: Many teachers are told to label students as 'visual', 'auditory' or 'kinaesthetic' learners and teach to that style. Research reviews (e.g., Pashler and colleagues, 2008) found **no good evidence** that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning. People do have preferences, but the content should decide the format: maps are visual for everyone, pronunciation is auditory for everyone. Use varied, meaningful representations for all.

steps.title: Worked example: a 5-minute retrieval starter
steps.body:
Class 7, start of lesson on 'Nutrition in plants':
- Q1 (last lesson): What gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
- Q2 (last week): Name two parts of a flower.
- Q3 (last month): What is a food chain? Give one example.
- Q4 (today's link): Where do you think plants get their food from?

Students answer silently on slates or notebooks, then you go through answers quickly. No marks recorded — it's practice, not judgement.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Plan a 4-question retrieval starter for a topic you teach or study: one from yesterday, one from last week, one from last month, one preview. Use it three times this week and notice what students remember.

statements.s: Re-reading notes is more effective than self-testing for long-term memory.
statements.why: Retrieval practice (self-testing) is generally more effective.

statements.s: Spacing study over several days usually beats cramming the same total time.
statements.why: The spacing effect is robust.

statements.s: Matching teaching to a student's 'learning style' is well supported by evidence.
statements.why: Reviews have found little evidence for the meshing hypothesis.

statements.s: Worked examples are especially helpful for novices.
statements.why: They reduce cognitive load while schemas form.

statements.s: Working memory can hold a large amount of new information at once.
statements.why: It is limited; break content into manageable steps.

quiz.q: The 'testing effect' refers to...
quiz.why: The testing effect means that practising recall strengthens memory more than re-reading. Retrieval makes learning last.

quiz.q: Interleaving means...
options: teaching only one topic per year
mixing different problem types in practice
quiz.why: Interleaving mixes different problem types in practice, which helps students learn to choose the right method for each problem.

quiz.q: Cognitive load theory suggests teachers should...
options: break content into manageable steps and remove distractions
present as much as possible at once
quiz.why: Working memory is limited, so cognitive load theory says to break content into manageable steps and remove distractions. Presenting everything at once overloads learners.

quiz.q: Which is the best evidence-based alternative to 'learning styles' teaching?
options: Using meaningful, varied representations suited to the content for everyone
quiz.why: Evidence does not support matching teaching to 'learning styles'. Instead use meaningful, varied representations suited to the content for everyone.

quiz.q: Retrieval quizzes work best when they are...
quiz.why: Low- or no-stakes retrieval quizzes let students practise recall without much anxiety. High stakes add pressure that hurts learning.

sources: Dunlosky et al. 2013, Improving students' learning
Pashler et al. 2008, Learning styles review

lessons.title: Planning lessons and checking understanding

story.title: Farhan's lesson that went wrong — and right

scenes.text: Farhan, a B.Ed trainee in Aligarh, teaches Class 6 fractions. He explains for 30 minutes, asks 'Any doubts?' — silence — and moves on.
The next day's homework shows most students added denominators. His mentor teacher says: 'Silence isn't understanding.'
Farhan re-plans with a clear objective, short explanation, a worked example, and a 'hinge question' where every student shows an answer on mini-whiteboards.
This time he spots the misconception in minute 12, re-teaches it, and 90% of the exit tickets are correct.

steps.title: Start with clear objectives
steps.body:
A good learning objective says what students will be able to **do**, using an observable verb.
- Vague: 'Students will understand fractions.'
- Clear: 'Students will add two fractions with unlike denominators and explain why a common denominator is needed.'

**Bloom's revised taxonomy** (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) offers six levels: **Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create**. A lesson can climb from lower to higher levels, but higher thinking needs solid knowledge underneath.

steps.title: A simple lesson structure
steps.body:
- **Retrieval starter** (5 min): review previous learning.
- **Hook and objective** (2–3 min): why this matters; what we'll be able to do.
- **Explicit explanation** (8–10 min): short, clear, with visuals.
- **Worked example(s)** ('I do') then **guided practice** ('we do').
- **Hinge question / check for understanding**: everyone responds.
- **Independent practice** ('you do'), with support for those who need it and challenge for those ready.
- **Exit ticket** (3 min): one or two questions that show whether the objective was met.

The **5E model** (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) is a popular alternative for inquiry-based science lessons.

steps.title: Formative assessment
steps.body:
**Formative assessment** means checking learning *during* teaching so you can adjust — as opposed to **summative assessment** (end-of-unit tests) that judges learning afterwards. Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam's influential review (1998) argued that good formative assessment can substantially raise achievement.

Techniques:
- **All-student response:** mini-whiteboards, slates, finger voting (1–4 for multiple choice), coloured cards.
- **Cold calling** with no hands up, kindly, so everyone thinks.
- **Hinge questions:** a multiple-choice question where each wrong option reveals a specific misconception.
- **Exit tickets.**
- **Feedback** that tells students what to do next, not just a mark.

steps.title: Worked example: a hinge question
steps.body:
**1/2 + 1/3 = ?**
- A) 2/5 — reveals 'add tops and bottoms'.
- B) 2/6 — reveals adding numerators but multiplying denominators.
- C) 5/6 — correct.
- D) 1/6 — reveals multiplying instead of adding.

If many choose A, re-teach common denominators with a visual (fraction strips) before moving on.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking 'Any doubts?' or 'Do you understand?' — students rarely say no.
- Taking answers only from confident hands-up students.
- Planning activities instead of learning ('students will make a poster' — but learn what?).
- Too much teacher talk, too little practice.
- Giving marks without guidance on how to improve.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write one measurable objective and one hinge question with three wrong options, each linked to a likely misconception, for a topic you know well.

activity.prompt: Arrange a well-structured lesson.

quiz.q: Which is a measurable objective?
options: Label the parts of a leaf and explain the role of chlorophyll
quiz.why: 'Label the parts of a leaf and explain the role of chlorophyll' uses observable verbs, so it can be measured. 'Understand' or 'appreciate' can't be seen or tested directly.

quiz.q: Formative assessment is used to...
options: check learning during teaching to adjust instruction
quiz.why: Formative assessment checks learning during teaching so the teacher can adjust instruction. Ranking at the end is summative.

quiz.q: A hinge question is designed so that...
quiz.why: A hinge question is designed so wrong options reveal specific misconceptions, making responses diagnostic.

quiz.q: Which is the highest level in Bloom's revised taxonomy?
quiz.why: In the revised Bloom's taxonomy the order is Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate and Create, so Create is the highest level.

quiz.q: Why is 'Any doubts?' a weak check?
options: Students rarely admit confusion publicly; silence isn't understanding
quiz.why: 'Any doubts?' is a weak check because students rarely admit confusion publicly, and silence isn't understanding. Use responses from all students instead.

sources: Black & Wiliam 1998, Inside the Black Box

lessons.title: Calm classroom management

story.title: Mr. Dsouza and the back bench

scenes.text: Mr. Leon Dsouza, in his first year teaching Class 9 in Goa, struggles with a group on the back bench who chat and laugh through lessons.
He tries shouting; it works for two minutes and then gets worse. One student, Nikhil, starts to openly challenge him.
A senior teacher advises: greet students at the door, teach routines explicitly, use names, move around the room, and talk to Nikhil privately rather than in front of others.
In a private chat Nikhil admits he can't follow the maths and jokes to hide it. With support and a seat change, he becomes one of the most engaged students.

steps.title: Relationships and routines first
steps.body:
Most classroom problems are prevented, not punished.
- **Relationships:** learn names quickly, greet students, show interest, notice effort, be fair and consistent.
- **Clear expectations:** a few positively phrased rules ('We listen when someone is speaking').
- **Routines taught and practised:** entering, starting work, distributing materials, group work signals, transitions, leaving. Practise them like any skill in the first weeks.
- **Engaging, well-paced lessons:** many behaviour problems come from confusion or boredom.

steps.title: Withitness and least-invasive responses
steps.body:
Jacob Kounin described **'withitness'** — the teacher's awareness of everything happening in the room, communicated to students. Scan the room, position yourself to see everyone, circulate.

Use the **least invasive response** that works, stepping up only if needed:
- 1. A look or pause.
- 2. Moving closer (proximity).
- 3. Saying the student's name in a sentence, or a quiet non-verbal signal.
- 4. **Positive narration**: 'I can see rows one and two are ready...'
- 5. A quiet, private reminder of the expectation and a choice.
- 6. A follow-up conversation after class.
- 7. Agreed school procedures and involving parents/counsellor when needed.

steps.title: The law in India
steps.body: The **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009**, Section 17, prohibits **physical punishment and mental harassment** of children. National guidelines also discourage humiliation, name-calling and public shaming. Corporal punishment is harmful and ineffective: research links it to worse behaviour, mental-health problems and damaged relationships. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Worked example: a private conversation
steps.body:
After class, calm and seated at the same level:
- *'Nikhil, I've noticed you've been chatting a lot in maths this week. That's not like the work I saw from you in June. What's going on?'*
- Listen. (He says he's lost since algebra started.)
- *'Thanks for telling me. Let's fix that. Can you come for 10 minutes on Thursday at lunch? And in class, I'll check in with you after the example.'*
- *'In return, I need you to keep the chatting for break time. Deal?'*

This separates the behaviour from the person, finds the cause and sets a clear expectation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shouting or sarcasm — quick compliance, long-term damage.
- Public confrontations that a student cannot back down from without losing face.
- Inconsistent rules for different students.
- Collective punishment of the whole class.
- Ignoring possible underlying causes: learning difficulties, hunger, problems at home, bullying. If you suspect abuse or neglect, follow your school's child-protection procedure (Childline: 1098).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write down the three routines you most need (e.g., starting work, transitions, packing up). For each, write the exact steps you'll teach and how you'll practise them in week one.

a.text: During your explanation, two students at the side are whispering and giggling. What do you do first?

choices.label: Pause, look at them calmly and continue when they stop.
choices.feedback: Least-invasive first step; often enough.

choices.label: Shout: 'You two, out of my class!'
choices.feedback: Escalates quickly and loses learning time.

b.text: They stop briefly, then start again a few minutes later. Next step?

choices.label: Walk over and stand near them while still teaching; use one student's name in a sentence.
choices.feedback: Proximity and name-dropping keep the lesson flowing.

choices.label: Give the whole class extra homework.
choices.feedback: Collective punishment feels unfair and harms relationships.

c.text: The class goes tense. One student answers back loudly. What now?

choices.label: Stay calm, say you'll talk after class, and return to the lesson.
choices.feedback: Good de-escalation: avoid a public power struggle.

choices.label: Argue back until they apologise in front of everyone.
choices.feedback: Public battles rarely end well for anyone.

d.text: After class you talk privately. One student says they're bored because the work is too easy. How do you respond?

choices.label: Thank them, agree to offer extension tasks, and restate the expectation about talking during explanations.
choices.feedback: You addressed the cause and kept the boundary.

end1.text: Calm, escalating-only-as-needed responses plus a private conversation solved the issue and improved the relationship.

end2.text: This path damaged trust and lost learning time. Try again with least-invasive steps.

quiz.q: Which Indian law prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment of children in schools?
quiz.why: The RTE Act 2009 (Section 17) prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment of children in schools. The IT Act and Companies Act don't cover this.

quiz.q: 'Withitness' means...
options: being aware of everything happening in the class
quiz.why: 'Withitness', from Kounin, means being aware of everything happening in the class. It helps prevent problems early.

quiz.q: Which is the least invasive response?
quiz.why: A pause or look is the least invasive response. Start small and escalate to calling parents, detention or sending out only if needed.

quiz.q: Why have difficult conversations privately?
options: So the student can respond without losing face
quiz.why: Hold difficult conversations privately so the student can respond without losing face. Public confrontations tend to escalate.

quiz.q: Persistent misbehaviour can hide...
options: learning difficulties, hunger or problems at home
quiz.why: Persistent misbehaviour can hide learning difficulties, hunger or problems at home, so look for causes.

sources: Kounin 1970, Discipline and Group Management in Classrooms
NCPCR guidelines on eliminating corporal punishment

lessons.title: Inclusive education

scenes.text: Diya, 9, in Class 4 in Nashik, is bright in discussions but her reading and spelling are far behind. A teacher writes 'careless, does not try' in her diary.
Her new teacher, Mrs. Kulkarni, notices letter reversals, slow reading and how hard Diya works. She talks to the school's special educator.
An assessment suggests dyslexia, a specific learning disability. The school agrees accommodations: extra time, reading questions aloud, structured phonics support.
By Class 6 Diya reads more confidently and tops her class in science projects. 'I'm not stupid,' she tells her mother. 'My brain learns differently.'

steps.title: What inclusive education means
steps.body:
Inclusive education means **all children learn together** in their local schools, with the support they need — not just being physically present, but participating and achieving.

In India, the **Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016** recognises **21 specified disabilities** (including specific learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, visual and hearing impairment, locomotor disability and others) and requires educational institutions to provide inclusive education and **reasonable accommodation**. **NEP 2020** also emphasises equitable and inclusive education. Inclusion also includes children from disadvantaged groups, girls, children of migrant workers, and those learning in a second language.

steps.title: Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
steps.body:
UDL (developed by CAST) means designing lessons that work for the widest range of learners from the start, rather than retrofitting. Three principles:
- **Multiple means of engagement** — the *why*: choice, relevance, varied challenge.
- **Multiple means of representation** — the *what*: text plus visuals, audio, real objects, clear vocabulary support.
- **Multiple means of action and expression** — the *how*: students show learning by writing, speaking, drawing, building or using technology.

UDL benefits everyone — captions help hearing-impaired students and also second-language learners.

steps.title: Common needs and simple supports
steps.body:
- **Dyslexia (specific learning disability in reading):** structured, systematic phonics; extra time; reading aloud of questions; audiobooks; assess knowledge orally where possible.
- **ADHD:** clear routines, short chunks, movement breaks, seating away from distractions, checklists, positive feedback.
- **Autism:** predictable routines, visual schedules, advance warning of changes, clear literal language, a calm space.
- **Low vision:** large print, seating, contrast, magnifiers.
- **Hearing impairment:** face the class when speaking, captions, seating, written instructions; respect for sign language.

Identification and diagnosis are done by qualified professionals; teachers notice, support and refer.

steps.title: Worked example: differentiating one task
steps.body:
Task: 'Explain the water cycle.'
- **Support:** labelled diagram with word bank; student arranges cards in order and explains orally.
- **Core:** draw and label the cycle and write three sentences.
- **Challenge:** explain how deforestation could change the local water cycle.

All students meet the same core objective; the route and support differ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Labelling children as 'lazy' or 'weak' without considering learning needs.
- Lowering expectations instead of providing support.
- Treating accommodations as 'unfair advantages' — they remove barriers, they don't give extra marks.
- Talking about a child's disability in front of classmates without consent.
- Ignoring the child's own voice in planning support.

scenes.text: Pooja, 18, from Ranchi, wants to teach young children. Her counsellor suggests a D.El.Ed or an integrated programme.
Her cousin Abhishek, with an MSc Chemistry, wants to teach Class 11–12 and plans a B.Ed.
Their friend Fatima already has a B.Ed and prepares for the CTET and her state TET to apply for government school posts.
All three keep checking NCTE and exam notices, because eligibility rules are updated from time to time.

steps.title: Regulator and stages
steps.body: Teacher education in India is regulated by the **National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE)**. School stages under **NEP 2020** follow a **5+3+3+4** structure: Foundational (ages 3–8), Preparatory (8–11), Middle (11–14), Secondary (14–18). Different stages need different qualifications.

steps.title: Main qualifications
steps.body:
- **D.El.Ed** (Diploma in Elementary Education, 2 years, after Class 12): for primary/elementary teaching.
- **B.Ed** (2 years, after a bachelor's degree): commonly for upper primary, secondary and senior secondary (subject teachers).
- **ITEP** (Integrated Teacher Education Programme, 4 years: B.A. B.Ed., B.Sc. B.Ed., B.Com. B.Ed.): introduced under NEP 2020, which envisions the 4-year integrated B.Ed as the minimum qualification for school teachers by 2030.
- **Early childhood** diplomas for pre-primary teaching.
- **B.Ed Special Education** (RCI-recognised) for special educators.

In 2023 the Supreme Court held that B.Ed holders are not eligible for primary (Class 1–5) teacher posts under the rules then in force, where a D.El.Ed-type qualification is expected. Rules evolve — always check current NCTE notifications and recruitment advertisements.

steps.title: Eligibility tests
steps.body:
- **CTET** (Central Teacher Eligibility Test, conducted by CBSE): **Paper I** for Classes 1–5, **Paper II** for Classes 6–8. The CTET certificate's validity was extended to lifetime in 2021.
- **State TETs** for state government schools.
- Recruitment exams (e.g., by central school organisations or state boards) for specific posts; postgraduate teacher (PGT) posts generally require a master's in the subject plus B.Ed.

Private schools set their own criteria but increasingly prefer B.Ed and TET-qualified candidates.

steps.title: Beyond school teaching
steps.body: Teaching skills open other paths: college and university teaching (usually master's plus UGC-NET or PhD), coaching and test-prep, curriculum design, educational content and ed-tech, teacher training, NGO education programmes, special education, adult literacy and corporate learning and development.

steps.title: Choosing your route
steps.body: Decide which **age group** you love teaching — this matters more than anything. Volunteer with that age group (tuition centres, NGOs, summer camps). Then choose the qualification for that stage, check recognition of the institution on the NCTE website, and plan TET/CTET timing.

questions.why: The RPwD Act 2016 requires schools to provide inclusive education and reasonable accommodation. This is a statutory duty.

questions.why: Novices benefit most from worked examples and step-by-step guidance, which reduce extraneous cognitive load while knowledge builds. Unguided discovery overloads them.
