options: Extra time and having questions read aloud
questions.why: Extra time and having questions read aloud support a student with dyslexia without lowering standards. Accommodation removes barriers, while free marks lower the standard.

questions.q: Interleaving maths practice mainly helps students to...
options: learn to choose the right method for each problem
questions.why: Interleaving maths practice helps students learn to choose the right method for each problem. It trains discrimination between problem types.

questions.q: Which plan best reflects evidence-based teaching for a new unit?
options: Clear objectives, explicit teaching with worked examples, frequent checks for understanding, spaced retrieval over weeks
Cover all content in one long lecture, test at the end
questions.why: Clear objectives, explicit teaching with worked examples, frequent checks and spaced retrieval over weeks combine several robust principles. One long lecture or daily high-stakes tests do not.

courses.title: Social work and NGO practice
courses.summary: What professional social work is, its values and six methods, the casework process and group work, community organisation and participatory tools, running NGO projects in India (registration, FCRA, CSR, monitoring), and careers through BSW and MSW.
outcomes: Learners can explain the purpose, values and six methods of social work
Learners can apply the casework process and stages of group development
Learners can use participatory tools for community needs assessment
Learners can describe NGO legal forms, FCRA, CSR and a basic project logframe
Learners can map BSW/MSW pathways and practice settings

lessons.title: What social work is

scenes.text: Rekha, 20, from Patna, volunteers every Sunday giving food at a railway station. She wants to 'do more' and asks a social worker, Mr. Joseph, what his job is.

He explains that he helps a family get a child back into school, links an elderly widow to her pension, runs a support group for young mothers, and works with the community to demand a working hand-pump.
'Charity meets today's need,' he says. 'Social work also asks why the need exists and helps people change it — with them, not for them.'
Rekha decides to apply for a BSW.

steps.title: A global definition
steps.body:
The International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) and the International Association of Schools of Social Work (2014) describe social work as a **practice-based profession and academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people**. Its principles include **social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversity**.

Professional social work in India has a long history; the country's first school of social work was established in Bombay in 1936.

steps.title: Core values
steps.body:
- **Dignity and worth of every person.**
- **Social justice** — challenging discrimination (caste, gender, disability, religion, class) and unfair systems.
- **Self-determination** — people make their own decisions about their lives.
- **Non-judgemental attitude** and **acceptance**.
- **Confidentiality** (with limits for serious harm and legal duties).
- **Empowerment and participation** — work *with* people.
- **Integrity and competence.**

steps.title: The six methods
steps.body:
Indian social work education traditionally teaches six methods:

**Primary (direct) methods:**
- **Social casework** — working with individuals and families.
- **Social group work** — working with groups for growth, support or action.
- **Community organisation** — helping communities identify needs and act together.

**Secondary (auxiliary) methods:**
- **Social welfare administration** — managing agencies, programmes and resources.
- **Social action** — organised efforts for social and policy change.
- **Social work research** — studying problems and evaluating interventions.

steps.title: Charity, welfare and social work
steps.body:
- **Charity:** giving to meet immediate needs (food, clothes). Valuable, but can create dependency if used alone.
- **Welfare:** organised services (pensions, schemes).
- **Social work:** professional, values-based practice that combines direct help with linking people to rights and services and changing systems.

Example: a child labour case. Charity: give the child a meal. Social work: assess the family, link to schemes and school enrolment under the RTE Act, involve child-protection services where needed, and work with the community on root causes.

steps.title: Pitfalls for beginners
steps.body:
- **Saviour mindset** — seeing yourself as rescuing 'helpless' people.
- Making decisions *for* people instead of *with* them.
- Photographing vulnerable people for social media without informed consent.
- Ignoring power differences (caste, gender, education, money) between you and the people you work with.

quiz.why: A saviour mindset is a beginner's pitfall because you should work with people, not for them. Respecting diversity, confidentiality and consent are good practice.

quiz.why: Social action is a secondary method of social work, along with administration and research. The primary methods are casework, group work and community organisation.

lessons.title: Casework and group work in practice

scenes.text: In a Chennai urban settlement, school social worker Ms. Selvi learns that Lakshmi, 13, has stopped attending school.
On a home visit she learns Lakshmi's mother is ill and Lakshmi is caring for two younger brothers.
Together they make a plan: the mother is linked to the government hospital, the boys to the local anganwadi, and the school agrees to a catch-up programme.
Lakshmi also joins a girls' group Selvi runs, where she meets others in similar situations. Six months later she is back in class.

steps.title: The casework process
steps.body:
Social casework (pioneered by Mary Richmond, *Social Diagnosis*, 1917) follows a process:
- **1. Intake and engagement:** first contact, building rapport, explaining role and confidentiality.
- **2. Study / assessment:** understanding the person-in-environment — family, health, income, housing, education, support networks, strengths and risks.
- **3. Social diagnosis / formulation:** what is the problem, why, and what resources exist?
- **4. Planning:** agreed goals and tasks with the client.
- **5. Intervention:** counselling, linking to services and schemes, advocacy, practical help.
- **6. Evaluation:** are goals being met?
- **7. Termination and follow-up.**

steps.title: Strengths-based practice
steps.body:
Rather than only listing problems, the **strengths perspective** asks: what is working? What skills, relationships, beliefs and community resources does this person have? Lakshmi's strengths: she is responsible and caring; her mother values education; a neighbour is willing to help.

Strengths-based plans feel more hopeful and are more likely to be followed. Tools like an **ecomap** (a diagram of the person's connections to family, school, health services, work, community) help both worker and client see the whole picture.

steps.title: Group work and group stages
steps.body:
Social group work uses the group itself as a source of support, learning and change. Types: support groups, educational groups, therapeutic groups, task and action groups (e.g., self-help groups).

Bruce Tuckman's stages of group development:
- **Forming:** polite, uncertain; the worker provides structure.
- **Storming:** conflict, testing; the worker helps manage disagreement.
- **Norming:** shared rules and trust develop.
- **Performing:** the group works effectively.
- **Adjourning:** ending; the worker helps members review and say goodbye (added in 1977).

steps.title: Worked example: a SMART case plan
steps.body:
Goal: Lakshmi returns to regular school attendance.
- Task 1 (worker, this week): refer mother to the government hospital and accompany on the first visit.
- Task 2 (mother and worker, in 2 weeks): enrol younger brothers at the anganwadi.
- Task 3 (school, from next month): 30-minute catch-up classes three times a week.
- Task 4 (Lakshmi): attend the girls' group weekly.
- Review: in 6 weeks, attendance above 80%?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing assessments *about* people rather than *with* them.
- Writing case notes with judgemental language ('lazy mother').
- Ignoring safety or child-protection concerns — follow procedures and, for children, contact child-protection services or Childline 1098.
- Ending a case abruptly without planning.

scenes.text: An NGO team led by Arif arrives in a village in Rajasthan planning to build toilets, because a donor wants that.
Instead of starting construction, Arif's team asks villagers to draw a social map on the ground with chalk and stones, showing homes, water sources and problems.
Women point out the biggest problem is walking 3 km for water. Toilets without water won't be used.
The NGO goes back to the donor with the community's priorities. A water project comes first, then sanitation. Both are used and maintained by a village committee.

steps.title: Community organisation
steps.body:
Community organisation helps people identify common needs, build their own capacity and act together. Jack Rothman described three broad models:
- **Locality development:** broad participation and self-help (e.g., a village improving its school).
- **Social planning:** experts and data-driven planning of services.
- **Social action:** organising disadvantaged groups to demand rights or redistribution of power.

Good practice mixes them carefully and always centres the community's voice.

steps.title: Participatory tools (PRA)
steps.body:
**Participatory Rural Appraisal** (popularised by Robert Chambers) uses visual, group-based tools so that everyone — including people who cannot read — can contribute:
- **Social map:** households, resources, who has what.
- **Resource map:** land, water, forests.
- **Transect walk:** walking across the area with residents, observing and discussing.
- **Seasonal calendar:** work, illness, income and food across the year.
- **Venn (chapati) diagram:** institutions and how important and accessible they are.
- **Problem ranking / pairwise ranking.**

Make sure women, Dalit and Adivasi communities, people with disabilities and the poorest households are heard, not only local leaders.

steps.title: NGOs in India: the basics
steps.body:
- **Legal forms:** a **trust**, a **society** (under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 or state laws), or a **Section 8 company** (Companies Act, 2013).
- **Tax:** registrations under the Income-tax Act (such as 12A/12AB for the organisation's exemption and 80G for donors' deductions).
- **Foreign funding:** requires registration or prior permission under the **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), 2010** (amended 2020).
- **CSR funding:** under **Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013**, companies meeting certain thresholds must spend at least **2% of their average net profits** of the preceding three years on CSR activities, often through NGOs.

This is general education, not legal advice; rules and thresholds change.

steps.title: Designing and measuring a project
steps.body:
- **Theory of change:** if we do X, then Y will change, because Z.
- **Logical framework (logframe):** a table linking **inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact**, with indicators, means of verification and assumptions.
- **Outputs vs outcomes:** '500 women trained' is an **output**; '300 women increased household income by 20% within a year' is an **outcome**.
- **Monitoring and evaluation:** baseline data, regular monitoring, end-line evaluation, and honest reporting of what didn't work.
- **Sustainability:** community ownership, local committees and maintenance plans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Donor-driven projects that ignore community priorities.
- Counting outputs and calling them impact.
- 'Poverty photography' without consent or dignity.
- Building infrastructure with no plan for maintenance.
- Poor financial transparency — keep accounts clean and publish reports.

lessons.title: Careers in social work and the NGO sector

scenes.text: A batch of MSW graduates meets three years after graduation in Delhi.
Joseph is a medical social worker in a cancer hospital. Nasreen is a protection officer working on child protection in her district. Tenzin coordinates a CSR education project.
Ritu evaluates programmes for a research organisation; Manoj works in HR and employee welfare in a factory.
'Same degree,' says Nasreen, 'but all of us still use the same skills — listening, assessing, linking, advocating.'

steps.title: Qualifications
steps.body:
- **BSW** (Bachelor of Social Work): usually 3 years (or 4 years with honours/research at many universities under NEP 2020), with supervised **fieldwork** placements.
- **MSW** (Master of Social Work): 2 years, with concurrent and block fieldwork and a research project. Common specialisations: family and child welfare, medical and psychiatric social work, community development (rural/urban), criminology and correctional administration, human resource management and labour welfare, disaster management.
- **M.Phil / PhD:** for teaching, research and specialised clinical roles (e.g., psychiatric social work).

steps.title: Practice settings
steps.body:
- Hospitals, mental-health services, de-addiction centres, HIV and palliative care.
- Schools and colleges.
- **Child protection:** under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 — district child protection units, Child Welfare Committees, children's homes.
- Government schemes and missions (health, livelihoods, women and child development).
- NGOs, CSR foundations, international development organisations.
- Correctional settings, courts and legal aid.
- Corporate HR and employee wellbeing.
- Disaster response and humanitarian work.
- Research, monitoring and evaluation.

steps.title: Skills employers look for
steps.body: Interviewing and counselling skills, case documentation, knowledge of schemes and laws, community mobilisation, local languages, report writing, basic data analysis (spreadsheets, surveys), project management, and ethical judgement. Fieldwork diaries, a portfolio of reports and good references matter a lot.

steps.title: Honest realities and self-care
steps.body: Salaries in many NGO roles start modestly and vary greatly; work can involve travel, difficult situations and emotional strain. Protect yourself with supervision, peer support, clear boundaries and rest. Burnout is common when organisations are under-resourced — choose employers who offer supervision and fair working conditions where you can.

a.text: You're a new NGO field officer. Your manager asks you to photograph malnourished children for a donor report, quickly, without asking parents. What do you do?

choices.label: Explain you'll seek informed consent from parents and take dignified photos, or none.
choices.feedback: Dignity and consent come first.

choices.label: Take the photos — the manager asked.
choices.feedback: This violates dignity and consent and can harm families.

b.text: Your manager agrees but says the donor wants 'impact numbers' this month, and you've only trained mothers so far. How do you report?

choices.label: Report outputs honestly (number trained) and explain when outcomes will be measured.
choices.feedback: Honest reporting builds long-term trust.

choices.label: Claim malnutrition dropped by 50%.
choices.feedback: Fabricating results is unethical and harms future funding and communities.

c.text: This choice harms people or breaks trust. What would you do instead?

choices.label: Go back and choose the ethical option.
choices.feedback: Try again.

end1.text: You protected dignity, followed consent and reported honestly — the foundations of trustworthy social work.

quiz.why: An MSW usually takes 2 years, including supervised fieldwork.

quiz.why: Report outputs honestly and explain the timeline for outcomes. Inventing or copying results breaks integrity.

questions.q: Which NGO legal form is created under the Companies Act, 2013?
questions.why: A Section 8 company is the not-for-profit company form under the Companies Act, 2013. Trusts, societies and cooperatives come under other laws.

questions.q: A donor wants a toilet project, but the community's top priority is water. The best approach is...
options: share community priorities with the donor and re-design together
questions.why: Share the community's priorities with the donor and re-design together. Participation and honest dialogue beat building toilets nobody prioritised or ignoring the donor.

questions.q: During casework you discover a 12-year-old is being made to work and beaten. What is the right step?
options: Follow child-protection procedures and contact child-protection services/Childline 1098
questions.why: A 12-year-old made to work and beaten needs child protection. Follow procedures and contact child-protection services or Childline 1098; don't keep it confidential or confront the employer alone.

questions.q: Why is 'saviour mindset' harmful?
options: It ignores people's agency and power differences
questions.why: A saviour mindset ignores people's agency and power differences. Good practice is to work with people rather than for them.

questions.q: Which logframe chain is correct?
questions.why: The logframe chain runs inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact, in that order. The other orders break the logic.

courses.title: Choosing a career: know yourself, explore, decide
courses.summary: A practical, reflective course for students and young adults: understand your interests, values and aptitudes; explore careers through real conversations and experiences; reality-test costs and pathways; make a decision with a Plan B; and talk to family about it calmly.
outcomes: Learners can describe their interests using the Holland RIASEC framework and identify core values
Learners can reflect honestly on aptitudes and skills, and understand the limits of aptitude tests
Learners can research careers through informational interviews, shadowing and official sources
Learners can use a weighted decision matrix and create a Plan B
Learners can plan a respectful conversation with family about career choices

scenes.text: Rhea, 15, from Kanpur, is expected to take PCM because 'everyone in the family is an engineer'.
She notices she loses track of time when designing posters for school events and explaining things to younger kids.
A career workshop introduces her to the RIASEC model. Her top codes are Artistic, Social and Investigative.

She starts exploring careers like UX design, architecture, teaching and psychology — some of which still use maths. 'I don't have to choose between me and my family yet,' she says. 'I just need more information.'

steps.title: Holland's RIASEC
steps.body:
Psychologist John Holland suggested that people and work environments can be described by six interest types:
- **R — Realistic** ('doers'): hands-on, tools, machines, outdoors, sport. *E.g., mechanic, engineer, electrician, farmer, physiotherapist.*
- **I — Investigative** ('thinkers'): analysing, researching, solving. *E.g., scientist, doctor, data analyst.*
- **A — Artistic** ('creators'): creativity, expression. *E.g., designer, writer, musician, actor.*
- **S — Social** ('helpers'): teaching, caring, counselling. *E.g., teacher, nurse, counsellor, social worker.*
- **E — Enterprising** ('persuaders'): leading, selling, starting things. *E.g., entrepreneur, manager, lawyer, marketer.*
- **C — Conventional** ('organisers'): order, data, detail. *E.g., accountant, banker, administrator.*

Most people are a mix; your top two or three letters (e.g., ASI) point to environments you may enjoy.

steps.title: Values: what matters to you
steps.body:
Interests tell you what you enjoy; **values** tell you what you need from work to feel satisfied. Examples: security, high income, helping others, creativity, independence, prestige, work–life balance, adventure, staying near family, social justice, learning.

A career that fits your interests but clashes with your top value (e.g., you love film but need stable income) can still work — but you'll need a plan for that tension.

steps.title: Worked example: clues from your life
steps.body:
Ask yourself:
- When do I lose track of time?
- What do people ask me for help with?
- Which school subjects or activities energise me, and which drain me?
- What problems in the world make me angry or curious?
- What did I love doing at age 10?

Rhea's answers: designing posters, explaining things, animal welfare, sketching. Pattern: Artistic + Social, with Investigative curiosity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing only by marks ('I scored high in maths, so engineering').
- Choosing by what friends choose.
- Treating one online quiz result as destiny.
- Thinking interests never change — they develop with experience, so keep exploring.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rank the six RIASEC types from most to least like you. Then write your top five values in order. Keep this note; you'll use it in the next lessons.

activity.prompt: Match each activity to its main RIASEC type.

items.text: Repairing a motorbike
Running a science experiment
Composing a song
Tutoring younger students
Starting a small business at a school fair
Organising the class accounts in a spreadsheet
Coaching a cricket team
Designing a costume for a play

quiz.q: RIASEC was developed by...
quiz.why: RIASEC was developed by John Holland in his theory of vocational personalities.

quiz.q: 'E' in RIASEC stands for...
quiz.why: In RIASEC, E stands for Enterprising, meaning leading, persuading and starting things.

quiz.q: Values in career choice refer to...
options: what you need from work to feel satisfied
quiz.why: Values in career choice refer to what you need from work to feel satisfied, for example security, helping or creativity. They are not just salary or marks.

quiz.q: Which is a common career-choice mistake?
options: Choosing only based on marks or friends
quiz.why: Choosing only on marks or friends is a common mistake, because marks show ability in a subject, not whether you'd enjoy the career.

quiz.q: Interests usually...
quiz.why: Interests usually develop with experience, so keep exploring. They are not fixed at birth.

lessons.title: Aptitude and skills: an honest reflection

story.title: Vikram's cricket and his Plan A

scenes.text: Vikram, 16, from Rajkot, dreams of playing cricket for India. He plays for his district under-16 team.
His coach, honest and kind, shares his performance data and explains how few players reach the top, and that the path is uncertain even for very talented players.
Vikram reflects on his strengths: tactics, reading the game, motivating teammates, and good grades in biology.
He keeps training hard while also exploring sports science, coaching and physiotherapy. 'Cricket stays my Plan A,' he says, 'but now I have a Plan B in the same world.'

steps.title: Aptitude, ability, skill
steps.body:
- **Aptitude:** a natural potential to learn certain things quickly (e.g., spatial reasoning, verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning, musical pitch, coordination).
- **Ability:** what you can do now.
- **Skill:** a learned capability developed through practice (coding, public speaking, bowling, counselling).

Aptitude helps, but **sustained, well-guided practice** develops most skills. Many people with average early aptitude become excellent through deliberate practice and good teaching.

steps.title: Aptitude tests: useful but limited
steps.body:
Aptitude and psychometric tests can give helpful information about reasoning strengths and interests. But:
- they measure a sample of abilities on one day,
- results depend on test quality, language and familiarity with such tests,
- they cannot measure motivation, values, grit or opportunity,
- no test can tell you your 'one perfect career'.

Use results as one input along with your own reflection, experiences and feedback from teachers and mentors. Prefer tests offered by qualified career counsellors or psychologists, and be wary of expensive tests that promise certainty.

steps.title: Transferable skills
steps.body: Some skills travel to almost any career: communication, teamwork, problem-solving, digital literacy, numeracy, writing, self-management, empathy, leadership and learning how to learn. Build them through school projects, sports, clubs, volunteering, part-time work and online courses. They make every Plan B stronger.

steps.title: Worked example: a skills inventory
steps.body:
Vikram's list:
- **Strong:** tactical thinking (captaincy), motivating others, physical fitness, biology.
- **Developing:** English writing, public speaking.
- **Evidence:** captained district U-16 team; 85% in science.
- **Feedback from others:** coach says 'reads the game brilliantly'; teacher says 'explains concepts well to peers'.
- **Careers that use these:** professional cricketer, cricket coach, sports scientist, physiotherapist, sports analyst, PE teacher.

steps.title: Ask for honest feedback
steps.body: Ask two or three people who know you well (a teacher, a coach, a relative, a friend): 'What do you think I'm good at? When have you seen me at my best?' Write down their answers without arguing. Patterns across different people are especially useful.

activity.prompt: Write your own skills inventory: three strong skills (with evidence), two skills you're developing, feedback others have given you, and three careers that would use these.
activity.hint: Evidence can be small: a project you led, a competition, a time someone asked you for help. Be honest, not modest or boastful.

quiz.q: A skill is...
options: a learned capability developed through practice
quiz.why: A skill is a learned capability developed through practice. It differs from a value and isn't fixed at birth.

quiz.q: Aptitude tests can...
options: tell you your one perfect career
give helpful information about some abilities, as one input
quiz.why: Aptitude tests can give helpful information about some abilities as one input. They can't name your one perfect career or replace reflection.

quiz.q: Which is a transferable skill?
quiz.why: Communication is a transferable skill, useful in almost any career. Knowing one software version is narrow.

quiz.q: Why ask several people for feedback?
options: Patterns across different people are more reliable
quiz.why: Ask several people for feedback because patterns across different people are more reliable and reduce individual bias.

scenes.text: Noor, 19, from Bengaluru, is choosing between law, journalism and public policy. Online videos make each one look either glamorous or terrible.
She politely messages five professionals through family friends and alumni groups, asking for 20 minutes to learn about their work. Three say yes.
The lawyer describes long hours and how much reading she does; the journalist talks about deadlines and changing media business models; the policy researcher describes data work and writing.
Noor spends a week volunteering at a legal aid clinic. She loves it. Her choice is now based on experience, not guesses.

steps.title: Informational interviews
steps.body:
An **informational interview** is a short conversation with someone doing a job you're curious about — to learn, not to ask for a job.

Good questions:
- What does a typical day or week look like?
- What do you enjoy most and least?
- What skills matter most?
- How did you get here? What would you do differently?
- What is the job market like now?
- What should someone my age do to explore this?

Be on time, keep it short, thank them afterwards.

steps.title: Try it before you choose
steps.body:
- **Job shadowing:** spend a day watching someone at work.
- **Volunteering:** NGOs, hospitals, schools, events.
- **Internships** and short projects.
- **Mini-projects at home:** write three articles, build a small app, design a poster series, coach a small group of kids.
- **Short introductory courses** (many are free online).

How you *feel* after real exposure is valuable information.

steps.title: Reality-test the path
steps.body:
For each option, find out from **official or reliable sources** (official exam and university websites, regulators, recent job listings):
- Entry requirements and entrance exams.
- Duration and total cost of education.
- Scholarships and education loans.
- Typical first jobs and realistic early salaries (from multiple sources).
- Where the jobs are (cities, sectors).
- Licensing or registration needed.
- Long-term growth and how technology is changing the field.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Relying only on social media or one relative's opinion.
- Believing extreme salary claims from advertisements.
- Ignoring total cost and time.
- Not checking whether a course or college is recognised by the relevant regulator.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a polite message asking a professional for a 20-minute informational conversation. Include who you are, why you're interested in their field, and that you're not asking for a job.

activity.prompt: Career exploration checklist for one option you're considering.
items: Read the official entry requirements and entrance exam details
Found the total cost and duration of study
Had at least one informational interview
Spent time shadowing, volunteering or doing a mini-project
Looked at recent job listings for entry-level roles
Checked whether registration or licensing is needed
Written down what I liked and disliked after real exposure

quiz.q: The main aim of an informational interview is to...
options: learn about the work and path
quiz.why: An informational interview is a conversation to learn about the work and the path into it. It is not a job request, so asking for a job immediately defeats its purpose.

quiz.q: Which is the most reliable source for entry requirements?
options: The official exam or university website
quiz.why: The official exam or university website is the most reliable and current source for entry requirements. Ads, guesses and social media posts may be outdated or wrong.

quiz.q: Job shadowing means...
options: spending time observing someone at their job
quiz.why: Job shadowing means spending time observing someone at their job. It gives real exposure to what the work involves.

quiz.q: Why check whether a course is recognised by the relevant regulator?
options: Unrecognised courses may not lead to registration or jobs
quiz.why: Check that a course is recognised by the relevant regulator, because unrecognised courses may not lead to registration or jobs. This protects your time and money.

lessons.title: Decide, plan B and talk to your family

scenes.text: Sameer, 17, from Lucknow, wants to study design. His father, a government officer, wants him to prepare for UPSC or engineering.
Instead of arguing, Sameer prepares: research on design careers, colleges and entrance exams, costs, three professionals he spoke to, and a Plan B.
He starts with, 'Papa, I know you want me to have a secure future. I want that too. Can I show you what I've found?'

His father is still worried but agrees: Sameer will attempt the design entrance and, as a backup, keep strong Class 12 marks for other options. 'You've thought about this more than I did at your age,' his father admits.

steps.title: A weighted decision matrix
steps.body:
1. List your options (e.g., Design, Engineering, Architecture).
2. List your criteria from your values (interest, job prospects, cost, fit with skills, location, family support).
3. Give each criterion a **weight** (1–5) by importance.
4. Score each option on each criterion (1–10).
5. Multiply score × weight and add up.

The highest total isn't an automatic answer — but if your gut disagrees with the numbers, ask why. That tension often reveals what you really value.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Criteria and weights: Interest (5), Job prospects (4), Cost (3), Skills fit (4).
- **Design:** Interest 9×5=45, Prospects 6×4=24, Cost 5×3=15, Skills 8×4=32 → **116**
- **Engineering:** Interest 5×5=25, Prospects 7×4=28, Cost 6×3=18, Skills 7×4=28 → **99**
- **Architecture:** Interest 7×5=35, Prospects 6×4=24, Cost 4×3=12, Skills 8×4=32 → **103**

Design scores highest for Sameer. He also notices architecture is close — a useful backup that shares many skills.

steps.title: Plan B (and C)
steps.body:
A Plan B isn't giving up on Plan A; it's what lets you pursue Plan A without panic.
- Choose a Plan B that **shares skills** with Plan A where possible (cricket → sports science; acting → media production; design → architecture or marketing).
- Set **checkpoints**: 'If I don't clear the entrance by my second attempt, I will...'
- Keep doors open: maintain marks, build transferable skills.
- Remember careers are rarely straight lines; many people change direction several times.

steps.title: Talking to family
steps.body:
- **Start with shared goals:** 'We both want me to be secure and happy.'
- **Show research**, not just feelings: costs, colleges, conversations with professionals.
- **Listen to their worries** and reflect them: 'You're worried design isn't stable.' Often worries are about security and status.
- **Offer a plan with checkpoints** and a Plan B.
- **Invite a trusted third person** (teacher, school counsellor, relative in the field) if conversations get stuck.
- **Be patient** — big changes in views can take several conversations.

steps.title: If it feels overwhelming
steps.body: Career pressure can cause real stress. If you feel hopeless, can't sleep or eat, or have thoughts of harming yourself, talk to someone you trust and contact **Tele-MANAS 14416** (mental health support) or **112** in an emergency. No career decision is worth your life, and there is always more than one path.

a.text: You want to study psychology; your mother wants you to do medicine. She says, 'Psychology has no future.' How do you begin?

choices.label: 'I know you want me to have a good future. Can I show you what I found about psychology careers?'
choices.feedback: Starting from shared goals lowers defensiveness.

choices.label: 'You never understand me!' and leave the room.
choices.feedback: Understandable feeling, but it closes the conversation.

b.text: She listens but says, 'What if it doesn't work out?' What do you say?

choices.label: Reflect her worry and share your Plan B and checkpoints.
choices.feedback: Addressing the real worry — security — builds trust.

choices.label: 'It will definitely work out, don't worry.'
choices.feedback: Reassurance without a plan rarely calms worried parents. Try sharing your plan.

c.text: Later you calm down. What's a good next step?

choices.label: Apologise for leaving, and ask for a time to talk calmly with your research ready.
choices.feedback: Repairing and preparing is mature and effective.

d.text: Your mother suggests asking your school counsellor's opinion too. Do you agree?

choices.label: Yes — a trusted third person can help both of us.
choices.feedback: Inviting help often breaks deadlocks.

choices.label: No — I've already decided.
choices.feedback: You may be right, but shutting out help can harden positions.

end1.text: You started from shared goals, listened, offered a plan and accepted support. That's how difficult family decisions move forward.

end2.text: The conversation stalled. Try again and see what happens when you invite a trusted third person.

quiz.q: In a weighted decision matrix, the weight shows...
options: how important each criterion is to you
quiz.why: In a weighted decision matrix, the weight shows how important each criterion is to you. It reflects your values, not the option's cost or your marks.

quiz.q: A good Plan B...
options: ideally shares skills with Plan A and has checkpoints
quiz.why: A good Plan B ideally shares skills with Plan A and has checkpoints. That lets you pursue Plan A calmly without giving it up.

quiz.q: The best way to start a career conversation with worried parents is...
quiz.why: Starting with shared goals, such as wanting you to be safe and happy, reduces defensiveness. Sarcasm, ultimatums or avoiding the talk make it harder.

quiz.q: Option A scores 8 on a criterion with weight 4. Its weighted score is...
quiz.why: The weighted score is score × weight: 8 × 4 = 32.

quiz.q: If career stress makes you feel hopeless, you can call...
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS, 14416, offers free mental-health support if stress feels hopeless. In an emergency call 112.

questions.q: RIASEC describes...
questions.why: RIASEC describes six interest types: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional. It is Holland's model.

questions.q: 'S' in RIASEC stands for...
questions.why: In RIASEC, S stands for Social, the helpers such as teachers, carers and counsellors.

questions.q: An informational interview is for...
questions.why: An informational interview is for learning about a job, not for getting hired immediately.

questions.q: Which is a value rather than an interest?
questions.why: Job security is a value, something you need from work. Fixing bikes, coding and drawing are interests.

questions.q: Which source is best for current entrance exam requirements?
questions.why: The official exam website is the best source for current entrance exam requirements. An old blog, meme or rumour may be out of date.

questions.q: Skills are mainly developed through...
questions.why: Skills are mainly developed through practice and feedback. Certificates alone, luck or birth do not build them.

questions.q: Which statement about aptitude tests is accurate?
options: They are one useful input but have limits
They identify your one perfect career
questions.why: Aptitude tests are one useful input but have limits. They can't name your one perfect career or measure motivation perfectly, so use them with reflection and experience.

questions.q: Weighted score for: Interest 7 (weight 5) + Cost 6 (weight 2)?
questions.why: Weighted score = 7 × 5 + 6 × 2 = 35 + 12 = 47.

questions.q: A would-be cricketer's Plan B that shares skills could be...
questions.why: Sports science or coaching shares skills and knowledge with cricket, so it keeps you in the same world. A random choice wouldn't share skills.

questions.q: Your matrix says Engineering, but your gut strongly says Design. The best response is...
options: ask why — the tension may reveal a value you under-weighted
questions.why: Ask why your gut disagrees, because the tension may reveal a value you under-weighted. Use the matrix to think, not just to obey.

questions.q: Your parents worry your chosen career isn't secure. The most effective response is...
options: reflect the worry and present research, a plan with checkpoints and a Plan B
questions.why: Reflect their worry and present research, a plan with checkpoints and a Plan B. This addresses the real concern, while arguing or giving up doesn't.

questions.q: Which combination gives the strongest basis for a career decision?
options: Interests, values, skills evidence, real exposure and reality-tested information
questions.why: The strongest basis combines interests, values, evidence of skills, real exposure and reality-tested information. Marks, friends or trends alone are thin evidence.

questions.q: Which statement about careers today is most accurate?
options: Careers are always a straight line
Many people change direction several times; transferable skills help
Only one career fits each person
questions.why: Many people change direction several times, and transferable skills help. Careers are not always a straight line, and a first choice isn't permanent.
